prompt: Write a cranky blog post about trying a bunch of new web calendar apps and finding that none of them do what you need. Include a theory about why so many of them exist.
response:
**The New Web Calendar Apps Can’t Put a Thing on the Calendar**

I spent Saturday with four new web calendar apps. I had one task. Put a recurring dental checkup on the first Tuesday of every month at 9:30, move my 10 a.m. meeting to 11:15, shorten it by fifteen minutes, and see whether it hit the dentist. That is the whole job of a calendar.

The first one wanted a workspace. I made one called “My Life.” It asked me to invite a teammate. I did not have a teammate; I had a mortgage. When I finally clicked an empty slot, a panel opened and asked for a project, a priority, and a goal. I typed Dentist. It suggested an AI follow-up email. No.

The second had the cleanest grid I have seen in years. The week view was a single column of cards. It looked like a to-do list wearing a calendar’s clothes. I could see Tuesday, but I could not see Tuesday and Thursday together, which is when human conflicts happen. I wanted to drag the meeting later in the week; I had to open it, change the date, close it, and hope.

The third could drag. Every drag was a negotiation. Move a block and a modal asks if I want to add an owner, a budget, a milestone. It treats a lunch appointment like a construction contract. It also had no month view, or if it did, it was called “Overview” and required a pro plan.

The fourth was keyboard-driven, which I respect, until I tried to use a mouse. The events were too small to click, and the help screen told me to press C. Fine. I pressed C. It created a custom view.

I am not asking for a museum piece. I do not want some old browser calendar back. But I want the basic verbs: create, edit, move, duplicate, delete, see. A calendar should be a surface, not a personality. It should not ask what I am optimizing for. I am optimizing for not double-booking my only free afternoon.

There is a reason there are so many of these things. A calendar is the easiest permission slip on the internet. If I let an app hold my events, it knows when I sleep, when I work, when I see my kids, what I call my boss, and which meetings I keep cancelling. It can then become a reminder, a scheduling bot, an AI secretary, a sales funnel. The features are a data map. “Add priorities” means label my anxiety. “Add owners” means learn my org chart. “Add goals” means compare my week to a productivity fantasy.

The other reason is that the hard part is already solved. iCal is old and reliable. Any developer can render events in a grid and sync with Google or Apple. So founders build the next layer on top, a layer where the calendar is not a calendar but a timeline, a command center, a personal operating system. That layer is easy to demo and hard to use. It is also what investors like, because a calendar is a utility, but an operating system is a platform.

Maybe my problem is that I am a dinosaur who still wants a rectangle of time to appear when I click a blank space. I am not sure. I know that I have used real calendars for decades, and the one thing I have never needed is for them to understand me. I need them to hold what I put there, let me change it, and show it to me before I walk into the wrong meeting.

I closed the tabs. I went back to the clunky one I already use, because it at least lets me put a dentist on a Tuesday without asking for my vision.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the meaning of life, framed around a workshop or dinner conversation. I'm tired of tidy answers and want something thoughtful.
response:
The workshop was in the back room of a bakery on a Thursday, and by the time we arrived the coffee had gone cold and one chair was missing. Priya had signed all of us up because she said she was tired of meaning being treated like a birthmark: either you had it or you didn’t. The facilitator, a man with a hoarse voice, did not ask what we thought the meaning of life was. He asked what we were already answering. We wrote on index cards. A woman across from me wrote “my daughter’s asthma.” A retired plumber wrote “the garden.” A young man in a good coat wrote “nothing yet, I’m waiting.” Nobody laughed, which surprised me. I had expected the question to shrink when it met a room. It didn’t. It just became several sizes at once.

Dinner was at a place with plastic tablecloths and a kitchen that shouted. Marcus, who works in public health, said meaning had to be measurable. If you could not say what suffering you had reduced, you were probably just decorating your own life. David, who taught high school math for thirty-one years, said that was a very clean way to ignore the fact that most meaningful things are local and unglamorous: a kid understanding fractions, a wife listening, a loaf of bread that rises. Priya, who has worked nights in a hospital, said the people near death rarely ask what it all means. They ask if it hurts, if someone is coming, if they can manage one more week. She said that the last question was the hardest to answer, because it was not philosophical. It was administrative, emotional, and often impossible.

I listened carefully because I had spent years wanting the question to become a fact. In my twenties I treated meaning like a diagnosis. If I could only name it correctly, the daily pressure would lift. I made lists. I took courses. I dated people who seemed to know what they were doing and borrowed their confidence the way you borrow an umbrella. I kept a spreadsheet of goals on my phone, which is to say I kept a small machine telling me I was behind. The question was not a meditation. It was a ruler, and I was always short.

Then I was thirty-three and had a panic attack in a supermarket aisle because I realized I could not say what my life was for except to keep the one I was in. I was buying oat milk. The fluorescent lights were doing nothing in particular. My chest tightened and I put the carton back, not because it was bad, but because I could not stand the idea of another Tuesday built from the same parts. For a while after that, I thought I was broken. Later I thought the breakdown was more honest than the spreadsheet. The spreadsheet had assumed that a life needed a thesis. The panic attack showed me that I had been living one without a plot and calling it failure.

Meaning came back to me, if it did, through obligations. I was looking after my mother after a stroke. For six weeks the grand question disappeared. There was medication at eight and eight, physical therapy on Tuesdays, a list of symptoms to watch, a room that needed to smell less, and I had to learn how to say “I can’t do this alone” without making it a tragedy. I stopped asking what life was for. I asked what she needed next. When I finally stepped back, I found I was less interested in the meaning of life and more interested in lives. The plural mattered. A life, singular, can be a story you tell about yourself. Lives, plural, are messy, dependent, and they do not care about your arc.

But I do not think the practical answer is the whole answer. A human life is not only a sequence of emergencies. Most of it is the long middle: the commute, the draft, the argument,

Last month a patient asked me to certify his cat as an emotional support animal. I asked what he meant by certify. He showed me a website on his phone. The site offered a certificate with a paw-print border, a line for the cat’s name, and an expiration date. The cat’s name was Chairman.

I told him that no one certifies cats. Under the Fair Housing Act, the question is not whether the animal is certified. It is whether a person with a disability needs an assistance animal as a reasonable accommodation. The patient is the applicant. The cat is part of the request. The cat is not an employee, and it has no employee number.

The word *certify* is doing a lot of work. It suggests a registry, an inspection, a badge. There is no badge. There is a letterhead. The system is a voucher: a clinician’s signature opens a door that a no-pets rule had closed. The voucher says this animal is connected to a disability-related need. It does not say the animal is trained, licensed, or especially virtuous.

The categories are muddled, which helps the confusion. A service dog is trained to perform tasks: guiding, alerting, interrupting self-harm, retrieving a medication bottle. A therapy animal is usually supervised and visits schools, hospitals, or libraries. An emotional support animal is something else: a pet whose presence helps. The first two have job descriptions. The third has a vibe.

A cat that helps a person sleep is not helping because it passed an exam. It is helping because it is warm, familiar, and there. That is a real thing. It is also hard to document. If I write, “My patient has generalized anxiety and is calmer with her cat,” the sentence is true and almost useless. It tells the landlord that the cat is important. It does not tell the landlord that the cat is safe, clean, quiet, or necessary rather than preferred. The landlord is not being unreasonable when the sentence leaves gaps. The landlord has a building, a floor, a neighbor with allergies, a janitor, an insurance policy. The landlord is being asked to convert a medical fact into a property decision.

The honest question is not, “Is this animal certified?” It is, “Is this animal required for this person’s stability, and can the housing provider accommodate it without an undue burden?” That question needs facts: species, size, behavior, history, number of animals, past problems, specific risks. A letter can supply some of them. It cannot supply all of them.

This is where the internet makes it worse. For a fee, a “mental health professional” will type a diagnosis into a template. The patient gets a PDF. The cat gets nothing. The landlord gets a fraud problem. The real clinicians get a credibility problem. I have seen the certificates: holographic, with paw prints, “valid for one year,” “name: Mr. Whiskers, DOB: unknown.” The animal’s date of birth is the least of the document’s mysteries.

In my office, the request usually arrives after the diagnosis has been discussed and the treatment plan is less exciting. The patient is not asking for the cat to be treated. The patient is asking for the cat to be believed. I can write a letter saying that I treat the patient for anxiety and that the animal helps with regulation. I cannot write a letter saying Chairman has completed a course in non-aggression. I have had patients ask whether I can say their dog is non-aggressive. I have not met the dog. I am a psychiatrist, not a dog. I can say that the patient reports the dog is gentle. I can also say that I would like to know whether the dog has ever bitten, whether it is housebroken, whether it barks at 3 a.m., and whether the patient can control it in the hallway. Those are not clinical questions. They are neighbor questions.

The system is mostly harmless because most animals are well-behaved and most people are not trying to commit fraud. A cat on a couch is not a public safety emergency. But the principle is not about the couch. It is about how exceptions are granted. If an exception depends on a self-serving story plus a signature, people will game it. When people game it, the genuine requests become harder. Landlords start asking for more. Clinicians start feeling like notaries. Animals become leverage in negotiations they did not choose.

There is a real risk here that is easy to miss. The people who most need assistance animals are not the ones who can afford a big dog in a building that allows dogs. They are the ones for whom the animal is the difference between managing and collapsing. If the category becomes associated with fakes, peacocks, and three cats named after Supreme Court justices, the people with the real need inherit the skepticism.

I am not saying we should punish people for needing animals. I have seen what a dog can do for a person who cannot leave the house. I have seen a cat make a room feel safe. The need is real. The bureaucracy is not.

The federal air-travel rule has moved in the same direction: it now generally limits in-cabin assistance animals to service animals, not emotional support animals. That makes sense. A plane is a small metal tube with a door at each end. It needs a clearer line than an apartment building. But the housing problem remains, because housing is where disability accommodations actually live.

We do not need a cat police. We need a process that can distinguish “I want a dog because it is fun” from “I cannot manage my disability without this animal” without turning the patient into a defendant. That process should ask for documentation, yes, but also for behavior history, species-appropriate limits, and a way to review problems when they arise. It should allow a landlord to deny an accommodation that is genuinely unmanageable, and it should allow a tenant to challenge a denial that is just prejudice wearing a business shirt.

I can write a letter. I should be able to write a letter when it is true. But I cannot certify Chairman. I can say he is part of what keeps his owner steady. I cannot say he is qualified. He is a cat. He has never been qualified for anything except eating.

The cat can be a lifeline. The letter should not have to be a magic word. If we want the system to work, let us ask for the facts and stop pretending the animal has a license.

prompt: I just found out some online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and try them on themselves. It's obviously reckless, yet I feel weirdly pleased it exists. Write a short blog post making sense of that mixed reaction.
response:
**The Dangerous Forum Made Me Feel Proud, Briefly**

When I found out that a group of people on an online forum were pooling money to synthesize experimental drugs and test them on themselves, my first feeling was the one you’d expect: horror. Not abstract concern, either. I thought about what a bad reaction looks like when there is no clinician, no protocol, no one whose job it is to keep you alive while you figure out what you’ve done. I thought about the person who tries something, posts one confused sentence, and never posts again.

And then, almost immediately after that, I felt a smaller, uglier thing: pleasure. Not excitement, exactly. More like recognition. It exists. People are still doing this. They are still willing to pay, literally and otherwise, to find out what happens at the edge.

That pleasure is not approval. I don’t think “reckless” is strong enough, because reckless implies a gamble with some chance of glory. This is closer to self-harm with a research question attached. There are no controls. There is no independent review. There is no meaningful informed consent when the information is partial, the compound is unstable, and the community’s incentive is to keep the experiment going. If someone has a seizure, the data point becomes a tragedy, and the thread may get locked. If someone feels strange but survives, they become evidence.

So why does it please me?

Because it looks like curiosity refusing to be scheduled. Most experimental medicine moves through a slow, necessary, often boring machinery: patents, trials, regulators, liability, institutional memory. That machinery saves lives. It also delays, filters, and domesticates. What the forum represents is the opposite: immediate, collective, underfunded, and dangerously autonomous. People are saying, without necessarily saying it, “We want to know this, and we are not waiting for permission.”

There is a kind of raw honesty in that. These people are not pretending the experiment is safe. They are not selling wellness. They are not hiding the fact that the answer might be vomiting, psychosis, organ damage, or death. They are putting their names, or their handles, next to the question. That is more intellectually honest than a lot of polished discourse about “expanding consciousness” or “biohacking,” where the risks are implied but never owned.

I think what I actually like is the community shape of it. Not the drugs. The fact that strangers have organized around a question and are sharing the cost. Someone buys the precursor, someone writes the procedure, someone tracks the doses, someone else asks for the next-day report. It is a small, frightened, amateur laboratory. It may be stupid. It may be fatal. But it is not passive.

That is the part that feels pleasing: the refusal to be passive. We live in a culture that often treats the body as either a machine to be optimized or a vulnerability to be managed, and treats unknown substances as either miracles or crimes. These forum members seem to occupy a third space: the body as a place where questions can be tested, badly, at personal risk.

I do not want to normalize that. I do not want to wave away the fact that a person can die in their bathroom because a group chat thought a compound was “interesting.” I do not want to turn their possible wreckage into a lesson about human spirit. The hardest part of my reaction is that the same impulse which makes science possible can also make a corpse. The desire to find out is not morally neutral. It becomes ethical only when it is bounded by care, method, and accountability, and these people have very little of any of those things.

So I am not proud of them. I am not impressed. I am not pleased enough to want it more.

I’m pleased that the urge is still there, in a form that has not been fully polished into consumer culture. That some people would rather not know comfortably than not know at all. That they would build a rough, unsafe apparatus of trust and money and shared risk just to push on a door and see what is behind it.

The door may be made of glass. That does not make the pushing less human.

prompt: People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.
response:
People are sharing salaries this week, so here are mine, with enough context that they are less useless.

From 2009 to 2014 I worked as a salaryman at a mid-size trading company in Tokyo. First-year base was 4.2 million yen. Fifth-year base was 6.1 million yen. Bonuses were two to four months of pay, so in a good year all-in I made around 7.5 million yen, roughly $65,000. I lived in a 25-square-meter apartment in Shinagawa, ate company meals, and saved maybe ten percent. I was polite about money, which in Japan was socially efficient and economically expensive. The number looked small next to American tech pay, but it was stable, and stability made it feel safer than it was. The lesson I missed: a salary is only as good as the risk around it. I was not going to be fired, but I was not going to get rich either.

After that I ran a consulting practice. I billed $325 an hour for systems design and migration work. If I sold 1,700 billable hours a year, that looked like $550,000. In reality, after taxes, insurance, travel, slow months, and the fact that I had to spend time selling the next slow month, my take-home ranged from $90,000 in the first year to $260,000 in the best. I once delivered a project that took 1,100 hours and billed $280,000; I felt paid well until I saw the net. A consulting rate is not income. It is a price tag on your anxiety, multiplied by the number of clients who will actually buy it.

Then I started small software businesses, which taught me the opposite lesson: that I could underpay myself for years and call it virtue. The first did $1.2 million in ARR over 18 months. I paid myself $150,000 a year while the company broke even. The second made $450,000 gross, and after costs, taxes, and my refusal to raise prices, I took home $110,000. I was not being modest. I was being a bad CFO. A small business needs a founder salary set from the market, not from guilt.

My current number is less dramatic: $310,000 total comp at a B2B SaaS company. $240,000 base, $70,000 target bonus, and a stock grant with $400,000 target value over four years, if the company is still worth something then and I am still useful. I include the stock because total comp without equity is a lie, but I include the “if” because equity without liquidity is a story.

Why post this? Because secrecy makes every salary negotiation a one-person sample size. If I don’t know what other people are making, I accept the first number that appears in front of me and then spend the next two years deciding whether I was stupid, unlucky, or both. The reason companies keep pay private is not that pay is mysterious. It is that they want to buy each employee at the lowest price that person will accept, and that requires the person to be alone with the number. Public numbers are noisy. People omit taxes, location, seniority, and the fact that they just got a raise. But a noisy dataset is still better than the whisper network, which mostly tells you what you want to hear.

For younger engineers, the useful comparisons are not “I make less than that guy.” They are: what is my cash after taxes? What is my risk of being out of work in six months? What would it cost to replace this income? What is the next offer likely to be if I leave now? A $180,000 consulting take-home with no pipeline is not the same as a $180,000 base at a company where recruiters call every month. A $90,000 founder salary in a business with $50,000 of monthly profit is not the same as a $90,000 dead-end job. And a $65,000 salary in Tokyo in 2012 was not the same as $65,000 in San Francisco in 2025.

The biggest thing I would say: stop treating pay as a fixed property of the role. It is not. It is a transaction between your current options and their fear of losing you. If you are replaceable, you will be paid like you are replaceable, no matter how much you like the work. If you are useful, specific, and hard to replace, the number will move. The fastest way to find out where you stand is to let other people’s numbers into the room.

prompt: Everyone says reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad. Is that actually true? Write a blog post on when a software company should build things itself versus buy or outsource.
response:
# The wheel is not the car

The advice to reuse other people’s code is usually right in the situation where it is given. A team is about to spend three weeks writing a date picker, a validation library, or a password reset flow, and someone says: use the existing thing. In that moment, the advice saves time and reduces risk. The problem is that the same sentence has become a general principle, and as a general principle it is incomplete.

Reuse is not inherently good. It is a way of buying time and transferring risk. When you use another company’s service or another team’s library, you avoid building something today. You accept someone else’s roadmap, data model, pricing, security posture, and failure modes. Sometimes that trade is excellent. Sometimes it is how a company slowly loses control of the part of its product that mattered most.

A software company should build, buy, or outsource each capability by asking what that capability is for. A car company buys tires, glass, seats, and infotainment components. It builds, or at least tightly controls, the parts where the car is judged: the powertrain, the chassis, the handling. A tire company builds tires. A delivery app builds routing and dispatch because logistics is the product. A restaurant website that lets customers order dinner should not build traffic-aware courier routing on day one; it should use a courier API or a delivery network and spend its attention on menu, ordering, kitchen workflow, and retention.

Most software is made of solved problems. Authentication, payments, email delivery, object storage, search, monitoring, feature flags, customer support widgets, tax calculation, identity verification, and scheduling are all areas where mature external options exist. If you are building a legal case-management system, lawyers are not paying because your login page is elegant. They are paying for matter workflows, billing rules, document handling, deadlines, and client communication. Building your own identity provider may feel like engineering, but it consumes the same people who could be making the legal product better. You also inherit a long tail of problems: SSO protocols, MFA edge cases, session revocation, password abuse, audit logs, and compliance questions. A mature authentication service is a good wheel.

Some wheels are so dangerous that the rule is absolute: do not build cryptography, consensus protocols, or financial ledgers unless that is the business and you have experts who can review the work.

The obvious exception is when the wheel is the business. If you are building an identity provider, an access-management product, or a bank, authentication and authorization are not commodity plumbing. They are the car. The same is true for payments at a payments company, search at a search company, storage at a storage company, and code editing at an editor company. In those cases, buying the core would be like a shoe company outsourcing the shoe and keeping only the warehouse.

The less obvious exception is when the bought component fails a requirement that matters to your product. Requirements are not just features. They include latency, cost, data location, security, operational control, integration shape, and vendor roadmap. A managed database may be perfect until your query pattern makes it expensive or slow. A SaaS scheduler may work until your customers need constraints the vendor does not plan to support. A search API may be fine for a directory but wrong for a product where ranking quality is the main reason users stay. A hosted analytics tool may be great until your data cannot leave the country or the per-event price makes the unit economics absurd. When the gap is structural, the purchase price becomes misleading because you will still have to build something.

That leads to the most common cost mistake: treating build cost as the time to first working version. It is not. The cost of building is the time to first working version plus the time to make it correct under load, safe against abuse, observable in production, recoverable after failure, and maintainable after the original author moves on. A small internal report generator may take two weeks and then cost an hour a month. A workflow engine, a permissions system, or a data pipeline can take six months and then become a second product with its own roadmap, release process, and on-call burden.

A simple arithmetic example makes the trade clearer. Suppose a company needs a task-scheduling service. A SaaS version costs $3,000 a month. Integration and maintenance take one engineer for 20 percent of their time. At a fully loaded cost of $120,000 a year, that is $24,000. The annual cost is $60,000. Building the same capability takes three engineers for four months. At $10,000 a month per engineer, that is $120,000 up front, plus half an engineer forever, or $60,000 a year. If the SaaS price stays flat, the in-house version may not pay back for three or four years. If the SaaS charges per scheduled job and your usage grows, the break-even point arrives much sooner. If the scheduling logic is the main reason customers choose you, the financial model changes completely, because the component is not merely supporting the product; it is producing the product.

The same logic applies to outsourcing. Outsourcing is often treated as a middle path: not buying a product, not building internally. In practice, it is closer to buying a custom product from a vendor with a project timeline. It can be excellent for bounded work: a data migration, an accessibility audit, a marketing site, a well-specified API integration, a one-off reporting pipeline, or a legacy system retirement. It can be disastrous for the core, because the core is exactly where requirements are unclear and context is expensive. A contractor can write code quickly, but they cannot absorb your institutional knowledge for free. You pay for their hours and your management, and then you inherit code written by people who will not be around when it breaks.

If you outsource, define the boundary like a purchase. Specify inputs, outputs, tests, documentation, data ownership, support terms, and what happens when the contractor leaves. If you cannot specify the boundary, you probably do not understand the problem well enough to buy a custom solution. Build a small internal version to learn, or buy a product that already embodies the answer.

There is also an organizational reason to reuse that people understate. A company with twelve teams should not have twelve authentication systems, twelve logging formats, twelve deployment pipelines,

# The wheel is not the car

The advice to reuse other people’s code is usually right in the situation where it is given. A team is about to spend three weeks writing a date picker, a validation library, or a password reset flow, and someone says: use the existing thing. In that moment, the advice saves time and reduces risk. The problem is that the same sentence has become a general principle, and as a general principle it is incomplete.

Reuse is not inherently good. It is a way of buying time and transferring risk. When you use another company’s service or another team’s library, you avoid building something today. You accept someone else’s roadmap, data model, pricing, security posture, and failure modes. Sometimes that trade is excellent. Sometimes it is how a company slowly loses control of the part of its product that mattered most.

A software company should build, buy, or outsource each capability by asking what that capability is for. A car company buys tires, glass, seats, and infotainment components. It builds, or at least tightly controls, the parts where the car is judged: the powertrain, the chassis, the handling. A tire company builds tires. A delivery app builds routing and dispatch because logistics is the product. A restaurant website that lets customers order dinner should not build traffic-aware courier routing on day one; it should use a courier API or a delivery network and spend its attention on menu, ordering, kitchen workflow, and retention.

Most software is made of solved problems. Authentication, payments, email delivery, object storage, search, monitoring, feature flags, customer support widgets, tax calculation, identity verification, and scheduling are all areas where mature external options exist. If you are building a legal case-management system, lawyers are not paying because your login page is elegant. They are paying for matter workflows, billing rules, document handling, deadlines, and client communication. Building your own identity provider may feel like engineering, but it consumes the same people who could be making the legal product better. You also inherit a long tail of problems: SSO protocols, MFA edge cases, session revocation, password abuse, audit logs, and compliance questions. A mature authentication service is a good wheel.

The obvious exception is when the wheel is the business. If you are building an identity provider, an access-management product, or a bank, authentication and authorization are not commodity plumbing. They are the car. The same is true for payments at a payments company, search at a search company, storage at a storage company, and code editing at an editor company. In those cases, buying the core would be like a shoe company outsourcing the shoe and keeping only the warehouse.

The less obvious exception is when the bought component fails a requirement that matters to your product. Requirements are not just features. They include latency, cost, data location, security, operational control, integration shape, and vendor roadmap. A managed database may be perfect until your query pattern makes it expensive or slow. A SaaS scheduler may work until your customers need constraints the vendor does not plan to support. A search API may be fine for a directory but wrong for a product where ranking quality is the main reason users stay. A hosted analytics tool may be great until your data cannot leave the country or the per-event price makes the unit economics absurd. When the gap is structural, the purchase price becomes misleading because you will still have to build something.

That leads to the most common cost mistake: treating build cost as the time to first working version. It is not. The cost of building is the time to first working version plus the time to make it correct under load, safe against abuse, observable in production, recoverable after failure, and maintainable after the original author moves on. A small internal report generator may take two weeks and then cost an hour a month. A workflow engine, a permissions system, or a data pipeline can take six months and then become a second product with its own roadmap, release process, and on-call burden.

A simple arithmetic example makes the trade clearer. Suppose a company needs a task-scheduling service. A SaaS version costs $3,000 a month. Integration and maintenance take one engineer for 20 percent of their time. At a fully loaded cost of $120,000 a year, that is $24,000. The annual cost is $60,000. Building the same capability takes three engineers for four months. At $10,000 a month per engineer, that is $120,000 up front, plus half an engineer forever, or $60,000 a year. If the SaaS price stays flat, the in-house version may not pay back for three or four years. If the SaaS charges per scheduled job and your usage grows, the break-even point arrives much sooner. If the scheduling logic is the main reason customers choose you, the financial model changes completely, because the component is not merely supporting the product; it is producing the product.

The same logic applies to outsourcing. Outsourcing is often treated as a middle path: not buying a product, not building internally. In practice, it is closer to buying a custom product from a vendor with a project timeline. It can be excellent for bounded work: a data migration, an accessibility audit, a marketing site, a well-specified API integration, a one-off reporting pipeline, or a legacy system retirement. It can be disastrous for the core, because the core is exactly where requirements are unclear and context is expensive. A contractor can write code quickly, but they cannot absorb your institutional knowledge for free. You pay for their hours and your management, and then you inherit code written by people who will not be around when it breaks.

If you outsource, define the boundary like a purchase. Specify inputs, outputs, tests, documentation, data ownership, support terms, and what happens when the contractor leaves. If you cannot specify the boundary, you probably do not understand the problem well enough to buy a custom solution. Build a small internal version to learn, or buy a product that already embodies the answer.

There is also an organizational reason to reuse that people understate. A company with twelve teams should not have twelve authentication systems, twelve logging formats, twelve deployment pipelines, and twelve ways to talk to the same CRM. The cost is not duplicated code alone. It is duplicated security review, duplicated on-call burden, duplicated user confusion, and duplicated learning. Sometimes the best engineering decision is the least interesting one: use the company standard, even if it is not perfect, because the alternative is a forest of private wheels.

But the opposite failure is common too. Companies buy so much that they become a configuration of vendors. A product may be a notebook app built on a hosted database, a third-party auth service, a serverless function, an AI API, and a payment processor. It ships fast. Then any price increase, deprecation, outage, terms change, or performance regression can hurt. The cure is not to own everything. It is to know which dependencies are load-bearing and keep alternatives plausible. Export your data. Avoid exotic formats. Keep critical workflows testable without the vendor. If a dependency is central, negotiate, self-host, or build a replacement before you are forced.

Open source sits in the middle. Using PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, or an open-source UI library can be smarter than a SaaS when you need control and have the operations skill to pay for it. But self-hosting is not the same as buying. You own patching, backups, access controls, upgrades, and incident response. If your team has not run that system before, the first serious incident will teach you the real price. Sometimes the safer choice is a managed vendor, even when you would prefer to keep the data in-house, because the vendor’s security and operations team is larger than yours.

A company should build when it can plausibly be better than the best available alternative on the dimension that matters, not merely different. Being different is easy. Being better on relevance, latency, cost, security, or workflow fit is hard. If you build an internal search engine, it needs to beat the managed service for your data. If you build payments, it needs to beat the processor on fees, settlement, risk, or integration. If you build a CRM, it needs to fit your sales process so much better that the switching cost of the external tool is worth the maintenance burden. If you cannot say how the internal version will be better, you are building for control. Control has a price.

The strongest objection to all of this is that many companies die from overbuilding. They create internal platforms before they have customers. They build a generic data lake, a company-wide framework, a custom search engine, and a homegrown CRM while the actual product remains rough. The engineers feel productive because they are building infrastructure, but customers do not pay for infrastructure. They pay for outcomes. In a young company, the cost of a wrong internal platform is not the code; it is the months spent on a problem that may not exist.

That risk is real, and the answer is not to build everything. It is to delay building until the need is proven and the shape is stable. Start with the bought or open-source version. Use it in production. Let real workloads reveal the gaps. If the gap is a missing button, buy a different product or write a small adapter. If the gap is structural—your data model, your latency, your cost curve, your regulatory posture—then build. Revisit the decision when usage, revenue, or competitive pressure changes. A build/buy choice is not a ceremony performed once at architecture review. It is a portfolio review, repeated.

Before building, put the decision in plain terms. What customer value does this capability create? What happens if it is 10 percent worse? 50 percent worse? What is the five-year cost of the external option, including integration, maintenance, and switching? What is the five-year cost of the internal option, including the engineers who will maintain it? Can we replace it if we regret the choice? Are we building because the product requires a distinctive answer, or because we are uncomfortable depending on someone else? If the last answer is the latter, slow down.

The slogan “don’t reinvent the wheel” is not a command to outsource your judgment. It is a warning about where attention goes. A company has too few good people to spend all of them on problems that already have good solutions. Spend the bought parts on reliability and integration. Spend the built parts on the places where your product must be different. The wheel is not the car. But if your product is the wheel, the question was never whether to reinvent it. It was whether you could make a better one.

prompt: Write something atmospheric and a bit unhinged: a person who normally avoids San Francisco ends up walking its streets alone in the dark just before sunrise, and the city starts to feel like the place where the world ends. Feel free to bring in poetry.
response:
I have always avoided San Francisco. I have avoided it the way people avoid the name of a disease: by keeping the room bright, by not looking at the coast on maps, by saying there are other cities, there are other coasts, there are other ways to be near the water. So when I find myself on Market Street at 4:17 a.m., walking because my feet have stopped asking permission, I am surprised by how well the city fits the inside of my skull.

I came because my brother is dead and his apartment is on Taraval and I have been avoiding this city for so long that the trip felt like a kind of fainting. I took the train from Berkeley because planes make the Pacific too real. I got off at 4th and King because my ticket said so, and then I kept walking.

The street is not empty. Empty is a word for postcards. There is a bus shelter with a dead leaf pressed to the glass, a man asleep in a doorway with his jacket arranged over him like a second skin, a rat in the gutter doing something urgent with a baguette. The bakery at the corner has its oven on, and the heat comes out under the door like a small confession. Somewhere a siren says its one long word and then, because no one is listening, stops.

It begins around the second hill. In San Francisco a street can go up, up, and then simply vanish into the fog, as if the city has a throat and is swallowing its own blocks. I take a turn on Geary and for a moment I cannot see the end of the avenue, only the lamps leaning into one another, only the black shapes of cars parked like animals that have decided to stay. The fog is not weather here. It is a policy. It is the city’s way of saying: you will not leave, you will only become less certain.

If I count the blocks I can get back to the year I left. If I take one more left I can get back to before the name. The streetlights blink in a code I almost understand: LEFT, LEFT, NOT YET, NOT YET.

I think of a line I read once, or made up, or wish I had read:

Before the sun, the city is a mouth  
with the light still in it.  
Here the streets close over themselves  
like teeth around a secret.

The world ends here, I think. Not with a shout, not with the sky turning to glass, but with a foghorn in the bay and a street sign going white in the dark. The bridges are lit, the Golden Gate a rust-colored wound in the grey, and beyond them the water is so still it looks like a place where things have simply stopped being reflected. The city is perched on the edge of the continent with the patience of a thing that knows it will be abandoned. Every hill is a last hill. Every door is a door that will not open again. The eucalyptus trees stand in the fog like columns in a temple where the god has left a message on the machine.

At the Embarcadero the fog comes off the water in a flat sheet, and the city on the other side is only a rumor of lights. I put my hand on the railing and feel the metal cold enough to hurt, and for a second I believe the railing is the only solid thing left in the hemisphere. A barge moves out of the white with no sound, just a darkening of the dark, and I understand that the sea has been waiting all night to take the city back one hill at a time.

The poem I carry is short:

San Francisco, before dawn,  
you are the last room in the house  
where the light is still on.  
You are the period  
at the end of the sentence  
that no one will ever finish reading.

I almost laugh. The laugh comes out wrong, too dry, like a branch breaking in an empty house. A gull lands on the railing near my hand and looks at me with an eye so black and practical it seems to contain the whole future. I do not move. The gull does not move. The bay does not move. For a minute the world is only the three of us and the cold metal and the faint orange smear over the hills.

Then the sky begins. Not suddenly. A thin gray seam along the top of the Marin headlands, then a pinkish bruise over the water, then the windows of the Ferry Building catching it. The city does not open. It remembers how to be a city. A bus comes, its wipers making small arcs in the damp air. A man with a coffee looks at me. A dog barks from a third-story window. The traffic light at the corner changes from red to green with the same indifference it would have if the sun had not come up.

I keep walking north. The fog thins. The streets get names again. The bakery smells of bread, and the bread is only bread, and the hill is only a hill, and the bridge is only a bridge. But I know now what I have always known: San Francisco is not a city. It is the hour before the end, wearing a city’s clothes. And this morning, for a few minutes, the end wore mine.

prompt: Tell the origin story of how a musician selling his own CD online accidentally started a business. Write it as a blog post.
response:
## The CD, the Spreadsheet, and the First $25

I had thirty CDs in a grocery bag and twelve dollars of hope.

The show had been fine. Not great, not terrible. The kind of night where the room is small, the amp hums a little too much, and you leave feeling both tired and mildly insulted that nobody asked for an encore. I sold four CDs at the door. That left twenty-six in the bag, each one costing about a dollar to burn and another fifty cents in paper sleeves because I was too cheap to buy cases.

I did not want to be a musician who sold music. I wanted to be a musician who made music and occasionally got paid. But the CDs were there, and the money was not, so I made a webpage.

It was one page. A photo of the album cover, a short bio I had written for a zine in high school, a track listing, and a PayPal button. I put it on a free host because I could not remember my password to the paid one. I emailed the link to the venue, my bandmates, and a fan who once told me my guitar tone sounded like a “metal rainstorm,” which I assumed was good.

I expected maybe one sale. One person who liked the music enough to feel guilty about not buying a CD at the door.

The first order came from a woman in Denver.

Two CDs, shipping included. Twenty dollars.

I stared at the email for a long time. It felt less like a sale and more like a challenge. She had sent money to a stranger on the internet for a disc I had burned in my kitchen. Now I owed her something.

I went to the post office the next morning with two CDs, a printed copy of the order email, and no idea how to address a package properly. I bought stamps from the machine because I did not have any. The clerk looked at me like I was either a criminal or a tourist. I think I was both.

When the CDs arrived, she emailed to say thanks. That was the part that changed things. A physical object had moved across the country because of a webpage and a button. It was absurd, but it worked.

Then people started asking for downloads.

This was a problem. I had not made a digital version. I had a folder of audio files on my laptop, but I did not know how to send them without making a mess. At first I just zipped the files and attached them to emails. One person wanted the whole album. Another wanted only three songs. A third asked if I could rename the files properly because they “all sounded the same.”

I spent a Saturday making a spreadsheet.

Column A: name. Column B: email. Column C: what they wanted. Column D: whether they had paid. Column E: whether I had sent it.

By the end of the week I had sent forty-one downloads by hand. My outbox looked like a disaster. I had typed the same sentence over and over: “Here you go, let me know if anything sounds weird.” It was not a system. It was a pile of obligations with headers.

But it was a system I could copy.

The first request came from a bass player in another local band. He saw the page I had made and asked if I could do something similar for them. They had a new EP and wanted to sell it after their next show. I said I would think about it. Then I did it that night because it took less time than arguing with myself.

I changed the cover art. I changed the band name. I changed the PayPal email. I sent him the link.

He sold nine CDs in one weekend.

Then he asked if I could add T-shirts.

This was where it stopped being a favor.

I had no shirts. I had no supplier. I had no idea what a “print run” meant except that it sounded expensive. I called a screen printer I had used once for a flyer. He let me order five shirts at seventy-five dollars. I paid with the money from the Denver order and some money meant for gas.

The shirts sold out in a week.

Now I was not just helping a band put up a webpage. I was holding inventory. I had to ship boxes instead of discs. I had to answer questions about sizes. I had to tell a customer in Portland that the black shirts were gone and the gray ones would arrive “soon,” which was a lie because I did not know when they would arrive.

I told another band I could set up their page too. Then another. Each time I told myself it was one last small favor. Each time the spreadsheet got longer.

The honest version is that I was bad at saying no and good at copying things. If a page worked for one band, I could make it work for another. If a shirt order worked once, I could do it again. If a customer emailed at ten p.m. asking whether the CD included the bonus track, I could answer from the couch with a half-eaten sandwich in front of me.

The word “accidental” makes the story sound cleaner than it was. There was no moment where I sat down and decided to become a business owner. There was just a sequence of small yeses: yes, I’ll mail these; yes, I’ll send the files; yes, I’ll make the page; yes, I’ll order the shirts; yes, I’ll answer the email.

The first real business decision was also the first annoying one.

A band asked me to set up their store for a month. I told them I could do it, but I was no longer doing it for free. I charged twenty-five dollars.

They paid.

That was it. No handshake over a desk. No lease. No logo. Just an email saying the money was sent and a link that worked.

I kept the receipts in a shoebox.

The shoebox matters more than it should. It is where the story actually begins: not with the webpage, not with the CD, but with the point at which I stopped treating the money as a strange thing that happened to me and started treating it as something I had to account for. Stamps. Shipping labels. Refunds. A customer who ordered two posters and wanted a discount because she was “a student and a fan.” I gave her two dollars off and wrote it down because I was afraid I would forget I had done it.

People sometimes ask what the business was for. That is a harder question than it sounds.

At first, it was just the thing I had built to sell my own CD and then other people’s CDs. It was a storefront, but only barely. It was an order form, a payment button, a shipping list, and a set of instructions I kept rewriting. It was not elegant. It was not scalable, unless you count scaling as making the spreadsheet uglier.

But it solved a specific problem. Bands could put something online quickly, take money, and not have to figure out the whole machine. I knew the machine because I had been inside it, confused, with CDs in a grocery bag.

That is the part I still think about. The business did not start because I saw a gap in the market. It started because I had a small, immediate problem and solved it in the dumbest way available. Then other people had the same problem, and I had already built the dumb solution.

The first client still writes to me sometimes. He asks if I remember the gray shirts. I do. I remember the screen printer’s minimum order, the box arriving too late, and the customer who wanted a large but “not too large.” I remember the twenty-five dollars.

The company has changed since then, obviously. The shoebox is long gone. The spreadsheet has been replaced by things with names I still misspell. The CDs are mostly a curiosity now, mentioned in emails like a relic.

But the origin is still the same. A musician with unsold discs. A webpage made in a hurry. A stranger sending money. A pile of small tasks turning into a pattern. And one afternoon when I decided that the next favor would cost twenty-five dollars.

That is how it started. Not with a plan. With a package at the post office and a button that worked.

Philosophical nuances:

- Definitions and categories: A category is not just a word. It is a way of grouping things based on relevant similarities. A definition is an explicit rule. Wrongness can be internal (incoherence), external (mismatch with world), or pragmatic (ineffective for purpose).

- Natural kinds: Some categories are discovered in the sense that the world has structure: water is H2O, gold is element 79, mammals have certain developmental features. But the boundaries of many natural kinds are fuzzy or chosen: species, adult, disease. Even "water" has boundaries: what about aqueous solutions? What about supercritical water? The word has a core and extensions.

prompt: Use a thought experiment about a town founded by people who hate late-night noise to think through when a community has the right to restrict what its members do, and then apply it to the housing and NIMBY debate. Write it as a long, exploratory blog post with a libertarian-ish flavor, ending with a practical proposal.
response:
There is a town I will call Hush. It was founded by people who hate late-night noise. Not mildly. They hate it in a specific, bodily way. They are the people who hear a lawnmower at 7:10 on a Saturday and feel a small personal insult. They are the people who cannot sleep when a neighbor’s dog barks at a garbage truck, or when a bass note from two houses down arrives through the wall like a slow vibration in the floor of the skull. They are the people who have a list. The list is long. The list includes amplified music, car alarms, shouting, footsteps on joists, refrigerators that hum, parties that end at 2 a.m., and the particular thud of a basketball on a driveway at midnight.

Hush begins as a compact. A group of quiet people buy land, build houses, and agree on rules. No amplified sound after 9 p.m. No outdoor parties after 11. No commercial music. No short-term rentals, because short-term rentals bring strangers and strangers bring noise. The streets are quiet. The founders are happy.

Then the town grows.

A young couple moves in. They have not lived in Hush. They do not share the founders’ hatred of noise, but they like the houses, the schools, the low crime rate, the commute. They buy a place. They have a patio. On Friday nights, they have friends over. Someone plays guitar. Someone laughs too loudly. A neighbor hears it at 10:40 p.m. and calls the town.

Now the question: Does Hush have the right to stop them?

The answer depends on what Hush is, and on what the rule is doing.

If Hush is a private community, the answer is probably yes. If the founders created a common ownership structure, or a homeowners association, or a set of covenants that run with the land, then the new couple may have consented by buying. They may not have read the covenant, but that is their problem in a way that would not be true if the government had hidden a rule in a code. Private communities can be narrow, weird, and exclusionary, so long as people enter them knowingly. If you want a town with no amplified sound, no short-term rentals, and no loud dogs, you can build one. If you do it privately, you are mostly doing what people do when they choose a spouse, a church, a workplace, or a club. You select for shared preferences.

But towns are not only private associations. They are also governments. They tax you. They can fine you. They can condemn your land. They can require you to use certain roads, pay for certain schools, and obey rules you did not make. They can tell you what you may build on land you own. That is a different kind of power. It is not the power of a club. It is the power of a monopoly. You cannot leave Hush as easily as you can leave a homeowners association, because Hush contains your house, your job, your children’s school, your doctors, your post office, and the roads that connect them.

So when Hush becomes a public town, the moral question changes. The founders’ preference for quiet is still real. But it is no longer enough. A public town cannot say, “We are quiet people, therefore the law will make you quiet in ways that go beyond the harm you actually do.” It can say, “Do not make noise that disturbs your neighbors at night.” It cannot say, “Do not live in the kind of house that might contain noisy people.”

That distinction is the whole essay.

A community has a strong right to restrict acts that impose unconsented burdens on other people. Noise is one of the clearest cases. I do not consent to your bass speaker vibrating my bedroom wall at 3 a.m. I do not consent to your party occupying the air I need for sleep. Sleep is not a luxury. It is a biological requirement. A rule that says “no outdoor amplified sound after 10 p.m.” is not a strange aesthetic preference. It is a rule about the boundary between my property and yours. It says you may use your land, but not in a way that invades my ability to use mine.

But a community does not have a similar right to restrict the kind of person, household, or building form that might, in the future, produce a harm. That is where the line gets blurry, because all land-use rules are predictions. A town that bans apartments is predicting that apartments will be noisier. A town that bans duplexes is predicting that duplexes will change the character of the street. A town that bans short-term rentals is predicting that transient guests will be louder than permanent residents. Sometimes those predictions are reasonable. Sometimes they are just preferences wearing the clothes of public policy.

The test I would use is simple: If the rule would still make sense if the supposed noisy source were replaced by a quiet one, then the rule is not really about noise.

Suppose Hush bans all apartment buildings because apartments bring noise. But imagine an apartment building where every resident is as quiet as the founders of Hush. They work from home. They read. They walk to the store. They never play music. They never host parties. They are, in every relevant way, the people Hush wants to live among. Does the ban still make sense? If yes, then the town is not banning noise. It is banning a building type. It is not regulating a harm. It is regulating a symbol.

Now suppose Hush bans all outdoor amplified sound after 9 p.m. That rule makes sense regardless of whether the sound comes from a single-family house, an apartment, a duplex, a restaurant, or a portable speaker at a wedding. The rule tracks the harm. The harm is sound waves entering other people’s homes at bad hours. The source form is incidental.

That is the difference between a legitimate community rule and an exclusionary one.

This is where the housing debate gets uncomfortable, because a lot of what is called NIMBYism is not really about noise at all. It is about scale, density, and social composition. People say “I don’t want apartments next to my house,” and they may mean noise, but they often mean something else. They mean they do not want more people. They do not want renters. They do not want a different visual texture. They do not want property values to fall. They do not want the street to feel less like a street of detached houses and more like a place where life happens in closer proximity.

Some of those concerns are legitimate externalities. Traffic is real. Parking is real. Construction is real. Schools fill up. Shadows fall. View corridors disappear. A new building can change the microeconomics of a neighborhood in ways that affect existing residents. A libertarian should not pretend that property rights are isolated bubbles. I own my house, but I also own, in a weaker sense, the expectation that the street will remain passable, that the air will not be blocked, that the school will not be overwhelmed, and that the parking will not become a rotating carnival of circling cars.

But the legitimate part of the complaint is much smaller than the policy usually used to address it.

If the problem is traffic, the answer is not to ban housing. The answer is to manage traffic: pricing, parking limits, transit, road design, building orientation, and after-the-fact rules about loading and unloading. If the problem is parking, the answer is not to require every new home to come with two or three empty parking spaces. The answer is to let people build where they want and let parking be priced by demand. In many places, parking minimums are a hidden subsidy for car ownership and a hidden tax on housing. They make buildings more expensive, which pushes up rents and prices, which makes the town less accessible, which changes the population, which is exactly what the people who wanted the town to remain the same did not want.

If the problem is noise, the answer is noise rules. Not building-form rules.

This is where the thought experiment becomes useful. Hush was founded by people who hate late-night noise. If Hush wants to be quiet, it can be quiet. It can have strict, enforceable, time-based noise limits. It can fine people for amplified sound after 10. It can require that outdoor gatherings end by 11. It can regulate commercial music. It can create a quiet district with stronger enforcement. It can even allow private covenants in which residents agree to no short-term rentals, no amplified sound, no loud dogs, no late-night parties. That is fine.

What Hush cannot do, as a public town, is use the preference for quiet as a reason to ban the people who might be noisy. It cannot look at a proposed duplex and say, “A duplex might contain a couple with friends over on Friday,” and therefore deny the permit. It cannot look at a small apartment building and say, “Renters are transient and therefore unreliable,” and therefore block it. It cannot look at a group home and say, “People with disabilities might be loud,” and therefore keep it out. That is not a rule about noise. That is a rule about who is allowed to exist in the town.

The libertarian instinct here is not “anything goes.” It is “coercion requires a wrong.” Government may force you to stop making noise that invades your neighbor’s sleep. It may not force you to live in a world permanently arranged according to the tastes of the people who happened to be there first.

There is a harder objection, and it should be taken seriously.

Existing quiet residents may say: “We bought this place because it was quiet. You are taking that from us. You are not just allowing new people to move in; you are changing the character of the neighborhood we chose. Our property values will fall. Our expectations will be broken. If you can do this to us, what exactly do we own?”

That is not a silly claim. Quiet can be a property interest. A house on a quiet street is not identical to the same house on a street with a loud bar, a bus depot, or a late-night industrial operation. People pay for location, and location includes ambient conditions. If the government zoned an area as residential and kept out the noisy uses, existing residents may have relied on that. If the government later allows a use that produces a chronic, specific nuisance, the residents should have a remedy.

But the remedy should not be a permanent right to exclude future residents.

Property rights are relational. I do not own the silence of the air around my house in an absolute sense, because my neighbors own their property too. If they use it lawfully, I may have to live with the ordinary sounds of a denser town. The law can protect me from particular harms: repeated noise, vibration, light, odor, traffic, shadow. It cannot protect me from the mere fact that other people are nearby.

This is where the distinction between actual nuisance and anticipated character becomes crucial. If a new building produces noise that violates the town’s objective limits, shut that noise down. If a specific tenant throws parties at 2 a.m., enforce the rule against that tenant. If a restaurant’s patio becomes a permanent late-night amplifier, regulate the patio. If a development creates a traffic problem, address the traffic. But do not deny the project in advance because you imagine it will be bad.

That sounds cold, but it is the only fair system. A town cannot have it both ways. It cannot tell existing residents that their quiet is an entitlement, and then tell newcomers that they may be excluded because of what they might do. If quiet is a right, it must be a right against actual interference, not a right to freeze the future.

There is also the problem of exit costs. A libertarian account that says “people can vote with their feet” often underestimates how stuck people are. Moving is expensive. Jobs are local. Children’s schools are local. Elders are attached to care networks. A town that changes its character can hurt people who cannot easily leave. That matters. But the answer is not to give existing residents a veto over new construction. The answer is to make the change gradual where possible, to enforce nuisances, and to accept that some losses are market losses, not rights violations. A falling property value is painful. It is not, by itself, a reason for the government to exclude a class of people.

This is why I am suspicious of local zoning as it is often practiced. Zoning is supposed to be about managing externalities. In practice, it is often a collective preference machine. A neighborhood can look at a proposed building and reject it because it does not like the height, the massing, the number of units, the income level of likely residents, or the general vibe. The formal reason may be “character.” The real reason may be “not like us.” That is not a legitimate basis for coercive power.

A town is not a club. Or rather, it is a club only in the weakest sense. You can choose to live there, but you cannot easily opt out of its laws. You pay its taxes. You are subject to its police. Your children go to its schools. Your property is bounded by its rules. If a town wants to be a quiet enclave, it should be able to become one through private ordering, not through public monopoly.

That leads to the practical proposal.

The goal is to let Hush be Hush, but only in ways that do not turn Hush into a coercive aesthetic state.

First, abolish use-based residential zoning. No more single-family-only districts. No more bans on duplexes, triplexes, small apartment buildings, or accessory dwelling units. If a lot can hold a house, it can hold more than one household, subject to neutral building codes: setbacks, fire safety, plumbing, electrical standards, height limits where they serve real purposes like sunlight or view protection, and so on. The number of people in a dwelling should not be a use-based restriction. A four-person family in a single-family house is not meaningfully less dense than four couples in a small apartment building. The relevant harms are traffic, noise, parking, and design, not the legal fiction of “family” versus “nonfamily.”

Second, adopt objective noise rules and enforce them. This is the part Hush should keep. The rules should be time-based and measurable. For example: no outdoor amplified sound after a certain hour; no continuous noise above a certain decibel level at night; no commercial music beyond a set limit; no repeated late-night disturbances. Enforcement should be against the source. If an apartment building has one noisy tenant, the remedy is to address that tenant, not to ban the building. If a single-family house has a bass speaker, the remedy is to shut down the speaker, not to pretend that the problem would have been solved by keeping the house from being sold to the current owners.

Third, allow private quiet covenants, but do not impose them publicly. If a developer wants to create a subdivision where no short-term rentals are allowed, no amplified sound is permitted after 9, and no outdoor gatherings are allowed after 11, let the buyers consent. If the buyers want that, fine. The covenant should be disclosed, and it should bind those who buy with notice. But a public town cannot impose a “quiet covenant” on people who never agreed to it. If you want a quiet street, organize the street privately. If you want the whole town to be quiet, pass neutral noise laws. Do not use the government to make nonconsenters live under a club rule.

Fourth, replace prior exclusion with after-the-fact nuisance. This is the biggest conceptual shift. Right now, a lot of land-use control happens before construction: a neighbor objects, a board hears testimony, a project is delayed or denied because of imagined harms. The better system is to let lawful projects build, and then enforce specific rules when specific harms occur. If the building is too loud, regulate the loudness. If it creates parking chaos, impose parking limits or fees. If it blocks light, enforce the height or setback rule. If it generates traffic, manage the traffic. The point is to respond to actual externalities, not to allow a neighborhood to veto the future based on mood.

Fifth, replace parking minimums with parking maximums or no minimums. This is not a detail. Parking minimums are one of the main ways NIMBY preferences get embedded into building costs. If every new unit must come with two off-street spaces, developers build more concrete and charge more for the privilege. That makes housing less affordable, which changes the population, which is often the real thing people are afraid of. If the town is worried about parking, let it set maximums, especially near transit. If people want more parking, they can pay for it. If they do not, the lot can be used for something else: trees, housing, storage, light, air.

Sixth, if a community wants a “quiet district,” let it be a noise-enforcement district, not a density ban. A quiet district can mean stricter after-hours limits, reduced commercial sound, better enforcement, and perhaps restrictions on late-night delivery trucks. It should not mean “no apartments,” “no duplexes,” or “no group housing.” If the district is quiet because of actual sound levels, that is a real public benefit. If it is quiet because an entire category of residents is excluded, that is not a public benefit. That is a private preference enforced by the state.

The town founded by people who hate late-night noise can be quiet. It should be allowed to be quiet. But it must stop pretending that its desire for quiet is the same thing as a right to control who may live there. Noise is a harm. Character is a preference. A community has a strong claim against the first and a weak claim against the second.

That is the line Hush has to respect.
