prompt: I keep noticing that more and more things in my life feel 'addictive' -- the internet, games, food. Is the world actually getting more addictive, and if so what should a person do about it? Write me an essay.
response:
The first thing to sort out is what “addictive” means. In medicine, addiction is not “I enjoy this too much.” It is a pattern where a person keeps doing something despite clear harm, has tried and failed to cut back, and feels driven to do it even when it conflicts with other goals. By that standard, most people who spend three hours on their phone are not addicted. They are using a tool that is very good at taking time. But the everyday sense of the word is also real: a thing is addictive when it creates a pull strong enough to override your plans. On that measure, yes, a lot of modern life has become more pulling.

The change is not mysterious. We have taken the mechanisms that used to require a casino, a candy store, a bar, a television set, and a pack of cigarettes, and put them into a device that is always in reach, knows what you do, and can signal you when you are about to stop. A slot machine works partly because the reward is uncertain: sometimes you win, sometimes you do not, and the near-miss makes the next pull feel urgent. Much of the internet runs on the same logic. A social feed gives you likes, comments, messages, and new videos at irregular intervals. A game gives you loot boxes, daily login bonuses, streaks, and “come back in two hours for a free chest.” A notification that someone liked your post is a small burst of social uncertainty: did they like it? who else saw it? should I reply? None of these is a drug, but they are rewards, and they are delivered by systems designed to keep you checking.

Infinite scroll matters more than it looks. A television program has an ending. A book has a chapter. A meal has a plate. A feed has no bottom. That removes the natural moment where stopping feels reasonable. You do not have to decide to keep watching in the same explicit way you would decide to buy another drink. The next item is already there. The same is true of many games: levels continue, timers refill, and the interface is organized around the next small gain. Food is a different case. Most food is not addictive in the way nicotine is, but the modern food environment makes eating frequent and effortless. Ultra-processed foods are cheap, convenient, and formulated to be highly palatable. They do not need to be chemically addictive to produce overeating when they are everywhere and eating happens by default.

Is the world actually getting more addictive? In one sense, yes: the average person is now surrounded by more continuously available, more personalized reward systems than any previous generation. In another sense, the old addictions are still there. Alcohol, tobacco, gambling, and sugar are not gone, and they are still destructive. The new layer is not replacing the old one; it is adding to it. A person can be managing a drinking problem and still lose two hours a day to a phone.

I am not certain how many people meet formal clinical criteria for behavioral addictions, because the diagnoses are newer and less consistently applied than those for alcohol or nicotine. I would not bet that most heavy users are clinically addicted. But clinical addiction is not the only harm. A person can lose sleep, attention, and hours without being unable to stop if forced. A student who could put the phone down if a parent stood over her is still losing the ability to sit with a difficult task. A worker who checks messages for twenty minutes every hour is not necessarily compulsive, but the work is fragmenting. The practical question is not whether the world has produced more addicts in the strict sense. It is whether it has produced more environments in which ordinary self-control is taxed all day long.

The strongest objection to that view is that it is a story people tell when they are lazy, lonely, or undisciplined. Humans have always binged. Plenty of people were ruined by television, cheap sweets, gambling halls, and drinking before anyone optimized a user interface. If the problem were only the environment, why do some people manage fine? That question matters. The environment is not acting on a blank slate. A person with untreated depression, attention problems, trauma, or social anxiety may be much more vulnerable to anything that offers quick relief and a sense of connection. A person with a structured day, meaningful work, and reliable friends will find it easier to put the phone down. The same feed can be a nuisance to one person and a trap to another.

But that does not show the world has not changed. It shows that a more powerful set of triggers has appeared, and that it will find the people who were already fragile. It also shows that blaming “the algorithm” can become a way of avoiding the fact that you chose, repeatedly, to keep using the thing. Both things are true at once: the design is deliberately sticky, and you are still the one who unlocks the screen.

What should a person do? Start by treating it like a diagnosis, not a moral failing. For a week, notice when you reach for the phone, the game, or the snack. What happened just before? Were you bored? Tired? Anxious? Did a notification arrive? Were you sitting in a place where the thing was already in your hand? The trigger matters. If the problem is notifications, turn them off. If it is the phone in bed, move the charger to another room. If it is snacks on the counter, do not keep them there. If it is loneliness, the answer is not a better blocker; it is more contact with other people.

Then change defaults instead of relying on intentions. Willpower is a bad system because it is usually tested at the worst moment: when you are tired, alone, or under pressure. Make the behavior you want the path of least resistance, and make the behavior you want to stop require extra steps. If you want to read more, put the book on the pillow and the phone in the kitchen. If you want to stop doomscrolling, log out of the apps on your phone and use them only on a computer, where opening a window is more effort. If you want to eat less junk, do not buy the bag; buy the smaller version, or buy nothing and plan the meal. Friction is not elegant, but it works because it gives the rational part of your mind a few seconds to intervene.

Replace the variable-reward loop with activities that have natural endings. This is not a moral upgrade; it is an attention repair. A workout ends. A chapter ends. A conversation ends when the other person leaves. Cooking a meal ends when the food is done. These activities also produce reliable feedback: your body feels different, the page is finished, the room smells like food. Modern feeds are good at producing the next hit. Ordinary life is good at producing completion. If your days are mostly open-ended stimulation, you will start to crave it, because it is the only thing that feels alive.

Social structure helps more than people admit. It is easier to stop when other people expect you to stop. A dinner at someone’s house limits phone use. A gym class at a set time limits gaming. A friend who texts you at a certain hour creates a reason to look up. You do not need to announce a “digital detox.” You just need some parts of your life to be arranged around other people and other obligations. Isolation is a major amplifier of compulsive use, because the phone becomes the only source of social feedback.

If the problem is severe, get help. If you have tried to cut back and failed, if the behavior is damaging your relationships, work, sleep, or mood, that is not a character flaw waiting for more discipline. It is a health problem. Therapy, support groups, and in some cases medical treatment can help with compulsive patterns the way they help with other addictions. Pretending that you should simply be able to stop is usually a delay tactic.

The aim is not abstinence. A person who can use social media for thirty minutes and then stop is not broken. A person who cannot stop for three hours is in trouble. The goal is control: the ability to choose when to start and when to end. That ability is built less by inner strength than by the layout of your life. Fewer hidden rewards, fewer invisible cues, more activities with known costs and known ends. The world has not become a uniform slot machine. It has become a place where slot-machine logic is mixed into ordinary life. The practical response is to take the uncertainty out of your days and make your environment less able to pay you to forget your intentions.

prompt: Is there a biological explanation for why people with anorexia can't just regain weight once they decide to? Speculate about it using what we know about obesity and the body's weight set point. Flag clearly that you're not an expert.
response:
I’m not an expert in eating disorders or obesity physiology, so treat this as an informed guess rather than a clinical account. The premise also needs a small correction: people with anorexia can regain weight, and many do. The better question is why a decision to regain it is not enough.

The most useful place to start is the obesity side, because it shows that body weight is not controlled the way people assume. The set point is better thought of as a defended range, not a fixed number. Fat cells secrete leptin; when energy stores fall, leptin falls, hunger rises, and energy expenditure drops. When a person with obesity loses weight, the same feedback loops push back: the body behaves as if it is starving even if it is still above a healthy range. Genetic differences in this system help explain why some people defend higher weights with less effort than others. That is why a decision to diet is not enough. The person has to keep choosing smaller portions against a system that is signaling need.

Anorexia is tempting to read as the reverse: a body that has set its point too low. But that reading runs into a problem. If a person is severely underweight, the homeostatic system should not be saying, “stay thin.” It should be saying, “energy stores are inadequate: eat, conserve, slow down.” Starvation produces low leptin, low thyroid activity, low sex hormones, bradycardia, cold intolerance, and a slowed gut. Those are not signs of a healthy preference for thinness; they are signs that the body is surviving a deficit. If the person simply followed the body’s homeostatic signals, weight would tend to return.

So the hardest objection to a simple biological explanation is this: the biology, at the level of energy regulation, is already pushing toward weight gain. The reason that push does not automatically produce recovery is that the person is not simply obeying homeostasis. They have a second regulatory target, a psychological set point, that sits below the biological one. In that target system, hunger is not a useful signal; it is a warning that the self is failing. A full stomach is not comfort; it is a sign of loss of control. Weight gain is not restoration; it is danger. The intellectual decision to recover can coexist with a felt expectation that eating will make things worse. The brain’s threat circuitry is still classifying food as a predator, even when the cortex says the goal is health.

That is why “just decide” does not work. Weight is not a direct object of volition. You can decide to gain weight the way you can decide to stop your hands from shaking, but the shaking is generated by systems that do not take orders from a single act of will. Eating is controlled by appetite, satiety, taste, fear, habit, memory, and gut feedback. If those systems are organized around avoiding weight gain, the output is restriction, no matter what the stated intention is.

There are also concrete biological reasons the path back is rough. A starved gut may empty slowly, so a small meal produces nausea, bloating, and a sensation of being overfilled. Metabolism is downregulated, so the body is very efficient at remaining small; gaining even a modest amount can require more food than the person’s intuition expects. Refeeding too quickly can cause dangerous electrolyte shifts, so medically safe regain is often slower than it looks from the outside. Food can also be less rewarding during energy deficit, while restriction can feel clean, controlled, and anxiety-reducing. The person is not merely being stubborn; the feedback environment for eating has become aversive.

The obesity analogy is therefore not that anorexia is “obesity in reverse.” It is that both conditions show how powerful weight-regulating systems are when they are misaligned with the person’s goal. In obesity, the body often defends a higher range than the person wants, and the environment makes overeating easy. In anorexia, the person has learned to defend a lower range than the body wants, and the fear system makes restriction feel like safety. The body is not usually locked into thinness. It is locked into preserving life under the conditions the person has imposed, while the person’s learned system keeps imposing those conditions.

One caveat: I am less sure how much of the low hunger sometimes seen in anorexia is due to true homeostatic adaptation versus fear-driven misinterpretation of hunger. Both are probably real, and they reinforce each other. The practical implication is that recovery often requires more than a decision. It requires making the felt system believe that gaining weight is survivable, and often it requires medical support to get through the nausea, metabolic drag, and refeeding risk.

"I’m not an expert in eating disorders or obesity physiology, so treat this as an informed guess rather than a clinical account.

The most useful place to start is the obesity side, because it shows that body weight is not controlled the way people assume. In the simplified set-point model, the body defends a range of weight. Fat cells secrete leptin; when stores fall, leptin falls, hunger rises, and energy expenditure drops. When a person with obesity loses weight, the same feedback loops push back: the body behaves as if it is starving even if it is still above a healthy range. That is why a decision to diet is not enough. The person has to keep choosing smaller portions against a system that is signaling need.

Anorexia is tempting to read as the reverse: a body that has set its point too low. But that reading runs into a problem. If a person is severely underweight, the homeostatic system should not be saying, “stay thin.” It should be saying, “energy stores are inadequate: eat, conserve, slow down.” Starvation produces low leptin, low thyroid activity, low sex hormones, bradycardia, cold intolerance, and a slowed gut. Those are not signs of a healthy preference for thinness; they are signs that the body is surviving a deficit. If the person simply followed the body’s homeostatic signals, weight would tend to return.

So the hardest objection to a simple biological explanation is this: the biology, at the level of energy regulation, is already pushing toward weight gain. The reason that push does not automatically produce recovery is that the person is not simply obeying homeostasis. They have a second regulatory target, a psychological set point, that sits below the biological one. In that target system, hunger is not a useful signal; it is a warning that the self is failing. A full stomach is not comfort; it is a sign of loss of control. Weight gain is not restoration; it is danger. The intellectual decision to recover can coexist with a felt expectation that eating will make things worse. The brain’s threat circuitry is still classifying food as a predator, even when the cortex says the goal is health.

That is why “just decide” does not work. Weight is not a direct object of volition. You can decide to gain weight the way you can decide to stop your hands from shaking, but the shaking is generated by systems that do not take orders from a single act of will. Eating is controlled by appetite, satiety, taste, fear, habit, memory, and gut feedback. If those systems are organized around avoiding weight gain, the output is restriction, no matter what the stated intention is.

There are also concrete biological reasons the path back is rough. A starved gut may empty slowly, so a small meal produces nausea, bloating, and a sensation of being overfilled. Metabolism is downregulated, so the body is very efficient at remaining small; gaining even a modest amount can require more food than the person’s intuition expects. Refeeding too quickly can cause dangerous electrolyte shifts, so medically safe regain is often slower than it looks from the outside. Food can also be less rewarding during energy deficit, while restriction can feel clean, controlled, and anxiety-reducing. The person is not merely being stubborn; the feedback environment for eating has become aversive.

The obesity analogy is therefore not that anorexia is “obesity in reverse.” It is that both conditions show how powerful weight-regulating systems are when they are misaligned with the person’s goal. In obesity, the body often defends a higher range than the person wants, and the environment makes overeating easy. In anorexia, the person has learned to defend a lower range than the body wants, and the fear system makes restriction feel like safety. The body is not usually locked into thinness. It is locked into preserving life under the conditions the person has imposed, while the person’s learned system keeps imposing those conditions.

That leaves one important caveat: I am less sure how much of the low hunger sometimes seen in anorexia is due to true homeostatic adaptation versus fear-driven misinterpretation of hunger. Both are probably real, and they reinforce each other. The practical implication is that recovery often requires more than a decision. It requires making the felt system believe that gaining weight is survivable, and often it requires medical support to get through the nausea, metabolic drag, and refeeding risk."

prompt: Lately everything is a kind of 'justice': economic justice, climate justice, intergenerational justice. Write a short essay on what changes, psychologically and morally, when we reframe helping people as pursuing justice.
response:
When a food bank hands a family a bag of groceries, the family is grateful; when a labor law guarantees a living wage, the worker is not grateful to the worker’s peers, but owed. The first is a gift; the second is a settlement. That difference is not only in scale. It is in the shape of the moral scene.

In the scene of help, one party is above, even if gently. The helper has resources to spare and may choose to use them. The recipient is in a position of need and, ideally, gratitude. This can be warm. It can also be humiliating, because it makes dependence visible and optional. A person who receives help is allowed to suffer if the helper tires, if public sympathy fades, or if the helper decides that another cause is more urgent. The relationship is personal, and personal relations can be withdrawn.

In the scene of justice, the need is not an accident to be soothed but a claim to be honored. The recipient is not asking for a gift; they are demanding what is due. That changes the psychology of both sides. The recipient no longer has to perform gratitude or prove worthiness. The helper no longer gets the moral credit of mercy. In its place comes something less flattering but stronger: responsibility. The person with power is not a benefactor; they are an agent of a system that must be made fair.

Morally, the move is from virtue to obligation. Helping is often a supererogatory act, good to do but not required in the same way that keeping a promise is required. Justice is different. If a right is recognized, failure to meet it is a wrong even if no one is personally at fault. This is why the language can feel so demanding. It makes moral failure structural. A company may not have decided to make a worker poor; the tax system, wage floor, and property rules may have done it. But if the outcome is an injustice, the question is not whether anyone feels sorry, but who is obliged to repair it.

This is the real power of the reframe. Compassion can be exhausted; it asks for feeling. Justice asks for institutions. A person can stop being moved without becoming a monster. A system, by contrast, can be changed. That is why climate change, once treated as a global tragedy, becomes more tractable when framed as intergenerational injustice: the problem is no longer that people are indifferent to distant children, but that present consumers and polluters are taking from people who have no vote in the matter. The moral demand becomes less “be kind to strangers” and more “stop making choices that impose costs on people who cannot consent.”

But the reframe has costs. Justice can make us suspicious of the very impulse that made us human to one another. If every need is a right, then kindness can look like a cover for failing to do the plain thing. If every relationship is a claim, then gratitude, apology, and forgiveness lose their place. The person who helps a neighbor after a flood is not enforcing a treaty; they are doing what neighbors do. To call the neighbor’s act justice is to flatten a moral texture that may be what keeps life livable.

There is also a danger of moral inflation. If poverty, weather, debt, and dying are all injustices, the word begins to sound like a banner rather than a judgment. Not every harm is a wrong. Some are accidents, tragedies, or the ordinary costs of a shared world. prompt: Newspapers, record labels and book publishers all complain that people won't pay for content anymore. Write an essay on whether that framing is even right, and what happens to publishing next.
response:
The phrase “people won’t pay for content anymore” is doing too much work. It makes a fact about one business model sound like a fact about human nature. A person may refuse to buy a CD, an album, or a local newspaper, yet pay for Spotify, Netflix, Audible, a newsletter, and a *New York Times* subscription in the same month. What the person is not paying for is the publisher’s old claim on the content. That is a different thing, and it matters.

Historically, publishers did not sell content alone. They sold bundles. A newspaper was news, local information, weather, advice, sports, prestige, and a regular place in the household. A record label was music plus promotion, retail placement, tour support, and a brand that told you what was worth listening to. A book publisher was a book plus distribution, reviews, author credibility, and a gate to the culture. When the internet separated the content from the channel, the bundles broke. The content could be copied, shared, streamed, or generated. The channel became a platform with its own incentives. Audiences did not stop paying; they stopped paying the tollbooth.

Music shows this cleanly. Streaming is a mass-market subscription service, and people use it. It solved the piracy problem for major labels in the sense that it gave listeners a cheap, legal, convenient default. But the value moved. The platform takes a large share, labels take a large share, and what reaches an individual artist is a fraction of a cent per stream. A million streams can be a few thousand dollars, depending on territory and plan, which is a living wage for almost nobody. At the same time, vinyl sales have done well again, often at prices that make no economic sense if the product were only audio. People buy vinyl for the object, the cover, the ritual, the signal it sends. They pay for music when it is packaged as identity, convenience, or access to a world. They do not pay for “content” as an abstract category.

Newspapers are the starkest test. The *New York Times* and the *Wall Street Journal* have shown that people will pay serious money for journalism when it is useful, branded, and tied to a sense of who they are. A Journal reader may pay because the paper helps with work. A Times reader may pay because the paper organizes a worldview. But local newspapers have declined in ways that cannot be explained by a simple refusal to pay. Local news is a public good in an uncomfortable sense: it watches over a town, but the benefit to any one resident is thin. A reader can get national news from a dozen free sources, and a local story often has little resale value outside a small geography. The failure is not that people will pay for information. It is that many forms of information are hard to make individually valuable enough to carry their own cost.

Books sit in between. Paper book sales have not collapsed; people still buy books as gifts, objects, markers of taste, and things to hold. The problem is more subtle. A reader who wants a story can borrow it, pirate it, wait for a cheap edition, or stream a similar story in another medium. The publisher must justify the price by being the source of trust, curation, author development, rights, and physical presence. Self-publishing has lowered the barrier to entry and flooded the market with titles that look like books but have no distribution or editorial weight. The result is not a market that rejects books. It is a market that has become harder to navigate, with bestsellers and niche communities thriving while the middle, the book that is neither a spectacle nor a specialized text, struggles.

The hardest objection to the “they still pay” answer is that the total amount people will pay for content may not be enough to support the number of professionals the old system employed. Content competes with every other use of time and money: food, housing, travel, games, video, relationships, sleep. A listener may value a song more than a stream’s price, but not more than the price of a coffee, a movie, or an hour of free YouTube. Free substitutes are often good enough. If the average consumer’s willingness to pay is low, then the industry’s complaint is economically rational, even if its language is not. The old model assumed a mass audience would each pay a small amount for a standard product. That assumption may have been wrong, or it may have depended on scarcity and gatekeeping that no longer exist.

That objection changes the diagnosis. If the market is too small to support many full-time creators through direct sales, publishing cannot keep pretending that every article, album, or book is a mass-market product. It has to sort content by what it actually is. Some content is advertising: it exists to build an audience for something else. Some is utility: weather, finance, how-to, sports scores, local alerts. Some is identity: news or music that tells a tribe what it believes. Some is status: the book on the shelf, the ticket, the subscription that signals membership. Some is civic infrastructure: local reporting, investigative work, public accountability. Each needs a different business model.

The next phase of publishing will probably be more fragmented and less uniform than the last. At one end, a few large branded publishers and platforms will keep selling convenience: all-you-can-eat subscriptions, algorithmic feeds, ad-supported free tiers. They will compete for the largest share of attention and take the largest share of revenue. Subscriptions will also rotate; people will keep a handful of paid services and churn the rest, so loyalty must be earned weekly, not annually. At another end, creators and small publishers will sell direct relationships: newsletters, memberships, events, courses, merchandise, licensed work, and community. The product will be less “content” and more “a channel you trust, with people like you, and a way to support the person or institution you already follow.” In between, catalogs will remain important. Music catalogs, book IP, sports archives, and classic journalism have value because they are finite, recognizable, and can be licensed repeatedly. But new work will be harder to fund unless it can be tied to an existing audience or a very specific niche.

Local and civic publishing will not be saved by scale. It will be saved by smaller, more explicit arrangements: local digital subscriptions, local advertising, memberships, philanthropy, public subsidies, cooperative ownership, and partnerships with libraries or schools. The scale will be modest. A town paper cannot become the next Netflix. It can become the next town forum, with a digital front page, a few paid columns, a community calendar, and a newsroom that is visibly accountable to the people who pay or benefit from it. That model may be less glamorous than the old newspaper, but it is more honest about the product.

AI will press on all of this. It will make generic content cheaper to produce, which means the commodity value of words, images, and audio will fall further. A competent essay, a stock photo, a jingle, or a product description can be made by a machine. That does not make human-made content worthless; it makes the human part more important. Trust, taste, accountability, and community become the things that cannot be fully automated. A reader may not care whether an article was written by a person if it is useful and verified, but a reader will care when the article claims to report, interpret, or represent a community. The flood of machine-generated content will likely increase the value of known names, institutional brands, and human curation, even as it destroys the market for anonymous, interchangeable writing.

So is the framing right? It is right if it means the old distribution rents are gone. Publishers once sat between creators and audiences and charged for the privilege of reach. That rent has been taken by platforms, eroded by search, or bypassed by direct channels. It is wrong if it means audiences no longer value content. They do, but they value it in specific forms: convenient, useful, socially meaningful, or directly connected to people they trust. Publishing next will not be a return to the old bundle. It will be a set of smaller, more explicit deals. Some content will be free because it is a loss leader. Some will be paid because it is a service. Some will be sold because it is an object or a badge. Some will be subsidized because it is a public good. The companies that survive will be the ones that stop saying “people won’t pay for content” and start saying, more accurately, “people won’t pay for this version of this product, delivered this way, at this price.”

Newspapers are the starkest test. The New York Times and the Wall Street Journal have shown that people will pay serious money for journalism when it is useful, branded, and tied to a sense of who they are. A Journal reader may pay because the paper helps with work. A Times reader may pay because the paper organizes a worldview. But local newspapers have declined in ways that cannot be explained by a simple refusal to pay. Local news is a public good in an uncomfortable sense: it watches over a town, but the benefit to any one resident is thin. A reader can get national news from a dozen free sources, and a local story often has little resale value outside a small geography. The failure is not that people will pay for information. It is that many forms of information are hard to make individually valuable enough to carry their own cost.

Books sit in between. Paper book sales have not collapsed; people still buy books as gifts, objects, markers of taste, and things to hold. The problem is more subtle. A reader who wants a story can borrow it, pirate it, wait for a cheap edition, or stream a similar story in another medium. The publisher must justify the price by being the source of trust, curation, author development, rights, and physical presence. Self-publishing has lowered the barrier to entry and flooded the market with titles that look like books but have no distribution or editorial weight. The result is not a market that rejects books. It is a market that has become harder to navigate, with bestsellers and niche communities thriving while the middle, the book that is neither a spectacle nor a specialized text, struggles.

The hardest objection to the "they still pay" answer is that the total amount people will pay for content may not be enough to support the number of professionals the old system employed. Content competes with every other use of time and money: food, housing, travel, games, video, relationships, sleep. A listener may value a song more than a stream's price, but not more than the price of a coffee, a movie, or an hour of free YouTube. Free substitutes are often good enough. If the average consumer's willingness to pay is low, then the industry's complaint is economically rational, even if its language is not. The old model assumed a mass audience would each pay a small amount for a standard product. That assumption may have been wrong, or it may have depended on scarcity and gatekeeping that no longer exist.

That objection changes the diagnosis. If the market is too small to support many full-time creators through direct sales, publishing cannot keep pretending that every article, album, or book is a mass-market product. It has to sort content by what it actually is. Some content is advertising: it exists to build an audience for something else. Some is utility: weather, finance, how-to, sports scores, local alerts. Some is identity: news or music that tells a tribe what it believes. Some is status: the book on the shelf, the ticket, the subscription that signals membership. Some is civic infrastructure: local reporting, investigative work, public accountability. Each needs a different business model.

The next phase of publishing will probably be more fragmented and less uniform than the last. At one end, a few large branded publishers and platforms will keep selling convenience: all-you-can-eat subscriptions, algorithmic feeds, ad-supported free tiers. They will compete for the largest share of attention and take the largest share of revenue. At another end, creators and small publishers will sell direct relationships: newsletters, memberships, events, courses, merchandise, licensed work, and community. The product will be less "content" and more "a channel you trust, with people like you, and a way to support the person or institution you already follow." In between, catalogs will remain important. Music catalogs, book IP, sports archives, and classic journalism have value because they are finite, recognizable, and can be licensed repeatedly. But new work will be harder to fund unless it can be tied to an existing audience or a very specific niche.

Local and civic publishing will not be saved by scale. It will be saved by smaller, more explicit arrangements: local digital subscriptions, local advertising, memberships, philanthropy, public subsidies, cooperative ownership, and partnerships with libraries or schools. The scale will be modest. A town paper cannot become the next Netflix. It can become the next town forum, with a digital front page, a few paid columns, a community calendar, and a newsroom that is visibly accountable to the people who pay or benefit from it. That model may be less glamorous than the old newspaper, but it is more honest about the product.

AI will press on all of this. It will make generic content cheaper to produce, which means the commodity value of words, images, and audio will fall further. A competent essay, a stock photo, a jingle, or a product description can be made by a machine. That does not make human-made content worthless; it makes the human part more important. Trust, taste, accountability, and community become the things that cannot be fully automated. A reader may not care whether an article was written by a person if it is useful and verified, but a reader will care when the article claims to report, interpret, or represent a community. The flood of machine-generated content will likely increase the value of known names, institutional brands, and human curation, even as it destroys the market for anonymous, interchangeable writing.

So is the framing right? It is right if it means the old distribution rents are gone. Publishers once sat between creators and audiences and charged for the privilege of reach. That rent has been taken by platforms, eroded by search, or bypassed by direct channels. It is wrong if it means audiences no longer value content. They do, but they value it in specific forms: convenient, useful, socially meaningful, or directly connected to people they trust. Publishing next will not be a return to the old bundle. It will be a set of smaller, more explicit deals. Some content will be free because it is a loss leader. Some will be paid because it is a service. Some will be sold because it is an object or a badge. Some will be subsidized because it is a public good. The companies that survive will be the ones that stop saying "people won't pay for content" and start saying, more accurately, "people won't pay for this version of this product, delivered this way, at this price."

prompt: Libertarians like to say that competition between private communities, each trying to offer the best rules, will protect freedom better than government can. The internet looks like a real-world test of that idea. Write an essay on whether it actually has, especially for unpopular speech.
response:
The libertarian claim has a simple shape: if one community forbids something, another will allow it, and users will vote with their feet. The internet makes that look testable because anyone can start a forum, a blog, a channel, or a protocol. The result is not a clean confirmation. For small and dispersed groups, the internet has indeed protected unpopular speech by giving it places to exist. For speech that needs to be heard by a mass audience, it has often done the opposite: it has concentrated the public square in the hands of a few private companies whose rules are shaped by advertisers, lawyers, app stores, payment systems, and the politics of the moment.

The first thing to notice is that the internet was not built as a single community. It is a stack. At the bottom are technical systems: domain names, routing, cloud hosting, content delivery, payment processing. Above them are applications: search, social networks, messaging, video. The libertarian image of competing towns works best at the application layer, where a new site can open in a day. But the application layer does not float free of the lower layers. A forum can be legal and popular and still be unreachable if its domain is disputed, its server provider drops it, its app is removed from the stores, or its payments are cut off. Parler after the January 6, 2021 attack is the clearest example. No court ordered it closed. Apple and Google removed its apps; Amazon Web Services and Cloudflare dropped it. The site survived by moving to smaller providers. That was not a free market in rules. It was a market in dependencies.

This matters because the value of speech depends less on the right to send a message than on the ability to reach an audience. A platform can ban you and your words will still be true; your audience will not. The internet has made it easier to start an alternative venue, but it has also made audiences cluster. The largest social networks are not just places where people talk; they are where their contacts, memories, notifications, and habits already are. Leaving is possible, but expensive. When a user is banned from a mainstream platform, the rival platform may allow the speech, but it may be a room with no one in it. The libertarian claim assumes that users will follow the speech. Often they do not. They follow their friends, their job, their news, and their arguments. If those are on the big platform, the big platform sets the terms.

The strongest case for the libertarian story is that private alternatives keep speech alive even when mainstream platforms kill it. The same conspiracy theorists, militia leaders, election deniers, religious dissidents, and political radicals who are banned on one site appear on another. If a government had tried to ban the same speech, it would have faced legal process, constitutional limits in some countries, and the practical problem of identifying speakers. Private bans are quicker and cheaper. But the test was not whether speech survives; it is whether freedom is protected. A speech act that can only be heard by people who already believe it is not the same as one that can challenge the mainstream. When Twitter suspended tens of thousands of QAnon-linked accounts in 2020, the movement did not disappear. It moved. But its center of gravity shifted to places with smaller reach and less access to people outside the movement. That is a real loss of freedom, even if it is not total suppression.

The internet has also shown that platforms do not compete primarily on the quality of their speech rules. They compete for attention, convenience, and advertiser confidence. A permissive rulebook can attract users who want less friction, but it can also attract content that scares advertisers and regulators. The result is usually a middle path: enough openness to keep engagement high, enough restriction to keep brand risk low. The phrase “best rules” hides a question: best for whom? If best means most attractive to the largest possible audience, the answer may be less speech, not more. This is not a market for liberty. It is a market for a product. The rules are features, and features are adjusted to make the product easier to sell. That is why mainstream platforms tend to converge. They may differ in tone, but they face similar pressures from card networks, app stores, legal liability, and the reputational cost of being the place where something awful happened. Competition can produce differences, but it does not necessarily produce a permanent niche for every kind of speech.

The libertarian argument also underestimates the role of government in shaping the private arena. In the United States, Section 230 shields platforms from most liability for user speech and encourages them to moderate without fear of being treated as publishers. That is a government policy, and it makes private gatekeeping safer. The European Union’s Digital Services Act tries to regulate the same power. In both cases, the question is not whether government or private actors control speech, but how the legal environment divides the power. The internet is not a natural experiment in private self-governance. It is a political artifact. If the claim is that private competition protects freedom better than government regulation, the internet complicates the claim because the private order has been built on legal permissions that reduce the cost of exclusion.

There is a harder point here. In a country with a strong First Amendment, the government often cannot do to a private platform what the platform can do to a speaker. The state cannot simply order Twitter to ban a politician because the state dislikes the speech. Twitter can. That is the most damaging result of the internet test for the libertarian claim: private actors have acquired a censorship power that the state, at least in the United States, is constitutionally barred from exercising in the same way. The internet has not shown that private competition is a better check on power than government. It has shown that power can move from public institutions to private ones without the constitutional brakes that used to apply.

But the government is not an ideal comparator. In authoritarian systems, the state can and does shut down platforms, criminalize speech, and force local compliance. The internet there is a tool of control, not a test of libertarian competition. The interesting case is the liberal state, where the government is limited but private platforms are not. There, the internet has produced a strange hybrid: speech is legally free but practically gated. A person may have the right to speak without state interference and still be unable to be heard because the main channels are privately administered. That is not the old problem of state censorship. It is a new problem of distribution.

This distinction matters for unpopular speech. The internet protects speech that can form a community: a minority religion, a political subculture, a stigmatized profession, a local grievance, a fringe theory. If the group is small enough, it can sustain itself on alternative platforms. The internet is a refuge. But it protects less well speech that needs to cross into the general public: a political campaign, a journalistic investigation, a mass protest, a moral controversy, a challenge to a dominant narrative. For that speech, being absent from the largest platforms is not a minor inconvenience. It is a loss of the public square. The libertarian model works best where the unit is the community. It works worst where the unit is the audience.

There are cases where the private-market story looks better. Decentralized protocols like Mastodon and, later, Bluesky have shown that federated or alternative systems can attract users when a dominant platform feels politically compromised. After the acquisition of Twitter by Elon Musk, a significant number of users and institutions moved to other services. That was not a complete replication of Twitter, but it was enough to show that the social graph can be partially portable. If the architecture makes migration cheap, private competition can discipline platforms. The problem is that migration is still costly, and the biggest audiences remain sticky. The lesson is not that competition fails, but that it needs conditions: open standards, exportable accounts, redundant hosting, and limits on the chokepoints that make a platform indispensable.

The internet has therefore tested the libertarian idea, but it has not confirmed it as a general solution. It has confirmed a narrower truth: multiple private venues make total suppression harder. They make it possible for unpopular speech to exist, to organize, and to find its own people. They have saved speech from the kind of monopoly that a single state broadcaster or a single licensed newspaper might have produced. But they have not produced a durable market in which freedom of speech is the winning product. They have produced a market in which attention is the product, and freedom is one of the variables that affects its sale.

The practical consequence is that if the goal is to protect unpopular speech, the question should not be only whether a government censors it. It should be whether the infrastructure of communication is open enough that no single private owner can decide who is heard. The internet shows that private communities can preserve speech, but they cannot guarantee its relevance. The libertarian promise that competition will protect freedom is real where alternatives are viable. It is hollow where the public square has become a private plaza with a few entrances.

The internet makes that look testable because anyone can start a forum, a blog, a channel, or a protocol. The result is not a clean confirmation. For small and dispersed groups, the internet has indeed protected unpopular speech by giving it places to exist. For speech that needs to be heard by a mass audience, it has often done the opposite: it has concentrated the public square in the hands of a few private companies whose rules are shaped by advertisers, lawyers, app stores, payment systems, and the politics of the moment.

The first thing to notice is that the internet was not built as a single community. It is a stack. At the bottom are technical systems: domain names, routing, cloud hosting, content delivery, payment processing. Above them are applications: search, social networks, messaging, video. The libertarian image of competing towns works best at the application layer, where a new site can open in a day. But the application layer does not float free of the lower layers. A forum can be legal and popular and still be unreachable if its domain is disputed, its server provider drops it, its app is removed from the stores, or its payments are cut off. Parler after the January 6, 2021 attack is the clearest example. No court ordered it closed. Apple and Google removed its apps; Amazon Web Services and Cloudflare dropped it. The site survived by moving to smaller providers. That was not a free market in rules. It was a market in dependencies.

This matters because the value of speech depends less on the right to send a message than on the ability to reach an audience. A platform can ban you and your words will still be true; your audience will not. The internet has made it easier to start an alternative venue, but it has also made audiences cluster. The largest social networks are not just places where people talk; they are where their contacts, memories, notifications, and habits already are. Leaving is possible, but expensive. When a user is banned from a mainstream platform, the rival platform may allow the speech, but it may be a room with no one in it. The libertarian claim assumes that users will follow the speech. Often they do not. They follow their friends, their job, their news, and their arguments. If those are on the big platform, the big platform sets the terms.

The strongest case for the libertarian story is that private alternatives keep speech alive even when mainstream platforms kill it. The same conspiracy theorists, militia leaders, election deniers, religious dissidents, and political radicals who are banned on one site appear on another. If a government had tried to ban the same speech, it would have faced legal process, constitutional limits in some countries, and the practical problem of identifying speakers. Private bans are quicker and cheaper. But the test was not whether speech survives; it is whether freedom is protected. A speech act that can only be heard by people who already believe it is not the same as one that can challenge the mainstream. When Twitter suspended tens of thousands of QAnon-linked accounts in 2020, the movement did not disappear. It moved. But its center of gravity shifted to places with smaller reach and less access to people outside the movement. That is a real loss of freedom, even if it is not total suppression.

The internet has also shown that platforms do not compete primarily on the quality of their speech rules. They compete for attention, convenience, and advertiser confidence. A permissive rulebook can attract users who want less friction, but it can also attract content that scares advertisers and regulators. The result is usually a middle path: enough openness to keep engagement high, enough restriction to keep brand risk low. This is not a market for liberty. It is a market for a product. The rules are features, and features are adjusted to make the product easier to sell. That is why mainstream platforms tend to converge. They may differ in tone, but they face similar pressures from card networks, app stores, insurance, legal liability, and the reputational cost of being the place where something awful happened. Competition can produce differences, but it does not necessarily produce a permanent niche for every kind of speech.

The libertarian argument also underestimates the role of government in shaping the private arena. In the United States, Section 230 shields platforms from most liability for user speech and encourages them to moderate without fear of being treated as publishers. That is a government policy, and it makes private gatekeeping safer. The European Union's Digital Services Act tries to regulate the same power. In both cases, the question is not whether government or private actors control speech, but how the legal environment divides the power. The internet is not a natural experiment in private self-governance. It is a political artifact. If the claim is that private competition protects freedom better than government regulation, the internet complicates the claim because the private order has been built on legal permissions that reduce the cost of exclusion.

There is a harder point here. In a country with a strong First Amendment, the government often cannot do to a private platform what the platform can do to a speaker. The state cannot simply order Twitter to ban a politician because the state dislikes the speech. Twitter can. That is the most damaging result of the internet test for the libertarian claim: private actors have acquired a censorship power that the state, at least in the United States, is constitutionally barred from exercising in the same way. The internet has not shown that private competition is a better check on power than government. It has shown that power can move from public institutions to private ones without the constitutional brakes that used to apply.

But the government is not an ideal comparator. In authoritarian systems, the state can and does shut down platforms, criminalize speech, and force local compliance. The internet there is a tool of control, not a test of libertarian competition. The interesting case is the liberal state, where the government is limited but private platforms are not. There, the internet has produced a strange hybrid: speech is legally free but practically gated. A person may have the right to speak without state interference and still be unable to be heard because the main channels are privately administered. That is not the old problem of state censorship. It is a new problem of distribution.

This distinction matters for unpopular speech. The internet protects speech that can form a community: a minority religion, a political subculture, a stigmatized profession, a local grievance, a fringe theory. If the group is small enough, it can sustain itself on alternative platforms. The internet is a refuge. But it protects less well speech that needs to cross into the general public: a political campaign, a journalistic investigation, a mass protest, a moral controversy, a challenge to a dominant narrative. For that speech, being absent from the largest platforms is not a minor inconvenience. It is a loss of the public square. The libertarian model works best where the unit is the community. It works worst where the unit is the audience.

There are cases where the private-market story looks better. Decentralized protocols like Mastodon and, later, Bluesky have shown that federated or alternative systems can attract users when a dominant platform feels politically compromised. After the acquisition of Twitter by Elon Musk, a significant number of users and institutions moved to other services. That was not a complete replication of Twitter, but it was enough to show that the social graph can be partially portable. If the architecture makes migration cheap, private competition can discipline platforms. The problem is that migration is still costly, and the biggest audiences remain sticky. The lesson is not that competition fails, but that it needs conditions: open standards, exportable accounts, redundant hosting, and limits on the chokepoints that make a platform indispensable.

The internet has therefore tested the libertarian idea, but it has not confirmed it as a general solution. It has confirmed a narrower truth: multiple private venues make total suppression harder. They make it possible for unpopular speech to exist, to organize, and to find its own people. They have saved speech from the kind of monopoly that a single state broadcaster or a single licensed newspaper might have produced. But they have not produced a durable market in which freedom of speech is the winning product. They have produced a market in which attention is the product, and freedom is one of the variables that affects its sale.

The practical consequence is that if the goal is to protect unpopular speech, the question should not be only whether a government censors it. It should be whether the infrastructure of communication is open enough that no single private owner can decide who is heard. The internet shows that private communities can preserve speech, but they cannot guarantee its relevance. The libertarian promise that competition will protect freedom is real where alternatives are viable. It is hollow where the public square has become a private plaza with a few entrances.

prompt: Write a post for software developers who have never thought about operations: what is it, how does your understanding of it tend to evolve, and how can an ordinary developer start getting better at it?
response:
**A developer’s first pass at operations**

If you have spent your time mostly inside the code, operations can feel like the unglamorous rest: servers, deploys, logs, dashboards, on-call. But for a running system, it is the part that decides whether your software behaves like a service or like a demo. A demo runs when you run it. A service has to run when no one is watching, when a machine dies, when traffic arrives in a burst, when a dependency changes, when a certificate expires, and when someone has to roll something back at 2 a.m.

I am not sure operations has one clean definition, because the tools keep moving. But the problem underneath is stable. A program is a set of instructions in a controlled environment. A production system is a set of processes, networks, data stores, queues, caches, DNS names, certificates, permissions, humans, vendors, and clocks. Operations is the practice of making that larger system do what you intended under uncertainty. It includes packaging, deployment, configuration, secrets, networking, storage, backups, monitoring, alerting, capacity, cost, incident response, and the unglamorous work of knowing what to do when something is not working.

The first misconception is that operations is separate from software. It is not. It is a different time scale. Code answers: what should this function do? Operations answers: what should the system do over hours, days, and months when assumptions fail? A function can be correct and still make the product bad if it takes 30 seconds on the slowest requests, if it retries in a way that doubles load during an outage, or if it writes a token to a log.

Another misconception is that if you use managed services, you do not need to think about operations. Managed services remove some work: patching, scaling, disk replacement. They do not remove the interface. You still choose regions, network boundaries, IAM roles, quotas, timeouts, data residency, version upgrades, export paths, billing limits, and failure semantics. A managed database is not “no database operations.” It is a database whose operator is a vendor, plus a customer who still has to understand failover, connection limits, slow queries, backups, and restore points. Serverless is not the absence of operations either. It pushes operations into event sources, permissions, concurrency, cold starts, payload sizes, timeouts, and the behavior of every function in the chain.

Understanding usually evolves in stages.

At first, operations is a place: the server, the deploy script, the dashboard. You learn that code in a repository is not a running thing. It needs a runtime, dependencies, environment variables, ports, permissions, and a way to restart. This stage is mostly surprise. You discover that your app works on macOS but not in the container, that the load balancer expects a health check, that the database connection pool fills up, that the “temporary” file is not temporary, or that the service cannot reach the internet from the subnet you put it in.

Next, operations becomes change safety. The central question is not “is it up?” but “can we change it without breaking it?” You start caring about deploy size, migrations, feature flags, configuration, rollback, and canaries. A small deploy is not a virtue because it is neat. It is a virtue because it limits the blast radius. If your release takes two hours and mixes a schema change, a config change, and a dependency upgrade, you have made debugging a historical investigation.

Then operations becomes behavior at scale. You stop asking only whether the service is up and start asking what users experience. Is p95 latency acceptable? Is the error budget being consumed? Is throughput bounded? Does the queue grow under normal peak? Does the cache evict in a way that hammers the database? Numbers matter here. If you serve 10,000 requests per minute and 1% fail, that is 100 failed requests per minute. If your SLO is 99.9%, you have about 43 minutes of downtime per month; if it is 99.99%, about 4 minutes. Those are not abstract. They decide how aggressively you can deploy, what you alert on, and whether a slow leak is an incident or a background tax.

Eventually operations becomes a social and cognitive system. Who knows what? Who is paged? What is the runbook? What do we fix now versus later? What do we automate because it is repeated? What do we delete because it is not worth maintaining? A system can be technically reliable and still fail operationally if the person on call has to reconstruct intent from Slack history, if every alert means nothing, or if the cheapest mitigation is to restart something no one understands.

The hardest objection is: if there are platform teams, SREs, and cloud consoles, why should an ordinary developer learn this? The answer is that platform reduces the surface, not the decisions. You will still choose query patterns, timeout values, retry semantics, state storage, cache invalidation, idempotency, and deploy boundaries. A platform can give you a queue, but it cannot tell you whether your consumer should acknowledge the message before or after writing to the database. It can give you a load balancer, but it cannot tell you whether your service should return 503 or 200 with stale data. Operations knowledge lets you make those choices deliberately instead of inheriting them.

It also changes how you write code. If you know a service will be restarted, you think about state. If you know logs will be searched by a human at 3 a.m., you write structured logs with request ids, user ids, and error codes. If you know a dependency can be slow, you add timeouts and backpressure. If you know a migration can fail, you make it reversible or staged. If you know a deploy can be rolled back, you avoid one-way changes unless you have a plan.

Take a simple endpoint that calls a payment provider. The function may be short, but the operational questions are not: what timeout is right? What happens if the provider times out after capturing money? Should a 429 be retried immediately? How do you tell a duplicate request from a new one? Those choices are made in code, but they only become visible under load or failure.

How do you start getting better? Do not begin by trying to master Kubernetes or build a monitoring empire. Begin by making one small service boring. Pick something you own or can influence, and answer a short list of questions in practice, not in your head: How is it started? Where does configuration come from? How are secrets stored? What happens when the process dies? What happens when a deploy fails halfway? How do I know it is broken before a user tells me? How do I roll it back? What data could be lost? What dependency is most likely to fail? Who is responsible when it does?

Then make the answers executable. A service that starts from a script in a README is less operable than one that starts from a repeatable, versioned command or image. A service whose config is hidden in code is harder to change than one that reads from environment variables or a config store. A service that logs “error” is harder to debug than one that logs the operation, identifier, duration, and error class. A deploy that can be undone is worth more than a deploy that is clever.

Add one user-visible metric and one operational metric. User-visible: success rate, latency, or throughput. Operational: queue depth, connection pool usage, disk space, certificate expiry, or error rate by route. You do not need many alerts. You need alerts that mean something: a human should be able to look at the page and take a first action. If every alert is “something is wrong,” the system will train people to ignore it.

Practice failure in a small way. Kill the process. Fill a temp directory. Point the app at a dead cache. Stop a dependent service. Make a DNS name unavailable for a minute in a dev environment. The goal is not to break production; it is to learn what the system tells you when it hurts. Many systems fail silently: they return 200 with empty data, they time out after 30 seconds, they queue forever, or they log a stack trace with no request context. You want to know that before a customer tells you.

Learn incidents as a discipline. When something breaks, the first job is usually mitigation, not root cause. Communicate what is known, what is not known, and what is being tried. If a rollback will restore users in five minutes, do it, then investigate why. A postmortem is useful only if it produces a change: a better alert, a smaller deploy, a timeout, a backup test, a runbook, a deletion. Without that, it is a confession.

Get better by noticing the seams. Every integration is a seam: DNS, API, database, message queue, CDN, certificate, auth provider, billing system, feature flag service. At each seam, ask what can fail and how the failure appears. A 401 from an identity provider is different from a timeout. A full disk is different from a locked file. A queue backlog is different from a poison message, a message that always fails and clogs the queue. Operations is mostly learning these differences well enough to act.

An ordinary developer does not need to become a full-time operator. But if you can look at your service and say, “I know how it starts, how it changes, how it fails, how I find out, and how I undo,” you already understand more operations than most code reviews test. That is not a credential. It is the difference between writing software and being responsible for software that lives.

A system can be technically reliable and still fail operationally if the person on call has to reconstruct intent from Slack history, if every alert means nothing, or if the cheapest mitigation is to restart something no one understands.

Paragraph 9: Hardest objection: If there are platform teams, SREs, and cloud consoles, why should an ordinary developer learn this? The answer is that platform reduces the surface, not the decisions. You will still choose query patterns, timeout values, retry semantics, state storage, cache invalidation, idempotency, and deploy boundaries. A platform can give you a queue, but it cannot tell you whether your consumer should ack before or after writing to the database. It can give you a load balancer, but it cannot tell you whether your service should return 503 or 200 with stale data. Operations knowledge lets you make those choices deliberately instead of inheriting them.

Paragraph 10: It also changes how you write code. If you know a service will be restarted, you think about state. If you know logs will be searched by a human at 3 a.m., you write structured logs with request ids, user ids, and error codes. If you know a dependency can be slow, you add timeouts and backpressure. If you know a migration can fail, you make it reversible or staged. If you know a deploy can be rolled back, you avoid one-way changes unless you have a plan. The code becomes easier to operate, not just easier to read.

Paragraph 11: How to start. Do not begin by trying to master Kubernetes or build a monitoring empire. Begin by making one small service boring. Pick something you own or can influence, and answer a short list of questions in practice, not in your head: How is it started? Where does configuration come from? How are secrets stored? What happens when the process dies? What happens when a deploy fails halfway? How do I know it is broken before a user tells me? How do I roll it back? What data could be lost? What dependency is most likely to fail? Who is responsible when it does?

Paragraph 12: Then make the answers executable. A service that starts with a script in a README is less operable than one that starts from a versioned image or a documented command. A service whose config is hidden in code is harder to change than one that reads from environment or a config store. A service that logs "error" is harder to debug than one that logs the operation, identifier, duration, and error class. A deploy that can be undone is worth more than a deploy that is clever.

Paragraph 13: Add one user-visible metric and one operational metric. User-visible: success rate, latency, or throughput. Operational: queue depth, connection pool usage, disk space, certificate expiry, or error rate by route. You do not need many alerts. You need alerts that mean something: a human should be able to look at the page and take a first action. If every alert is "something is wrong," the system will train people to ignore it.

Paragraph 14: Practice failure in a small way. Kill the process. Fill a temp directory. Point the app at a dead cache. Stop a dependent service. Make a DNS name unavailable for a minute in a dev environment. The goal is not to break production; it is to learn what the system tells you when it hurts. Many systems fail silently: they return 200 with empty data, they time out after 30 seconds, they queue forever, or they log a stack trace with no request context. You want to know that before a customer tells you.

Paragraph 15: Learn incidents as a discipline. When something breaks, the first job is usually mitigation, not root cause. Communicate what is known, what is not known, and what is being tried. If a rollback will restore users in five minutes, do it, then investigate why. A postmortem is useful only if it produces a change: a better alert, a smaller deploy, a timeout, a backup test, a runbook, a deletion. Without that, it is a confession.

Paragraph 16: Get better by noticing the seams. Every integration is a seam: DNS, API, database, message queue, CDN, certificate, auth provider, billing system, feature flag service. At each seam, ask what can fail and how the failure appears. A 401 from an identity provider is different from a timeout. A full disk is different from a locked file. A queue backlog is different from a poison message. Operations is mostly learning these differences well enough to act.

Paragraph 17: An ordinary developer does not need to become a full-time operator. But if you can look at your service and say, "I know how it starts, how it changes, how it fails, how I find out, and how I undo," you already understand more operations than most code reviews test. That is not a credential. It is the difference between writing software and being responsible for software that lives.
