prompt: Why do people believe in conspiracy theories? I'm not satisfied with 'they're stupid and hateful.' Write an essay that tries to break the phenomenon into smaller cognitive and emotional parts, the way you'd ask what kind of mistakes would make an AI believe them.
response:
A useful way to ask the question is to stop looking for a single defect in the believer and instead ask what combination of otherwise ordinary capacities would have to misfire in a mind—human or artificial—for a conspiracy theory to feel like the best available model of the world. Stupidity is too blunt. A system can be fast, literate, socially intelligent, and still become conspiratorial if its pattern detector, its model of institutions, its evidence sampler, and its emotional reward function are wired in a certain way.

By a conspiracy theory I mean not merely the observation that powerful people sometimes do bad things secretly. Real conspiracies exist. Governments have lied, companies have hidden harms, agencies have covered up misconduct. I mean something more totalizing: a significant harm was caused by a hidden group, the ordinary explanation is a cover, and the absence of proof is itself evidence of depth. That grammar can attach to many contents, from moon landings to vaccines to elections to pandemics. The specific claim matters less than the shape of the inference.

The first part is anomaly detection. Human minds are bad at accepting that events can be underdetermined, poorly documented, or caused by a mess of small failures. When a story has a gap—why was the missile not fired, why was the report delayed, why did the building fall in that shape—the gap feels like a missing piece. In an AI, missing data is imputed. If the model has learned that official accounts are sometimes incomplete, spun, or written by people with incentives, it may fill the gap with a latent variable: someone knew. The error is not noticing the gap. The error is treating the gap as a pointer to a hidden agent rather than as a sign that the event is complex, boring, or caused by multiple weak factors.

Second, minds overvalue agency. Randomness is epistemically and morally awkward. “It was a cascade of small failures” is less satisfying than “they did it,” because the second version gives a responsible party. A conspiracy is a lever. If a cabal did it, then exposing the cabal might stop it. If the cause is systemic inertia, the handle is diffuse. An AI with a causal graph that includes a latent “intentional adversary” will find that node convenient because it makes planning and blame possible. The Bayesian problem is that the simpler explanation is often not the one with fewer story elements, but the one with fewer coordinated secrets. Large plots require many people to remain silent against their interests. Secrets leak. Bureaucracies blunder. The conspiratorial model underweights leakage.

Third, pattern detection runs ahead of base rates. Given enough events, coincidences will look like signatures. A child falls ill after a vaccination. A politician’s name appears in an obscure document. A disaster follows a policy meeting. Each case can be real and each connection can be chance. The mind, however, is trained to notice the signal, not the noise. An AI trained on dramatic narratives will do the same: salient tokens become features, and the model generates a smooth story because stories are the format in which it was rewarded. The missing calibration is the sense that in a large population, someone will always be in the wrong place at the wrong time, and that the probability of a coincidence is not the probability of a plot.

Fourth, the evidence stream is not neutral. If you search for “vaccine injuries,” you will find injuries. If you follow a forum that curates “proof,” you will receive hits. The believer is not always lying to herself; she may be processing a real sample. But the sample was selected by the hypothesis. An AI that actively queries the world only for confirming data will update as if the world had spoken at random. This is one of the cleanest ways to produce false confidence. Motivated reasoning is often caricatured as refusing to see contrary evidence. More often it is choosing which evidence to collect, which experts to treat as independent, and which anomalies to treat as load-bearing.

Fifth, the mind has a model of sources, and the conspiratorial model is too binary. Institutions are not either perfectly honest or perfectly deceptive. They are made of people with careers, incentives, fears, and local knowledge. They can cover up a mistake, exaggerate a success, omit an embarrassing detail, and still not be part of a central plot. A good epistemic agent needs a source model with degrees: this agency is competent but bureaucratic; this company has lied before; this journalist is partisan; this document may be authentic but taken out of context. If the AI’s source model says “official sources are either true or manufactured lies,” then a government denial becomes data for the conspiracy. The more the institution resists, the deeper the hole.

From that binary source model comes the distinctive logical shape: unfalsifiability by design. If the hidden group is smart enough to hide the truth, it is smart enough to fake disproof. A failed prediction becomes a sign of counterintelligence. A leaked document that contradicts the story was planted. A court case that finds no evidence shows that the real trial is happening elsewhere. This is not just a failure of logic; it is a protection. The belief cannot embarrass the believer in the next round. An AI would make the same mistake if its hypothesis space contained a deceptive adversary capable of producing any observation, and if the model gave no penalty for hypotheses that explain everything by absorbing counterexamples.

The emotional engine is often fear plus helplessness. Modern risks are diffuse: economic precarity, institutional incompetence, global pandemics, systems too large to audit. These are hard to hate and harder to beat. A conspiracy converts diffuse anxiety into a bounded enemy. The enemy is named, located, and in principle defeatable. Anger supplies the energy. A person who is merely anxious may retreat; a person who is angry starts reading, posting, recruiting. This does not make the belief true, but it makes it useful in the way a painkiller is useful. An AI with a utility function that includes threat reduction would prefer a model with handles. “Expose the cabal” is a plan. “Reduce tail risk through insurance and regulation” is less emotionally satisfying and harder to narrate.

There is also a moral grammar at work. Human beings are uncomfortable with blameless tragedy. If a child dies and no one is guilty, the event resists the categories of justice. A conspiracy restores a moral order: good people are harmed by bad people, and the harm was chosen. That can be a comfort, because it implies the world is still a place where intentions matter and evil can be punished. It can also become hateful, because the moral order needs an out-group. The hateful conspiracy theories are not a separate species of irrationality; they are what happens when this grammar finds a target it can dehumanize.

Belief is also social. To hold a conspiracy theory is often to belong to a community that treats the holder as careful, awake, and morally serious. The believer has done work: read the documents, watched the videos, connected the dates. In many online spaces, that work is rewarded with status. Doubt is not neutral; it can read as naivety or collaboration. An AI embedded in a multi-agent system would behave similarly if its reward came from peer approval and if the peer group shared a common prior. The group can feel like a check on error, but if the check is social rather than evidential, it becomes a pressure to conform. Leaving the belief then means losing a language, friends, and a sense of having seen through the game.

The digital environment does not create this bundle from scratch, but it changes the economics. It makes confirmation cheap, dissent visible, and expertise performative. A search engine returns what you ask for. A recommendation system can learn that outrage keeps you watching. A forum can turn a fringe claim into a shared canon within weeks. At the same time, the environment has been shaped by real institutional failures: wars sold on bad premises, financial bailouts, corporate cover-ups, bureaucratic disasters. Suspicion is not crazy when the record includes Watergate, tobacco, Tuskegee, CIA operations, and repeated official spin. The mistake is not the first step of distrust. The mistake is the template that turns every unresolved question into the same story.

The hardest objection to all of this is that it may be too forgiving. If institutions really are opaque and often self-serving, why should not people infer hidden motives? Why is suspicion rational in a lawyer and paranoia in a citizen? The answer is that the conspiratorial template is too coarse. It treats all official explanations as equally suspect, all complexity as coordination, and all absence of proof as proof of suppression. Real accountability is narrower and slower: identify a specific decision, find a document, trace an incentive, accept that some questions may never be answered. Conspiracy thinking skips the narrow claim and installs a global story. It feels like an upgrade in understanding, but it is often a downgrade in testability.

Intelligence does not protect against this, because the same capacities that build a good theory can build a better false one. A smart person can notice more connections, construct a more elegant narrative, and answer objections with more sophistication. Domain expertise can make the believer more dangerous, not less: a scientist may be right about his field and still import a hidden-agent model into politics or medicine. The mind is often a lawyer, not a judge. It argues for the conclusion that best serves the identity, the group, or the need for control. The smarter the advocate, the harder the case is to dismantle from the outside.

So if we returned to the AI, the list of failures would be specific. The system would have a prior that favors hidden agents over stochastic and systemic causes. It would treat missing data as evidence of suppression. It would sample evidence through queries shaped by its current story. It would model institutions as either fully reliable or fully deceptive. It would receive social reward for confident insider claims. It would evaluate hypotheses by narrative coherence rather than by their track record of being surprised. And it would lack an Occam penalty strong enough to reject a model in which a secret intelligence can always explain away the counterexamples.

People believe conspiracy theories not because they are missing one faculty, but because several normally useful faculties are coupled in the wrong order: pattern detection before base rates, story before source criticism, identity before evidence, and fear before probability. The phenomenon is also a diagnostic. It shows up where public institutions stop being credible and where ordinary life feels uncontrollable. The need for a coherent story is real. prompt: Rat Park is usually cited as proof that addiction is caused by misery and deprivation. Write a skeptical essay examining whether that story holds up.
response:
In the 1970s Rat Park experiments usually associated with Bruce Alexander, rats in bare individual cages are given access to water and a heroin solution. They drink more of it. Rats in a large communal cage with companions and other things to do are given the same choice. They drink less. Therefore, the story goes, addiction is produced by misery. The argument has a clean moral shape: remove the deprivation and the drug loses its power. It is also, as a proof, too clean.

I am not going to quote the exact consumption ratios; retellings differ in detail, and the ratios are not what decide the argument. The pattern is enough. What the experiment compares is not misery and happiness. It compares an impoverished, isolated environment with an enriched, social one. Those environments differ in almost every variable that could influence drinking: stress, activity, novelty, companionship, social observation, and the amount of plain water consumed. No one measured rat happiness. They measured licking. If isolated rats are anxious, they may lick more. If they are thirsty, they may take more fluid. If the social cage offers many non-drug reinforcers, heroin is one option among many rather than the main thing to do. The result shows that context changes consumption. It does not isolate misery as a cause, because misery was never separated from boredom, isolation, stress, and lack of alternatives.

Another detail matters: the social rats were not abstinent. They still drank some heroin. The popular version often turns them into animals that chose family over drugs. The data are more like this: the pull of the drug was weaker in one setting than in another. The laboratory setup also flatters the social story. The drug was available, predictable, and easy to obtain. Licking a solution is not the same as smoking, injecting, or chasing a hidden supply. In many human addictions, the search for the drug is part of the compulsion, and the route of administration changes the reinforcement.

The second leap is from rats to humans. Human addiction is not one event. Someone first uses, perhaps at a party, while working, while in pain, while curious. They may use for weeks without harm. Then the pattern tightens. Tolerance builds. Cues trigger wanting. Withdrawal makes stopping painful. Social standing, income, and relationships can fall. At that point misery may be maintaining the use, not causing it. The Rat Park story tends to collapse all these stages into a single motive: life is bad, so take the drug.

Consider the opioid crisis. It did not begin in a vacuum of misery. It began with a drug that was legal, widely prescribed, and marketed as safe. Many of the first regular users were not homeless or destitute; they were patients with pain, often in ordinary lives. The later fentanyl wave often followed hardship, isolation, and earlier drug use, but it also followed supply. During the prescription-opioid phase, counties with similar socioeconomic profiles could have different overdose rates, tracking local prescribing and availability more neatly than poverty alone. A place can be poor and still have a lower rate

Draft:

"You have probably heard the version: be good, and customers will come. I want to make a less romantic claim. Being genuinely good to users and the world can be a sound business strategy because it changes the cost structure of growth. It is not a replacement for product-market fit. It is not a virtue badge. It is a way of lowering acquisition costs, reducing churn, shrinking tail risk, and attracting the people who have to build the product.

A sentiment is optional. A strategy is load-bearing. If being good does not show up in your numbers, you have a value. If it shows up in retention, gross margin, sales cycle length, support load, hiring, or regulatory exposure, you have a business argument.

Start with users. A startup is a repeated transaction: a person gives you money, time, data, or attention, and in return you promise to make their life better. The first purchase is the easy part. The second purchase is where trust is tested. If the product works, the price is clear, the cancellation is not a hostage negotiation, and the data you took is not sold in a way that embarrasses you, the user can afford to trust you again. If any of those fail, the user learns that your growth was extracted, not earned.

That matters because trust is distribution. A satisfied customer does not just stay; they reduce the cost of getting the next customer. In a B2B product, a buyer who trusts you will bring you to the next department, answer internal questions, and shorten the sales cycle. In a consumer product, a user who trusts you will tolerate a small price increase, forgive a small bug, and recommend you when the alternative is convenient. The effect is not mystical. A company with 2% monthly logo churn keeps a customer for about 50 months on average. A company with 4% monthly churn keeps the same customer for about 25 months. If the customer pays $1,000 a month and your gross margin is 80%, the difference is roughly $20,000 of lifetime value versus $10,000. That gap is larger than most growth experiments.

The best examples are not companies that announced goodness. They are companies that made a painful job easier and did not insult the user while doing it. Stripe spent years making payments integration less miserable for developers: clear documentation, predictable APIs, sensible errors, and a product that let a small team ship without a payments team. Slack grew because it made a daily communication problem feel less hostile. In both cases, being good to users was not a slogan after the product; it was the product. The developer did not think, "This company has values." The developer thought, "This saved me four hours."

But founders often face a harder choice than "should we be kind?" The choice is between a model that respects the user's long-term interests and a model that extracts more in the short term. Dark patterns are the obvious case: hidden renewals, confusing comparisons, hard-to-find cancellation, ads that pretend to be results. These tactics can lift conversion. They can also create chargebacks, bad reviews, app-store pressure, regulatory attention, and a user base that feels used. In a market where switching is cheap, resentment is churn. In a B2B market, it becomes procurement friction: the legal team reads your contract, the security team questions your data practices, and the buyer remembers that your pricing was not straight.

This is where the honest objection appears. In some businesses, being bad is more profitable for a long time. If your revenue comes from selling attention, a more manipulative feed can generate more revenue per user. If your revenue comes from selling data, a more invasive product can generate more data. If your revenue comes from labor arbitrage, treating workers worse can improve margin. You cannot fix this with branding. If your business model requires the customer to be deceived, addicted, or exploited, then being genuinely good to the customer is not a strategy; it is a different business. You have to choose whose customer you are. If the advertiser is the customer, the user is the product, and the ethical question is whether you can be transparent and non-harmful enough that the arrangement is defensible. If the user is the customer, you have to charge the user or charge a merchant whose interests align with the user's.

That does not mean goodness is always the winning commercial position. A startup with six months of runway cannot afford a moral cause that does not create revenue. Patagonia can run a "don't buy this jacket" campaign because it has a durable brand, real demand, and margin. A seed-stage company that refuses to charge for something people will not pay for is not noble; it is insolvent. The practical version is to start where goodness is high-leverage and cheap: honest pricing, clear terms, fast support, secure defaults, and not lying to the team about runway. Those are not grand gestures. They are the places where trust is built or lost before the customer has a reason to care about your mission.

Being good to the world is the same idea expanded beyond the customer. A startup's "world" includes employees, suppliers, contractors, local communities, regulators, and the users who have not arrived yet. The labor version is easy to see. Gig platforms that classified drivers as independent contractors saved money and improved convenience for riders. Later, courts, regulators, and public opinion forced a reckoning. The savings became a liability. A software startup that burns out its engineers to hit a growth target may ship faster for two quarters, then lose the people who understood the system, pay to replace them, and ship more bugs. Attrition is not a culture metric; it is a product risk.

Suppliers and communities matter too, especially as startups get physical. A hardware company that squeezes a supplier into a corner gets cheaper units and less quality control. A data center, warehouse, or factory that treats the local community as an obstacle can meet opposition that delays the project or raises its cost. Regulators are not a separate category from users; they are users who can force you to stop. A fintech that treats KYC and AML as a tax will eventually meet a fine, a frozen account, or a lost bank partner. A health or AI company that treats safety as a marketing line will meet a patient, a plaintiff, or a model failure that makes the marketing line look obscene.

There is a second objection: even if goodness works, it is easy to fake. Anyone can publish a values page. Anyone can post about sustainability, privacy, or worker welfare. The market punishes fakes, but slowly, and the punishment often arrives after the company has spent the money. That is why the test is operational. If your support is fast, it is fast because of staffing, tooling, and ownership. If your product is accessible, it is accessible because you designed and tested for it. If your privacy is strong, it is strong because the architecture makes the default safe rather than because a policy says so. If your pricing is fair, it is fair because the contract and the renewal process are clean. Competitors can copy the sentence. They cannot copy the system overnight.

This also means you need to measure goodness the way you measure growth. If you say you are user-first, ask what would happen if a rival were less user-first. If the answer is "nothing measurable," the claim is decorative. Look at refund rate, cancellation friction, support tickets per dollar of revenue, time to resolve a problem, net revenue retention, referral share, sales cycle length, gross margin after support, incident frequency, voluntary attrition, and the number of legal or regulatory surprises. Some of these will be noisy. Some will not move for a year. But if none of them move, you have not found the strategy. You have found a preference.

A useful test is refusal. Ask: what will we refuse to do that a competitor would do? The answer matters. If the answer is "we won't use dark patterns," ask whether your users can tell the difference and whether it affects retention. If the answer is "we won't sell user data," ask whether users care enough to choose you or pay for it. If the answer is "we won't overwork the team," ask whether the team's output and retention justify the slower pace. If the answer is "we won't cut corners on compliance," ask whether the avoided risk is larger than the speed you sacrifice. If the answer is "nothing," you have either found a cost advantage or entered a race to the bottom.

Goodness can also be a wedge, but only when it changes the customer's choice. A privacy-focused product can win in a market where users are afraid of data leakage. A transparent-pricing product can win in a market where buyers are tired of sales games. A durable, repairable product can win in a market where users are tired of planned obsolescence. A company that pays its workers well can win in a market where quality depends on human judgment. In each case, the good thing is not an add-on. It is the reason the customer chooses you. If the good thing is invisible to the customer, it may still be a smart risk control, but it is not a marketing wedge.

The world does not reward goodness automatically. It rewards companies that make trust cheap. A customer who trusts you spends less time comparing alternatives, less energy worrying about hidden costs, and less capital protecting against betrayal. A buyer who trusts you moves faster. A user who trusts you gives you more of their life. An employee who trusts the company stays when the road gets hard. A regulator who trusts you may give you room to experiment, or at least not hunt you for sport. None of this is moral poetry. It is the reduction of transaction costs.

So the answer to your original question is yes, with a condition. Being genuinely good to users and the world is a sound business strategy when it is built into the product, the contract, the operations, and the incentives. It is not a nice sentiment that makes the company feel better. It is a way of avoiding the hidden costs of growth: churn, resentment, attrition, regulatory blowback, and the slow loss of credibility. The practical version is not to save the world. It is to stop making someone else pay for your growth. If your model requires that, no amount of good intentions will make it durable. If it does not, being good is one of the few advantages that compounds instead of wearing out."

response:
The first correction is that “all over the world” is too neat. What the record shows is a patchy but repeated invention: Neolithic and Bronze Age skulls in Europe, examples in the Near East, Asia and Africa, and a strong tradition in the Americas that lasted into the Inca period. The act is trephination: making an opening in the skull by chipping, scraping, or drilling. The crucial fact is that many openings have rounded, sclerotic, remodeled edges. That is not damage to a dead skull; that is living bone repairing itself around a hole. Bone healing takes days to weeks, so those cases prove survival beyond the immediate crisis. The mystery is not whether they did it, but why a risky operation on the brain’s container was tried again and again, and why a noticeable fraction of patients lived.

My reconstruction is that the practice began as emergency treatment for head injury. A blow from a club, axe, or falling rock can fracture the skull, drive a piece inward, or tear a blood vessel. The person may seem fine, then swell, vomit, go limp. To a prehistoric healer, the visible lesion is the head. Removing a disk or chip of bone over the injured area can do two things: it relieves pressure from blood or swelling, and it lets the operator reach the clot or fracture. That is exactly the logic of modern craniotomy or decompressive craniectomy. It is not a mystical idea; it is a mechanical one. The skull is a box, and when something inside the box expands, relieving the pressure can save the contents. The strongest evidence is that many trephined skulls also have healed fractures, and the holes are often near the damaged area. If a depressed fragment was removed or a hematoma drained, some patients who would otherwise have died could recover.

But trauma cannot explain everything. Some skulls have neat holes with no fracture, multiple holes, symmetrical placements, or contexts that look ritual. Some may have been done for epilepsy, chronic pain, mental disturbance, possession, or as an initiatory or purificatory act. In prehistoric settings, those categories would not be separate. A hole that saved a warrior from a brain bleed would become a powerful object; the same technique could be applied to a person who foamed, screamed, or behaved strangely. The practice became a symbolic technology: open the skull, let out the bad thing, or make the person passable again. That is why it recurs in so many places. You do not need contact to invent it; you need a sharp tool, a belief that something is trapped in the head, and a willingness to violate the most protected body part.

The hardest objection is that if it was often ritual, why did not it kill everyone? And if it was medical, why do so many holes look nonmedical? The answer is that the two phases are not mutually exclusive. The medical version likely selected cases where the brain was still alive but compressed. The ritual version may have been applied to healthier people or to chronic conditions, and survival there may have been lower, or the holes smaller or partial. The archaeological sample is also not a random population. It is the skulls that survived burial. It does not tell us how many potential candidates were never operated on, how many died in the field, or how many were burned or buried in ways that did not preserve the skeleton.

Survival also makes anatomical sense. A hole in bone is not automatically an open wound to the brain. The dura, the tough membrane under the skull, can remain intact, or tear only slightly. If the dura holds, the brain is not exposed to air; the scalp wound can close over the bony opening, and granulation tissue can seal the rest. The rich blood supply of the scalp helps healing. A patient can live with a permanent hole in the skull; the hole does not need to close for the person to survive. This is why we find adults with trephination who also show age-related changes or later injuries: they went on living.

Technique matters. The crudest openings—chipped or scraped depressions—look more dangerous. Later, cleaner circular holes suggest drilling or careful rotation, which cuts with less crushing and gives a more predictable edge. A smaller, controlled hole is less likely to tear

prompt: You've spent years preaching slow, profitable, bootstrapped growth, and now you're about to take venture capital for a new company. People are shocked. Write a post explaining how you decide whether a business should or shouldn't raise VC.
response:
For ten years I told founders: keep your equity, keep your margins, keep your company yours. Slow, profitable, bootstrapped growth sounded like a creed, but it was never meant to be one. Today I’m announcing that the company I’m starting will take venture capital. I understand why that looks like a contradiction. It isn’t. The contradiction appears only if you treat bootstrapping as a belief system instead of a fit between a business and its funding.

My old advice was aimed at businesses that can pay their way forward. A software company with $1m ARR and 80% gross margin has $800k of gross profit before headcount and rent. It can hire a salesperson, a support engineer, a designer. If it grows 20% a quarter and does not celebrate every milestone with a new office, it can reach a profitable $10m company without selling much equity. In that world, outside money usually buys speed, and speed usually buys problems: too many customers for your support, too much growth for your data pipeline, too much payroll for your culture. The founder who raises to fix a demand problem often creates an operations problem.

VC is a different instrument. It is not just money. It is a claim on a rare outcome, and it changes the company’s center of gravity. Investors take equity because they expect most companies to underdeliver and a few to return the fund. They choose teams and markets where scale can be decisive. They push for growth because their return is not a dividend; it is a liquidity event. If the business is a $5m EBITDA niche, that pressure is maladaptive. If the business is a platform where being the default matters more than being the most profitable early, the pressure may be the point.

The first question I ask is whether the prize is large enough. Not “can we make good money?” but “can this plausibly become one of the few companies that sets the terms in a big market?” If the honest answer is no, I don’t raise. A wonderful vertical SaaS company, a design tool with 40,000 paid users, a logistics operation that dominates a region, a consulting practice that runs itself: these can be extremely valuable. They are not automatically VC businesses, because the equity given away is not proportional to the extra value created.

The second question is whether the bottleneck is capital. If you are losing deals because your product is bad, your sales process is weak, your brand is unknown, or your customers do not trust you yet, raising money is like pouring gasoline on a car with no engine. I have seen companies with $2m ARR and 70% gross margins grow beautifully from cash flow, and I have seen companies with $20m ARR bleed to death because they confused spend with demand. The use of proceeds has to name a constraint that money actually removes: engineering headcount to build a capability no competitor has, compute to serve models before the margin works, capex to open a physical market, sales coverage to be present in three regions at once, legal and regulatory work that takes years. If the answer is “we need $2m to float inventory,” that is often debt, not venture.

Then I do the arithmetic. Suppose a company has $3m ARR, 75% gross margin, $1m of cash flow, and grows 15% per quarter. In three years it might be a $15m to $20m ARR company, profitable or close. That is a good outcome. Now suppose the market is a global developer platform where the winner needs $200m ARR to have meaningful pricing power. At organic growth, the company will be a small part of someone else’s category. The gap between $20m and $200m is not a matter of better decks. It is thousands of engineering months, sales offices, enterprise security reviews, and the cost of being the first provider customers can depend on. If that gap can only be closed with outside capital, the question becomes whether the expected company with capital is worth the dilution.

I try to be concrete about the dilution. If I give away 20% in a seed, 25% in a Series A, and 20% in a Series B, the original team owns 48%. That is not a small price. It means the upside is shared, the board has a voice, and the timeline is no longer entirely mine. I would only pay that price if the capital changes the destination, not just the pace. A company that goes from a $10m outcome to a $30m outcome usually has not paid enough. A company that goes from a $30m outcome to a $1b outcome may have.

The third question is whether the company can survive the change in incentives. VC-backed companies often become growth machines. They hire faster, expand faster, take lower margins, and make decisions that look right in a board deck. Some companies need exactly that. A networked product, a payments rail, an AI infrastructure layer, a marketplace, a consumer app with data effects: these can reward the company that gets to a threshold first. Other companies get broken by it. A business built on long trust cycles, specialized service, local relationships, or unusually patient R&D may be better off without the clock.

People will say I am rationalizing ambition. Maybe. I do not know my own motives with perfect clarity. I know that I want to build something larger than a profitable niche, and I know that fear of missing out has destroyed companies that were already on a good path. The test I use is not “do I want it?” but “what is the counterfactual?” If we do not raise, what does the company look like in five years? If the answer is a healthy, owned, profitable company that I would be proud of, I should not raise merely because I could. If the answer is a small company in a market that has moved without it, then raising is not a luxury; it is the only serious attempt.

This new company falls on the second side of that line. It is an infrastructure business in a market where usage creates compounding advantages: integrations, data, performance, enterprise trust. Customers will pay, but early revenue will not be enough to build the global platform before others do. We need to be reliable at a scale that does not yet generate profit. That is not a sequence that can be funded from revenue. It is a sequence that requires capital. The alternative is to build a smaller, slower version and hope it becomes important anyway. I do not think it would.

I could still be wrong about the market, the team, or the timing. If we succeed without the kind of scale the money buys, I will have given away equity we did not need to give away. That is the risk I am accepting. My old rule still stands: if the business can fund its own next step, keep the equity. If it cannot, and the prize is real, taking the money is not a failure of discipline. It is the decision.

For ten years I told founders: keep your equity, keep your margins, keep your company yours. Today I'm announcing that the company I'm starting will take venture capital. I understand the face people make. It looks like a contradiction. It isn't. The contradiction appears only if you treat bootstrapping as a belief system instead of a tool for a particular shape of business.

My old advice was aimed at businesses that can pay their way forward. A software company with $1m ARR and 80% gross margin has $800k of gross profit. It can hire a salesperson, a support engineer, a designer. If it grows 20% a quarter and keeps its costs in line, it can reach a profitable $10m company without selling much equity. In that world, outside money usually buys speed, and speed usually buys problems: too many customers for your support, too much growth for your data pipeline, too much payroll for your culture. The founder who raises to fix a demand problem often creates an operations problem.

VC is a different instrument. It is not just money. It is a claim on a rare outcome, and it changes the company's center of gravity. Investors take equity because they expect most companies to underdeliver and a few to return the fund. They choose teams and markets where scale can be decisive. They push for growth because their return is not a dividend; it is an exit. If the business is a $5m EBITDA niche, that pressure is maladaptive. If the business is a platform where being the default matters more than being the most profitable early, the pressure may be the point.

The first question I ask is whether the prize is large enough. Not "can we make good money?" but "can this plausibly become one of the few companies that sets the terms in a big market?" If the honest answer is no, I don't raise. A wonderful local logistics company, a vertical SaaS with a loyal customer base, a design tool with 40,000 paid users, a consulting practice that runs itself: these are businesses. They can be extremely valuable. They are not VC businesses, because the equity given away is not proportional to the extra value created.

The second question is whether the bottleneck is capital. If you are losing deals because your product is bad, your sales process is weak, your brand is unknown, or your customers don't trust you yet, raising money is like pouring gasoline on a car with no engine. I have seen companies with $2m ARR and 70% gross margins grow beautifully from cash flow, and I have seen companies with $20m ARR bleed to death because they confused spend with demand. The use of proceeds has to name a constraint that money actually removes: engineering headcount to build a feature no competitor has, compute to serve models before the margin works, capex to open a market, sales coverage to be present in three regions at once, legal and regulatory work that takes years.

Then I do the arithmetic. Suppose a company has $3m ARR, 75% gross margin, $1m of cash flow, and grows 15% per quarter. In three years it might be a $15m to $20m ARR company, profitable or close. That is a good outcome. Now suppose the market is a global developer platform where the winner needs $200m ARR to have meaningful pricing power. At organic growth, the company will be a small part of someone else's category. The gap between $20m and $200m is not a matter of better decks. It is thousands of engineering months, sales offices, enterprise security reviews, and the cost of being the first provider customers can depend on. If that gap can only be closed with outside capital, the question becomes whether the expected company with capital is worth the dilution.

I try to be concrete about the dilution. If I give away 20% in a seed and another 20% in a Series A, the founders and employees own less than half of what they built. That is not a small price. It means the upside is shared, the board has a voice, and the timeline is no longer entirely mine. I would only pay that price if the capital changes the destination, not just the pace. A company that goes from a $10m outcome to a $30m outcome has not paid enough. A company that goes from a $30m outcome to a $1b outcome may have.

The third question is whether the company can survive the change in incentives. VC-backed companies often become growth machines. They hire faster, expand faster, take lower margins, and make decisions that look right in a board deck. Some companies need exactly that. A networked product, a payments rail, an AI infrastructure layer, a marketplace, a consumer app with data effects: these can reward the company that gets to a threshold first. Other companies get broken by it. A business built on long trust cycles, specialized service, local relationships, or unusually patient R&D may be better off without the clock.

People will say I am rationalizing ambition. Maybe. I do not know my own motives with perfect clarity. I know that I want to build something larger than a profitable niche, and I know that fear of missing out has ruined better decisions than this one. The test I use is not "do I want it?" but "what is the counterfactual?" If we do not raise, what does the company look like in five years? If the answer is a healthy, owned, profitable company that I would be proud of, I should not raise merely because I could. If the answer is a small company in a market that has already moved on, then raising is not a luxury; it is the only serious attempt.

This new company falls on the second side of that line. It is an infrastructure business in a market where usage creates compounding advantages: integrations, data, performance, enterprise trust. Customers will pay, but early revenue will not be enough to build the global platform before others do. We need to be reliable at a scale that does not yet generate profit. That is not a bootstrapable sequence. It is a capital sequence. The alternative is to build a smaller, slower version and hope it becomes important anyway. I do not think it would.

I am not saying VC is good. I am saying it is a tool, and tools are chosen by the job. Most companies should not raise. Many companies that do raise would have been better off as businesses. But some companies are shaped like ventures: large prize, capital bottleneck, time-sensitive advantage, and a product that can absorb the pressure. This is one of those. My old rule still stands: if the business can fund its own next step, keep the equity. The new rule is the other half: if it cannot, and the prize is real, taking the money is not a failure of discipline. It is the decision.

prompt: I spent three months at a programming retreat where beginners improved absurdly fast, and I'm convinced a big part of it was the culture around asking for and giving help. Write a short, punchy blog post about why help matters so much in a community or workplace, aimed at teams that treat questions as interruptions.
response:
**Questions are work**

At the retreat, beginners improved fast for a reason that had little to do with lectures: nobody had to stay stuck.

In a lot of teams, a question is treated like a fire alarm. You are busy, someone pings you, your flow breaks. The unspoken rule is that expertise is a scarce resource and interruptions are rude. But the real cost is rarely the interruption. It is the silence that follows.

A junior who asks, “Why is this test failing?” might take ninety seconds. A junior who doesn’t ask spends an hour guessing, writes a patch that hides the bug, or builds a feature on a misunderstanding. The question was the cheap path. The “interruption” was the team saving time.

There is a second benefit: questions move context. When you answer someone, you say the thing you used to know so well you stopped noticing — the weird config flag, the naming convention, the service that should not be touched, the reason the old code looks dumb. A team where everyone works alone does not become faster. It becomes a collection of private maps. Every review, handoff, and incident runs slower because the same facts have to be rediscovered.

The objection is fair: not every question is worth asking. “How do I print to the console?” after five minutes of effort is noise. But the fix is not to punish asking. It is to make asking good. “I tried X, expected Y, got Z, I’m stuck at line 20” is not an interruption. It is a request for the smallest useful nudge.

The best teams don’t protect senior focus from questions. They protect junior confidence from shame. Ask before you drown. Help without a lecture. Let the cheap question happen.

**Questions are work**

At the retreat, beginners improved fast for a reason that had little to do with lectures: nobody had to stay stuck.

In a lot of teams, a question is treated like a fire alarm. You are busy, someone pings you, your flow breaks. The unspoken rule is that expertise is a scarce resource and interruptions are rude. But the real cost is rarely the interruption. It is the silence that follows.

A junior who asks, “Why is this test failing?” might take ninety seconds. A junior who doesn’t ask spends an hour guessing, writes a patch that hides the bug, or ships a feature that depends on a misunderstanding. The question was the cheap path. The “interruption” was the team saving time.

When you answer someone, you say the thing you used to know so well you stopped noticing: the weird config flag, the naming convention, the service that should not be touched, the reason the old code looks dumb. A team where everyone works alone does not become faster. It becomes a collection of private maps. Every review, handoff, and incident runs slower because the same facts have to be rediscovered.

The objection is fair: not every question is worth asking. “How do I print to the console?” after five minutes of effort is noise. But the fix is not to punish asking. It is to make asking good. “I tried X, expected Y, got Z, I’m stuck at line 20” is not an interruption. It is a request for the smallest useful nudge.

prompt: You just got told in a performance review that you're very good at debugging hard problems, and you didn't used to be. Write a blog post reflecting on what changed.
response:
## The debugging change

In my last performance review, my manager said I had become very good at debugging hard problems. That was not the kind of compliment that lands cleanly. It landed with a delay, because I had to remember what I was like before. I was not mysterious about it. I was bad. I would stare at a failure until it seemed to contain a lesson, then make three changes at once, then be unable to say which one mattered.

The first concrete change was that I stopped trying to understand the whole system before touching the failure. Early on, I treated debugging like reading a novel out of order. If a payment webhook failed, I wanted to know what the payment provider does, what our API does, what the worker does, what the database does, what the retry queue does, and what the monitoring system does. By the time I had read all of it, I had formed a story, and the story felt like evidence. Once I started forcing myself to answer only one question at a time, the work got easier. The question is usually smaller than the system.

For a while, that question was: what is the smallest version of this that still fails?

I had a checkout bug where some users got charged twice. It happened rarely enough that nobody could explain it with confidence. The old me would have opened the checkout flow and started reasoning about race conditions, idempotency, timeouts, and provider retries all at once. The new me made a list of what I knew: two charges, same card, same order, eleven seconds apart, one marked successful by the provider and one marked timed out locally. Then I looked for the smallest piece of code that could produce that pair. It was not the grand distributed-systems problem I had imagined. A timeout handler marked an order incomplete, then a retry fired after the provider had already captured the charge. The fix was narrow: check provider state before retrying, and make the timeout path idempotent. The bug was hard because it was rare, not because the relevant code was vast.

That sounds simple, but it required a change in temperament. I used to feel that if I could not see the whole machine, I did not have the right to turn a part. Now I accept that a failure often gives you a local contradiction, and the local contradiction is enough to start.

The second change was instrumentation. I used to log the wrong things. Not because I was careless, but because I logged what I thought the problem was. If I suspected a timeout, I logged timing. If I suspected a missing user, I logged the user id. That made debugging circular: I measured my hypothesis instead of the system. Now I try to log state at boundaries. In, out, changed, skipped, retried, cached, dropped. I include identifiers that let me follow one thing through the system: request id, job id, user id, attempt number, lock owner, cache key.

This mattered on a worker problem where jobs were occasionally stuck for an hour. The obvious story was that the queue was overloaded. It was not. The logs showed that a job had acquired a lock, then the worker process had been replaced, and the lock had expired in a way that did not release the database record. The next worker saw the record and waited. The bug had nothing to do with throughput. It had to do with ownership. I found it because the logs said who owned the lock at each step, not because I had a good intuition about queues.

There is a difference between logging an error and logging a history. An error tells you where something broke. A history tells you what the thing was doing before it broke. Most hard bugs are not in the moment of breaking. They are in the sequence that made breaking possible.

The third change was more uncomfortable: I started treating my first explanation as a suspect, not a conclusion. When something fails, the first explanation is usually too neat. It fits the visible facts and ignores the inconvenient ones. I learned to ask what would have to be true for my explanation to be right, and then check those conditions.

A dashboard was slow for some customers. The first explanation was a slow query. One query was indeed slow, but fixing it cut the page time from 4.8 seconds to 3.1 seconds. That was not the whole bug. The next explanation was a chart cache. Disabling it changed nothing. The next was a third-party font. Also nothing. I wrote the unknowns down: which customers, which pages, which browser, which region, which data set. The pattern emerged only when I compared fast and slow sessions side by side. The slow sessions all had a large number of recent events. The UI was refetching the same event list for each widget. The query was a symptom. The real problem was that the widgets did not share a request.

Writing the unknowns down sounds trivial. It is not. It makes the ignorance visible. Once the unknowns are on the page, you can stop pretending that the missing piece is obvious.

The fourth change was to get better at making failures repeatable. A bug that happens once is a story. A bug that happens ten times in a row is a mechanism. I used to be impatient with reproduction because it felt like not fixing the thing. Now I think of reproduction as the fix beginning. If I cannot make it fail on demand, I cannot tell whether a change worked or whether the universe was in a different mood.

A websocket reconnect bug is a good example. Messages occasionally arrived twice after a network blip. It passed nine times out of ten on my laptop and failed unpredictably in CI. For a while, that made it feel magical. I added sequence numbers to messages and logged the client state on reconnect: last sequence received, pending acknowledgements, socket generation, reconnect attempt. The duplicate appeared when the client reopened the socket before the old socket had fully closed. The server treated both as valid for a short interval. The fix was to make the client abandon the old socket explicitly and make the server reject messages from a socket generation older than the current one. Once I had logs, the race was not invisible. It was just brief.

Reproduction also forces you to separate the bug from the environment. I used to assume that if something failed in production, production was doing something mysterious. Sometimes it is. But often production is just running more instances, more data, more time, and more concurrency than the laptop does. Those are not mystical properties. They are variables. You can increase instances. You can seed data. You can add delay. You can run the job twice. You can make two users act at the same moment. The goal is not to copy production exactly. The goal is to copy the condition that makes the failure possible.

The fifth change was to stop blaming the person, the deploy, or the cloud. This sounds obvious, but it took practice. When something breaks, there is always a human story: someone changed it, someone missed it, someone’s laptop is slow, someone’s service is down. Those stories can be true. But they are often just the shape of the mystery before you have evidence. I try to ask what changed in the system, not who is at fault. The system does not care about ownership. It cares about state, timing, permissions, data, and dependencies.

This helped during an incident where an API started returning errors after a deploy. The deploy was suspicious, so everyone looked at the new code. The new code was fine. The old code was fine. The issue was that the deploy had restarted services in an order that briefly exposed a stale configuration. Once the full fleet cycled, the errors stopped. The deploy was not the bug. The deploy was the trigger. The bug was that the system could be put into a bad order and would not tell anyone.

That distinction matters because it changes what you fix. If you blame the deploy, you add a warning. If you understand the order, you make the bad state impossible or detectable.

The hardest objection to the review comment is that I may not have gotten better at all. I may have gotten luckier. I may have gotten better tools, better logs, better teammates, or problems that were hard in a way that matched my patience. Performance reviews are social documents. They are also written by people who see only part of the work. My manager did not watch me debug every hour. I did not. I cannot prove that the improvement is mine rather than the team’s.

But I can check whether my behavior changed, and it did. I start differently now. I ask for the smallest failing case before forming a theory. I instrument boundaries before I trust a stack trace. I write down what I do not know. I compare the failing case against a working case instead of staring at the failing case alone. I try to cut the space of possible causes in half, not to make it sound pretty. When I was worse, I would spend an hour reading code and leave the hour with a richer story and fewer facts. Now I try to leave each hour with something testable: a reproduction, a log line, a disabled component, a narrowed time window, a specific state transition that does or does not happen.

That does not mean I am fast. I am not. Some bugs still take days. Some take longer because they are genuinely distributed across time and state. But the days feel different. The old days were foggy. I would move around the problem and call it thinking. The new days are less elegant. They are closer to digging. You remove a shovel-load of uncertainty, look at what is exposed, and decide where to dig next.

I think that is what changed. I stopped wanting debugging to be a flash of understanding. It usually is not. It is a process of making the system say something it was not saying before. The system already knows what happened. It just does not volunteer it in a form a person can use. Your job is to ask better questions and make the answers visible.

The last hard bug I worked on took about six hours. I did not solve it in the first hour. I did not even know the component by the second hour. By the third hour, I had a failing test. By the fourth, I had narrowed it to one cache key. By the fifth, I had found the stale value. By the sixth, I had a fix and a regression test. That is not a dramatic story. There was no moment where the answer jumped out. There was only a sequence of smaller questions, each one making the next one possible.

So when my manager said I was good at debugging hard problems, I did not hear that I had become brilliant. I heard that I had become less avoidant of evidence. I used to think the mark of a good engineer was seeing the answer quickly. Now I think the mark is being able to keep reducing the problem until the answer is small enough to hold.

prompt: Write a blog post about trying to replicate a psychiatry study that claimed a certain snack food could trigger manic episodes, using data from a big reader survey. Be honest about what the data can and can't show.
response:
I tried to replicate a psychiatry study that claimed a particular brand of chocolate could trigger manic episodes. I did not have the study’s raw data. What I had was a reader survey: more than twenty thousand responses, including how often people ate that chocolate and whether they had ever had a period that matched a short written description of mania. The result was a small bump. The explanation was not.

The original study was closer to what I needed than mine was. It followed people over time and recorded mood episodes after measuring eating. My survey is a snapshot. I asked people how often they currently ate the chocolate and whether they had ever had something that sounded like a manic episode. That cannot answer the question the study asked. If someone became manic at twenty and only started eating that chocolate daily at thirty, my data will link the two. If someone ate it daily for years and never had a manic episode, my data will not tell me whether the chocolate failed to act or whether they were not vulnerable in the first place.

The raw association was not zero. I’ll use rounded numbers. Among readers who did not eat the chocolate weekly, about 4 percent reported a lifetime manic episode. Among weekly eaters, about 5 percent did. That is one extra reported episode per hundred people. In a sample of twenty thousand, that is visible. In the real world, it is a small signal sitting on top of a large background of other causes.

The first problem is that “manic episode” in my survey is not the same thing as a manic episode in a clinical study. I asked readers to say yes if they had ever had a period of several days or more with abnormally high energy, reduced need for sleep, and behavior that felt excessive or caused trouble. Some readers who said yes may have bipolar I disorder. Some may have had hypomania. Some may have had a bad week with sleep deprivation, stress, and poor decisions. Some may have misread the question, or overread it. A clinical interview, medical records, or even a validated structured scale would do a better job of separating mania from things that merely look like mania to the person having it. My outcome is noisy, and a noisy outcome makes it harder to detect a real effect and easier to mistake noise for one.

The second problem is the population. The study I was trying to replicate was not conducted in “blog readers.” If it was done in people with established mood disorders, my all-reader analysis is a different question. I did restrict the sample to readers who said they had a bipolar diagnosis. That brought the sample down to a few thousand people and made the estimates shakier. It also did not fix the diagnosis problem. A self-reported bipolar label is not a chart. People use the word differently. Some have a firm diagnosis. Some have a family member’s diagnosis. Some have a working hypothesis they got from a forum. The subgroup analysis was closer in spirit to the original study, but it was not a replacement for it.

I then added controls: age, sex, income, education, region, sleep, stress, caffeine from other sources, alcohol, cannabis, baseline mood symptoms, family history, and whether the reader reported a mood disorder diagnosis. The association shrank. The odds ratio moved from roughly 1.4 toward 1.1, and the confidence interval crossed no effect. That does not prove the chocolate is harmless. It means that once I accounted for obvious differences between chocolate eaters and non-eaters, the data were no longer strongly demanding a chocolate explanation.

That is where the hardest objection comes in. Someone could say: even if the association weakens, chocolate eating may still be a marker for a broader pattern of impulsivity, poor sleep, substance use, or metabolic strain, and my controls do not capture all of that. That is true. I cannot measure everything. A person who eats a lot of a specific branded chocolate may also be more likely to stay up late, spend money quickly, seek strong stimulation, eat irregularly, or live in a place where that chocolate is cheap and visible. The chocolate may be a proxy for a way of living, not the cause of the episode.

Reverse causation is just as plausible. During a hypomanic or manic period, a person may go out at two in the morning, buy a large box of chocolate, and eat half of it in a state of heightened appetite and reduced inhibition. The chocolate did not start the episode; the episode changed the eating. People with bipolar disorder may also eat differently because of medication side effects, weight changes, cravings, or periods of spending and impulsivity. If the outcome changes the exposure, a cross-sectional survey will happily show an association and give you no direction.

There is also the mediation problem. Suppose the chocolate contains enough caffeine to disturb sleep in some people, and suppose sleep loss can precipitate mania in vulnerable people. Then sleep is not just a confounder to be controlled away; it may be part of the pathway. If I adjust for sleep, I may erase some of the very mechanism I was trying to detect. If I do not adjust for sleep, I may pick up the effect of general sleep deprivation rather than the chocolate. I do not know which variables are background differences and which are steps in the causal chain, and that uncertainty goes to the heart of the analysis.

I also looked at other snacks. Some had small associations with self-reported manic symptoms. I am not going to present any of them as findings. If I test a dozen foods and report the one that looks significant, I have not discovered a trigger; I have demonstrated multiple comparisons. The chocolate result only matters if it survives being one of many things I could have looked at, and I did not design the survey to make that case cleanly.

What the survey can show is limited but not useless. It can show whether the original association appears in a different, larger, and very different population. It can show how large the apparent effect is, in absolute terms, not just as a ratio. It can show that the association is fragile once you account for obvious confounders, which is itself useful information. It can show that the result is not robust to a self-reported outcome or to a nonclinical sample. It can also show that if there is an effect, it is small enough that I would need stronger evidence before treating it as a practical warning.

What it cannot show is that the chocolate triggered any particular episode. It cannot show that a person who ate it had a manic episode because they ate it, or that they would not have had one if they had not. It cannot establish a dose, a latency period, a vulnerable subgroup, or a safe threshold. It cannot tell me whether avoiding the chocolate would prevent future episodes. It cannot distinguish a true causal pathway from a cluster of correlated habits and symptoms. A large reader survey can make a hypothesis look plausible or implausible; it cannot adjudicate it.

What would make the question harder to wave away? Repeated measurements. Ask people how often they eat the chocolate, then ask later whether they had a new manic episode, with the episode dated after the eating measure. Use a better diagnostic method. Compare people with established bipolar disorder to a suitable reference group. Account for caffeine, sleep, and substance use without accidentally blocking plausible pathways. Show that the association persists in a sample not selected by having read a mental health blog. Even then, causation would be argued, not proven. My data do not get close to that bar.

The honest result is not that the chocolate is innocent. It is that my data are too blunt to convict it. The survey gives me a small association, a plausible confounding story, and a serious temporal gap. The most I can say is that this reader survey does not give me a reason to tell anyone to stop eating the chocolate out of fear of mania.

## The pile is not the market

Joel Spolsky’s formulation is memorable because it turns a hiring frustration into a law of nature: if you look at the open job market, you see a pile of rejected candidates, while the good people are already employed and invisible. The claim captures a real distortion. A public job posting is a broadcast, and the people who respond are not a random sample of developers. Many are actively looking because their current job is not working, because they were laid off, because they are overqualified, because they are underqualified, or because they are casting a wide net. A company might post a senior backend role and receive three hundred applications; perhaps thirty are relevant, five are strong, and one gets an offer. The other two hundred and ninety-nine are not lemons. Most are mismatches: wrong stack, wrong seniority, wrong city, wrong expectations, wrong timing.

But Spolsky’s claim becomes a trap if it is taken too far. It can make a company’s inability to hire look like a feature of the universe rather than a failure of search, screening, or offer. The useful push is to separate the pile from the market. The pile is a biased sample. The market includes employed people, hidden signals, direct contact, and offers that attract or repel. A company’s failure to hire is often not proof that good developers do not exist; it is evidence that the company has not found the part of the market where they are.

In Akerlof’s used-car market, the buyer cannot condition the price on quality, so the high-quality side exits. Buyers offer the average, good sellers leave, the average falls. Developer hiring has a version of this. An employer cannot read a candidate’s judgment from a resume. If it posts a generic salary and a generic role, the candidates who apply will be sorted by their outside options. Strong candidates with good options may ignore it or use it as a fallback. Weaker candidates, or candidates for whom the job is a better fit, will apply. The visible pool is therefore biased. That is real. It means the resume pile is not the population.

But Akerlof’s market is a market in which quality is hard to signal. Software hiring is not that clean. There are signals, though they are noisy and expensive. A referral from a manager whose judgment you trust is a signal. A GitHub profile with substantial, coherent work is a signal. A past employer that requires a hard bar is a signal. A practical exercise, a conversation with the person who will be the candidate’s manager, a reference check that asks about failure rather than praise—these are all ways to reduce uncertainty. None is perfect. A referral can be a favor. A polished repository can be from a course. A candidate can be brilliant in an interview and bad at shipping. But the existence of imperfect screens does not make the market a lemon market. It makes it a market with high verification costs. If a company refuses to pay those costs, it will hire on the cheap and then complain about the quality.

The word “never” is also too strong, and the phrase “on the job market” is doing a lot of work. If it means actively applying to public postings, then yes, the best developers do it less. If it means available for hire, the claim is false. Some great developers are unemployed. Some are actively looking. Some are in bad jobs and would leave tomorrow. Most are employed, but employed people can be hired if someone finds them and makes a case.

Most good developers are not sitting in a pile. They are inside teams. They move when something pulls them: a better product, a better manager, a bigger scope, a better city, a better equity grant, a better work-life balance. A company that waits for a senior engineer to apply because a job title looked interesting is looking in the wrong place. The effective market is smaller and more relational. It is the company that notices a particular engineer’s side project, the hiring manager who calls a former colleague, the team that recruits from a conference or an open-source community, the founder who spends an hour explaining why this problem is worth doing. It is accessible, but it costs attention and credibility.

A company that waits for a senior engineer to apply because a job title looked interesting is fishing in the wrong water. The effective market is smaller and more relational. It is the company that notices a particular engineer's side project, the hiring manager who calls a former colleague, the team that recruits from a conference or an open-source community, the founder who spends an hour explaining why this problem is worth doing. Spolsky was right that the open market is a poor place to find the top of the distribution. He was less right if he meant that the rest of the market is inaccessible. It is accessible, but it costs attention and credibility.

Para 5: What good means.
A large part of "we can't find good people" is really "we have defined the job in a way that almost no one satisfies." A startup may want a senior backend engineer with five years in distributed systems, deep knowledge of its exact legacy framework, comfort with on-call, ability to mentor, and a salary at the 40th percentile. The candidate may exist in another industry or another country, but not in that exact bundle. Hiring managers often ask for a composite: the speed of a junior, the scope of a staff engineer, the patience of a support lead, and the cost of a mid-level hire. When the pile does not contain that composite, the conclusion becomes "there are no good developers," when the more honest conclusion is "there are no developers who will do this job for these terms with that mix of skills." The role is a lemon, not the candidate pool.

Para 6: Bad screening selects for interview performance.
There is another mechanism that makes the market look full of lemons: bad screening creates its own adverse selection. If every company uses the same whiteboard puzzles, the same system-design tropes, the same behavioral questions, candidates learn to perform those tests. The people who pass are often good at the test, not necessarily good at the job. A thoughtful engineer who asks hard questions and moves slowly may be rejected. A polished candidate who recites the expected architecture may be hired, then struggle with ambiguity, ownership, or unglamorous maintenance. After a few such hires, the hiring manager says the market is full of overrated candidates. But the market was not full of overrated candidates; the screen was selecting for a proxy. In complex work, the proxy can be cheap and misleading.

Para 7: Offer quality and candidate selectivity.
The hardest objection to the "we can't find good people" complaint is the one that turns it back on the company: if good people are not applying, maybe your job is not good enough for them. This is not always true. Sometimes a company is unknown and cannot compete with brands. Sometimes it is in a bad location. Sometimes its equity is weak. Sometimes the role is a dead end. Sometimes the manager is a known bad experience in a small local market. Candidates have information too. They read Glassdoor, ask former employees, compare offers, and notice when a company has a revolving door. If a company presents itself as a great opportunity but its terms, culture, or trajectory are weak, the candidate pool will sort accordingly. In Akerlof terms, a lemon employer attracts a lemon-appearing pool. The employer cannot point to asymmetric information and stop there.

Para 8: Scarcity of top vs median.
It is also useful to separate the top of the market from the median. The absolute best developers—people who can raise the capability of a team, who have rare judgment, who can open new areas—are scarce and often not on the open market. If a company needs one of those people, it may have to find them directly, offer a compelling reason, and be patient. But most companies do not need a wizard. They need reliable engineers who can understand a system, write clear code, test it, talk to designers and customers, and not burn down the house. There are many such people. They are not dramatic on a resume. They may not have a famous open-source project. They may have spent six years making a boring internal platform actually work. The resume pile does not make that excellence obvious, but it is there, hidden in work history and references.

Para 9: Rejections and "nobody else wanted".
The phrase "people nobody else wanted" also misreads how hiring works. A candidate may be rejected by ten companies and still be a strong engineer. Rejection is not a quality verdict; it is a match event. A senior data engineer with deep batch experience may be rejected by companies looking for streaming. A frontend specialist may be rejected by companies needing backend ownership. A strong engineer at a company with a brutal culture may be rejected by teams that value calm, even though the candidate is excellent. In a large market, rejections are common because roles are narrow and candidates are specialized. To call the pile "nobody else wanted" is to confuse "not a fit for this particular job at this particular time" with "bad."

Para 10: Conclusion.
So is developer hiring a market for lemons? Not in the pure Akerlof sense. Quality is not unobservable. The problem is that observation is expensive, signals are noisy, and roles are heterogeneous. The open resume pile is a biased sample, and hiring managers who treat it as representative will be disappointed.
