prompt: Congressional voting data gets turned into a left-right scale without anyone telling the algorithm what left and right are. Could something like that work for morality? Write an essay exploring whether you could discover what 'good' means statistically from ordinary life decisions.
response:
The congressional trick is not that a computer understands politics. It is that votes are numerous, repeated, and pulled by a few large forces. A member may vote on taxes, courts, military spending, foreign aid, and local projects. Most of those votes are not independent. They move together because they are caused by shared interests, party discipline, constituency pressure, and a small number of organizing issues. A low-dimensional model can exploit that redundancy. It does not need to know that one pole is liberal. It only needs the votes to contain a dominant direction of disagreement. Humans then look at the extreme positions and name the direction.

That is the part worth separating. The algorithm discovers structure. The naming is interpretive. If we fed it votes from a single-issue legislature, the axis might be “how much to spend on lighthouses.” If we fed it a body divided mainly by region, the axis might be region. The scale is not a political truth; it is a compression that happens to line up with our prior categories.

Could morality do the same? The tempting answer is yes. People make moral decisions all the time. They lie or tell the truth, keep or break promises, punish or forgive, help or ignore, share or hoard. If those decisions are generated by underlying values, maybe a model can recover the values. We could collect millions of ordinary choices and ask what latent variables best explain them. Perhaps we would find a “goodness” coordinate.

But the first obstacle is that ordinary decisions are not clean moral samples. Most choices are not primarily moral. Choosing a restaurant reveals taste, convenience, hunger, and price sensitivity. Choosing a job reveals ambition, risk tolerance, and local labor markets. Choosing whom to be friends with reveals proximity, shared interests, and identity. All of these can have moral traces, but the trace is thin. If we feed the model everything people do, it will mostly learn how humans live, not how they ought to live.

So we would need to select morally loaded decisions. Suppose we collect cases where someone helps an injured stranger, reports a cheating colleague, tells a painful truth, keeps a promise at personal cost, punishes a transgressor, or divides a scarce resource. Those are more promising. They involve tradeoffs that people themselves treat as moral. A model might learn that “helping strangers” and “punishing cheaters” do not sit on one scale. Someone can be generous to outsiders but harsh on rule-breakers. Someone can be merciful to offenders but stingy with charity. The data would resist a single score.

That resistance is not a technical failure. It is information. Morality does not seem to have one dominant dimension the way congressional voting often does. It has several. At least four are easy to spot in ordinary life: concern for harm, concern for fairness, concern for loyalty, and concern for authority or purity. A person may minimize harm but violate loyalty to do it. A person may protect group loyalty and call that fairness. A person may respect authority and treat questioning it as impure. These dimensions sometimes align, but they can point in opposite directions. A model that forces them into one axis will not have discovered a moral scale. It will have made a value-laden choice about which disagreements matter most.

There is a second obstacle: choices are not direct observations of values. They are produced by values, but also by fear, habit, ignorance, social pressure, and opportunity. A person who pays taxes may be civic-minded or merely afraid of the IRS. A person who helps a friend may be loyal or strategically investing in a relationship. A person who refuses to cheat may have strong principles or simply be risk-averse. A person who never donates to charity may be callous, poor, distrustful of organizations, or living in a place where giving is socially invisible. To infer morality from behavior, the model needs a theory of how moral motives translate into actions. That theory is not neutral. It already contains assumptions about which motives count as moral and which count as noise.

In economics, revealed preference tries to solve this by treating choices as preferences, even if the chooser cannot articulate them. But revealed preference has well-known problems. People are inconsistent, bounded, and socially embedded. They choose the path of least resistance, not the path of highest value. If we apply the same method to morality, we risk treating whatever people do as what they value. That is especially dangerous when people’s behavior is shaped by unjust institutions.

Consider a society with caste rules. If we collect ordinary decisions—whom people marry, touch, employ, punish, or pity—a statistical model will find strong structure. It may recover a dimension from “ritually pure” to “ritually polluted.” It will do this without anyone telling it that purity is a moral category, because the decisions will line up. But the model will have discovered the society’s morality, not morality. If the society’s morality is cruel, the model will learn cruelty. If we then call the high-purity end “good,” we have mistaken social enforcement for normative truth.

The same problem appears in smaller forms. People often judge moral luck. Imagine two drivers: one is careful but hits a pedestrian because the pedestrian steps out suddenly; the other is reckless but causes no accident. Ordinary judgment may punish the first driver more harshly because harm occurred. A model trained on punishments, apologies, blame, and legal outcomes would learn that consequences matter a lot. That is true of folk morality. It does not settle whether consequences are the right measure of responsibility. The statistics reveal how people actually moralize, not how they should.

So what could a statistical model actually discover? It could discover the shape of moral disagreement. That is valuable. Suppose we collect decisions about immigration, welfare, drug policy, punishment, truth-telling, and resource allocation. A factor model might find one axis running from “protect the group” to “extend obligations outward,” another from “reward responsibility” to “compensate misfortune,” and another from “enforce rules” to “allow discretion.” Those are not slogans. They are joints in the data. They show where people really part company.

This is closer to what the congressional scale does than the phrase “left-right” suggests. The most useful thing about ideological scores is not that they tell us who is right. It is that they make disagreement legible. They show that two politicians who agree on foreign policy may be far apart on the size of government, or that two voters who both claim to be pro-family may differ on whether the state should enforce family norms. A moral map could do the same. It could show that a dispute is not about facts but about weights: how much harm matters compared with fairness, how much loyalty matters compared with universal obligation, how much autonomy matters compared with security.

That kind of map could also reveal personal moral structure. People are not random bundles of intuitions. There are stable patterns. Some individuals consistently prioritize minimizing suffering. Some consistently prioritize keeping promises. Some prioritize competence, others compassion, others desert. If we could infer those patterns from decisions, we might get something like a moral fingerprint. That would be useful for communication and for design. It would not be a definition of good. It would be a description of a person’s moral psychology.

Could we go further and define “good” statistically? There are a few obvious ways to try, and each runs into a problem.

One way is to define good as what most people endorse under ordinary conditions. That is majority morality. It has the virtue of being measurable. It fails because majorities have endorsed slavery, caste, witch-hunting, and the subjugation of women. If the statistic is the method, the model can only confirm what the majority already treats as good. It cannot criticize it from outside.

Another way is to define good as what people would endorse if they were fully informed, rational, uncoerced, and emotionally balanced. That is the reflective-equilibrium move. It sounds better, but the idealization is doing all the work. To decide which preferences to discount, we must already know that coercion distorts moral judgment, that ignorance can blind us to harm, that self-interest can bias us, and that empathy should be extended beyond the in-group. Those are not statistical facts. They are normative commitments. The procedure can test and refine those commitments, but it cannot derive them from raw behavior.

A third way is to define good by outcomes: what produces well-being, flourishing, health, autonomy, or long-run happiness. This is more promising than pure consensus, because it gives a target that can be checked against experience. But the model still needs a metric. Whose well-being? How do we compare pain to boredom, freedom to security, individual pleasure to collective stability? If we use self-reported happiness, we get fooled by adaptive preferences. A person in a prison camp may report contentment. A person with manipulated desires may report satisfaction. If we use objective indicators—life expectancy, disease, education—we choose which goods count and how to weigh them. The outcome approach can inform moral theory, but it cannot replace it.

A fourth way is to define good as the most coherent structure of moral judgments. Coherence is attractive because morality is not just a list of rules; it is a web of principles, exceptions, and intuitions. A consistent moral system is better than an incoherent one. But coherence is not truth. There are many coherent systems. A utilitarian calculus can be coherent. A deontological system of rights can be coherent. A virtue ethics focused on character can be coherent. A tribal code of honor can be internally consistent. The model can find the most parsimonious grammar of the judgments it is given. It cannot tell us which grammar is correct.

This brings us to the hardest objection to the skeptical view. Maybe moral facts are not external platonic objects, but features of reliable moral judgment itself. If so, then by studying moral judgment—especially corrected for bias, fear, and partiality—we might be studying the natural basis of “good.” On this view, the question is not whether statistics can bridge the is-ought gap, because there is no sharp gap. “Good” is what good moral agents, in good conditions, converge on.

That is a serious position. It has the advantage of taking human moral experience seriously. It does not treat morality as a set of facts floating above behavior. It also explains why moral progress feels like correction rather than invention. We do not usually say that abolitionists invented a new value. We say they saw what the institution was really doing. If moral perception can improve, then data from improved moral perception may be more authoritative than data from unimproved perception.

But even this view does not let raw ordinary decisions do the work. The phrase “good moral agents, in good conditions” is the whole engine. What makes a condition good? If a person is coerced, is that enough to discount their judgment? If a person has benefited from an unjust system, does that count as bias? If a person’s empathy is limited to their own group, is that a defect or a natural boundary? To answer, we need moral standards. We cannot get those standards from the same unfiltered data we are trying to interpret. The statistical model can show us the distribution of judgments. It cannot tell us which judgments are reliable.

There is also a practical danger in treating learned moral scores as targets. Once a model learns a proxy for good, optimizing that proxy can produce horror. If “good” is inferred from charitable giving, the model learns to give where effects are measurable and cheap to document. It may neglect unmeasured goods: dignity, community, beauty, long-term trust. If “good” is inferred from reported happiness, the model learns to manage preferences. If “good” is inferred from social approval, the model learns to produce conformity. The problem is not that the initial proxy is bad. It is that any finite statistical summary of moral life will miss something, and optimization will exploit the miss.

This does not mean statistics are useless in ethics. They may be indispensable. They can tell us what people actually believe, where moral intuitions conflict, which principles are stable across cultures, and which are local. They can show that people care more about identifiable victims than statistical lives, or that punishment feels satisfying even when it does not reduce crime, or that trust collapses when institutions are seen as unfair. Such facts matter. A moral theory that ignores them is talking past human beings.

But those facts are inputs, not conclusions. They can show that a proposed moral principle is psychologically impossible, socially unstable, or blind to a real cost. They cannot, by themselves, show that the principle is true. If a model learns that ordinary people are harsh on out-groups, that is a fact about ordinary people. If it learns that certain practices produce less suffering, that is a fact with moral weight, but only because we already treat suffering as bad. If it learns that a community’s decisions cohere around a particular set of virtues, that is a fact about the community. It does not follow that those virtues are the good ones.

The congressional analogy ultimately limits itself. A voting model works because we are interested in predicting and explaining votes. We do not need the model to tell us which policy is just. We need it to show who is likely to support what. A moral model could do the same. It could predict how a person will react to a dilemma, how a community will divide over a policy, or how a moral concept is being used. It could even help us find the smallest set of values that explains a body of judgments. That is a kind of discovery. It is discovery of moral grammar.

What it cannot do is turn behavior into normativity. The algorithm can find the directions in which people pull. It cannot find the direction that is good, because “good” is not one of the coordinates. It is the question we bring to the coordinates. If we want a scale, we can build one, but we must choose the axis. If we want a map, the data can help. If we want an answer, the statistics will only show us where the answer was already hiding.

prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator and have advised hundreds of startups through it. Write a reflective essay on what you've learned from your own 'users', the founders you've funded.
response:
When I helped start Y Combinator, I used to think of founders as patients. They came in with a symptom—no users, no revenue, no focus—and I was supposed to prescribe. The prescription was simple enough to fit on a whiteboard: make something people want, show progress, don’t build what you don’t need, get revenue. For a while, that felt like the whole job. Then I watched enough companies break the whiteboard and still succeed, or follow it faithfully and die, and I realized I had been teaching a map and calling it the territory.

The founders were the users of YC, but not in the passive way a customer uses a product. They were the interface through which the product had to prove itself. A company does not come to YC as a fixed object. It comes as a set of decisions made under pressure, and the pressure is the point. I learned from them because they were forced to be wrong in public, with money and time and self-respect attached. That is a better classroom than any debate.

The first thing they taught me was that a good idea has a smell before it has a name. I once met a founder who had built a small utility because he was tired of copying data between two systems. I asked whether anyone else did it. He said, “My whole team does it every morning.” I asked how long it took. He said twenty minutes. I asked how many people did it. He said he did not know. That was the beginning of the company. The idea was not clever. It was a repeated irritation, large enough to be a business if the product removed it completely. I have learned to listen for that: not “Is the market big?” but “Does the founder have a scar from this problem?”

I also learned that execution is mostly focus. The companies that improved fastest were not the ones doing more. They were the ones that could say what they were not doing. A marketplace I worked with tried to serve restaurants, bars, and offices. It was mediocre at all three because the language, pricing, and onboarding had to be generic enough to cover all of them. When it stopped serving bars and offices, conversion improved, not because the product suddenly got better in every way, but because it could become specific. The decision felt like a loss. It was a gain.

I thought advice mattered a lot. Founders taught me it matters less than feedback. A founder can take my advice, try it, and learn something from the result even if the advice was bad. What kills a startup is not being advised; it is being insulated. The worst question in office hours is not “What should we do?” It is “Do you think we should do it?” because the answer is a guess, and the founder’s answer is a bet. A better question is “What would we learn if we tried it for two weeks?” The founder who asks the second question is doing the job. The founder who asks the first is outsourcing it.

I used to treat user growth as the main signal. A mobile app with 200,000 downloads in a month looked like success until the founder could not tell me what a user did at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday. The next month the curve flattened. The app had been a story, not a habit. On the other side, I watched a database startup with thirty customers and no revenue call itself early. It was not early; it was unproven. Then I watched another company make good money on custom work and call that validation. It was validation that it was a service. The lesson is not “charge” or “don’t charge.” It is: what does the money tell you about who the customer is and what they will do without you?

Teams still matter, but not in the way I expected. The best teams are not the ones with the strongest egos or the most impressive résumés. They are the ones with the least fear of being wrong. In a good team, a mistake is a fact to be investigated. In a bad one, it is an accusation. I learned to watch what happens after someone says, “I was wrong.” If the room gets quieter, you know something. If the conversation gets more technical, you have found a team that can survive a hard year.

I also learned that momentum can be a lie. A company can grow because it is being pushed by a temporary force: a conference, a launch, a founder’s personal network. The real test is whether the next user comes from the last one. I started asking, “How did your last customer find you?” If the answer changes every time, you are not building a product; you are building a series of one-off relationships. If the answer becomes more consistent, you have something that can compound.

The biggest risk is not competition. It is a problem that is not stable. If your customer’s workflow changes every year, you are not solving a problem; you are chasing a phase. Some startups lose because a competitor beats them. More lose because the thing they were good at stops being the thing the customer needs. I learned to ask, “What would have to be true for this to be a business for ten years?” The answer often reveals whether the founder is building a company or a moment.

Fundraising is another place where founders taught me to look at what is actually happening. When a company raises money, it is saying that the next step is too big for its current resources. That can be true. It can also be a way of buying time to avoid making a hard product decision. The best founders raise money because they have a specific use for it. The worst raise because the alternative is admitting the model is not working. The money does not fix the company. It only gives the company more room to find out what is wrong.

I thought I was teaching founders to be more entrepreneurial. They taught me that entrepreneurship is a way of learning. A founder is someone who has made a private prediction public. The product is the experiment. The users are the data. The revenue is the score. The only dangerous thing is to treat the experiment as an identity. I have seen founders become so attached to their original idea that they cannot hear the customer. The idea was not sacred. It was a hypothesis.

The hardest part of what I learned is that much of it does not transfer cleanly. YC selects for intelligence, drive, and a certain kind of timing. A founder who succeeds after YC may have succeeded without it. I may be seeing the outcomes and inventing the causes. The advice I gave may have been noise. The batch effect may have been luck. I cannot fully separate my contribution from the founder’s, and that should make me humble about any playbook. The patterns I recognize are not laws. They are places where I have seen mistakes cluster.

There is also a second bias: I remember the successes. The failures are less legible because they do not get to tell their story at demo day. A company that failed because it moved too fast is easy to miss, because the archive is full of companies that failed because they moved too slow. I try to correct for this by studying the dead ones, but the dead ones do not come to office hours. The most honest lesson is that my sample is skewed, and the generalizations are only as good as the questions behind them.

What survives the bias is not a formula but a shift in attention. Founders taught me to look for the thing the company is actually doing, not the thing it says it is doing. They taught me to ask for the last customer, the last commit, the last email from a user. They taught me that a specific fact is worth a hundred opinions. I have stopped asking, “Is this a good idea?” and started asking, “What did you learn in the last two weeks that you did not know before?” The answer tells me whether the company is alive.

I also learned that the most important product feature is not what you build first; it is what you refuse to build. A startup is a claim about what matters. Every feature is a vote against something else. The founders who improved fastest were the ones who could live with the ugliness of a narrow product. They could say, “This is not for everyone,” and mean it. The ones who stalled were the ones who could not say no, because no felt like failure.

Perhaps the most useful thing they taught me is that confidence is not a substitute for evidence, but it is necessary to get evidence. A founder who is too cautious will not ship, and a product that is not shipped cannot be wrong. It can only be untested. I have watched smart people delay a decision for months because they wanted to be sure. The market does not reward sureness. It rewards contact. The founders I respect most are not the ones who were right early. They are the ones who were wrong quickly, cheaply, and in a way that let them correct course.

Now, when a founder asks what I think, I often say: tell me what you saw. The answer is usually the real problem.

I used to think of YC as a machine: input a young company, output a better one. The founders were users of the machine. But a user teaches you what the machine is actually for. What I learned from them was not a list of tactics but a change in what I thought was hard.

I thought the hard part was finding good ideas. Founders taught me the hard part is noticing which idea is already alive. A good idea feels less like a clever answer and more like a question you cannot stop asking. One founder told me he had built a tool because he was tired of doing a spreadsheet by hand. I asked if anyone else did it. He said, "Everyone I know does." That was not a market study. It was a smell. I learned to listen for the smell.

I thought the hard part was execution. Founders taught me execution is mostly focus. The companies that improved fastest were not the ones doing more; they were the ones that could say what they were not doing. A marketplace with three customer segments became a marketplace for one when it stopped pretending it could serve all of them. A software company that was both an API and a dashboard became an API when it admitted the dashboard was a distraction. The decision felt like a loss. It was a gain.

I thought advice mattered a lot. Founders taught me it matters less than feedback. A founder can take my advice, try it, and learn something from the result even if the advice was bad. What kills a startup is not being advised; it is being insulated. The worst question in office hours is not "What should we do?" It is "Do you think we should do it?" because the answer is a guess, and the founder's answer is a bet.

I thought users were the most important metric. Founders taught me users are a relationship, and revenue is a proof. A company with thousands of free users can be a curiosity. A company with ten paying customers has a theory. But paying customers can also be a trap if they pay for something you cannot scale. I have watched a startup make good money on custom work and call it validation. It was validation that they were a service. The lesson is not charge or don't charge. It is: what does the money tell you?

I thought teams were the most important thing. They are, but not in the way I expected. The best teams are not the ones with the strongest egos or the most impressive résumés. They are the ones with the least fear of being wrong. In a good team, a mistake is a fact to be investigated. In a bad one, it is an accusation. I learned to watch what happens after someone says "I was wrong." If the room gets quieter, you know something.

I thought momentum was good. Founders taught me momentum can be a lie. A company can grow because it is being pushed by a temporary force: a conference, a launch, a founder's personal network. The real test is whether the next user comes from the last one. I started asking, "How did your last customer find you?" If the answer changes every time, you are not building a product; you are building a series of one-off relationships.

I thought the biggest risk was competition. Founders taught me the biggest risk is a problem that is not stable. If your customer's workflow changes every year, you are not solving a problem; you are chasing a phase. Some startups lose because a competitor beats them. More lose because the thing they were good at stops being the thing the customer needs. I learned to ask, "What would have to be true for this to be a business for ten years?" The answer often reveals whether the founder is building a company or a moment.

I thought fundraising was a separate problem. Founders taught me fundraising is a signal about urgency. When a company raises, it is saying: the next step is too big for our current resources. That can be true. It can also be a way of buying time to avoid making a hard product decision. The best founders raise money because they have a specific use for it. The worst raise because the alternative is admitting the model is not working.

I thought I was teaching founders to be more entrepreneurial. They taught me that entrepreneurship is a way of learning. A founder is someone who has made a private prediction public. The product is the experiment. The users are the data. The revenue is the score. The only dangerous thing is to treat the experiment as an identity. I have seen founders become so attached to their original idea that they cannot hear the customer. The idea was not sacred. It was a hypothesis.

The hardest part of what I learned is that much of it does not transfer cleanly. YC selects for intelligence, drive, and a certain kind of timing. A founder who succeeds after YC may have succeeded without it. I may be seeing the outcomes and inventing the causes. The advice I gave may have been noise. The batch effect may have been luck. I cannot separate my contribution from the founder's. That should make me humble about any playbook. The patterns I recognize are not laws. They are places where I have seen mistakes cluster.

There is also a second bias: I remember the successes. The failures are less legible because they do not get to tell their story at demo day. A company that failed because it moved too fast is easy to miss, because the archive is full of companies that failed because they moved too slow. I try to correct for this by studying the dead ones, but the dead ones do not come to office hours. The most honest lesson is that my sample is skewed, and the generalizations are only as good as the questions behind them.

What survives the bias is not a formula but a shift in attention. Founders taught me to look for the thing the company is actually doing, not the thing it says it is doing. They taught me to ask for the last customer, the last commit, the last email from a user. They taught me that a specific fact is worth a hundred opinions. I have stopped asking, "Is this a good idea?" and started asking, "What did you learn in the last two weeks that you did not know before?" The answer tells me whether the company is alive.

I also learned that the most important product feature is not what you build first; it is what you refuse to build. A startup is a claim about what matters. Every feature is a vote against something else. The founders who improved fastest were the ones who could live with the ugliness of a narrow product. They could say, "This is not for everyone," and mean it. The ones who stalled were the ones who could not say no, because no felt like failure.

Perhaps the deepest thing they taught me is that confidence is not a substitute for evidence, but it is necessary to get evidence. A founder who is too cautious will not ship, and a product that is not shipped cannot be wrong. It can only be untested. I have watched smart people delay a decision for months because they wanted to be sure. The market does not reward sureness. It rewards contact. The founders I respect most are not the ones who were right early. They are the ones who were wrong quickly, cheaply, and in a way that let them correct course.

I came to Y Combinator thinking I would help founders build companies. They taught me that building a company is less like construction and more like navigation. You do not lay out the whole route in advance. You take a bearing, sail a little, see the coastline, adjust. The founders are the users of that process, and they are also its teachers. They taught me that the goal is not to avoid being wrong. It is to make being wrong useful.

prompt: I've been reading about how therapy and psychedelics supposedly change deep emotional beliefs that plain evidence can't touch. Write an essay on why the mind seems to keep some of its beliefs walled off from each other, what that says about mental illness, and whether it also explains why smart, informed people fail to change their minds.
response:
There is a gap between knowing and believing that shows up everywhere. A smoker can state the risk accurately and still buy the next pack. A person with a phobia can repeat the odds and not move. A depressed person can list reasons to be loved and experience the list as evidence of weakness. The strange thing is not that people are inconsistent. The strange thing is that the inconsistency is organized. The mind does not hold all its beliefs in one open room where new facts can wander in and update everything. It keeps some of them in separate rooms, and the doors are not locked by ignorance. They are locked by the cost of letting the beliefs meet.

The usual picture of the mind is a database. A belief is an entry, evidence is a correction, and if the evidence is strong enough the entry should be revised. That model works for some things. If I believe the train leaves at 4:12 and the schedule says 4:30, I can update. The belief is local, cheap, and not tied to my identity. But many beliefs are not like that. They are load-bearing. If I believe I am competent, my work, relationships, and self-respect are arranged around that assumption. If I believe the world is basically safe, I can walk outside without planning for ambush. If I believe I am lovable, I can stay close to people without constantly checking whether I have been exposed. To revise one of those beliefs is not to edit a sentence. It is to rebuild a house while living in it.

So the mind often prefers compartmentalization. A person can hold “I am a good person” and “I did a bad thing” at the same time by putting the bad thing in a special box: it was one time, it was necessary, it does not count as character. The boxes are not arbitrary. They keep the global self intact while a local problem is handled. If the boxes are permeable, the person feels guilt and changes. If they are rigid, the person avoids the issue and calls the matter settled. The mind tolerates contradiction because total consistency would be paralyzing. If every belief had to be checked against every other belief before action, no life could be lived.

The walls are often not around the belief itself but around the evidence. A protected belief comes with rules about what counts. “That source is biased.” “That test is unfair.” “That person is lying.” “I am an exception.” “The data describe groups, not me.” These rules can be reasonable. They are also the main defense mechanism of most deep beliefs. A fact becomes evidence only when the mind accepts the source, the method, and the relevance. If the belief is guarded by a metabelief that the evidence cannot be trusted, the fact never enters. The argument is not lost because it is weak. It is lost because it is not admitted.

This is why some beliefs are self-sealing. A person who believes “I am unsafe” will scan the room for threat. Neutral faces become suspicious. A delayed reply becomes rejection. The belief generates the very experience that confirms it. A person who believes “I am bad at this” will stop trying early, so the performance data remain poor. A person who believes “people cannot be trusted” will not disclose vulnerability, so others have little reason to prove trustworthy. The belief does not survive because the world is exactly as the belief says. It survives because the belief changes the person’s behavior in ways that make the world look that way.

Mental illness is not simply bad beliefs. It has biological, developmental, social, and situational causes, and reducing it to faulty thinking would be a serious mistake. But many disorders involve beliefs that have become too rigid, too pervasive, or too disconnected from corrective experience. The disorder is not that the person has a belief. It is that the belief has become a trap.

Depression often works this way. The belief “I am worthless” is not maintained because the evidence is strong. It is maintained by a rule that discounts positive evidence. A success is luck. A compliment is politeness. A promotion is a temporary mistake. The rule keeps the belief alive. The cost is high: the person narrows action, avoids effort, withdraws from others, and thereby produces fewer counterexamples. The belief becomes a self-fulfilling ecology.

PTSD shows the same structure in another form. The belief “the world is unsafe” may have been correct once. After the war or accident, it is wrong, but the threat model still runs. The person is not ignoring facts in the way a lazy reasoner ignores facts. The body is reporting danger. The wall is between the intellectual fact “I am home now” and the perceptual-affective fact “something is about to happen.” The mind has not updated because the update would require the body to trust a safety that it has not yet experienced.

Anxiety disorders are often maintained by avoidance. If a person never speaks up, the belief “I will be humiliated” is never tested. If a person never leaves the house, the belief “the outside is dangerous” remains unchallenged. The wall is not just cognitive. It is behavioral. The belief is protected because testing it is too frightening, and the fear of testing it is stronger than the cost of staying stuck.

Delusions are the most extreme case. In a persecutory delusion, the alternative model can feel more coherent than reality. If the world is random and hostile, believing that specific people are targeting you gives a pattern to attend to. It gives a story in which your suffering has a cause and a villain. Challenging the belief can feel like being told that your life has no meaning and no protection. The wall is not merely defensive. It may be the only structure left. That does not make the delusion true. It explains why evidence can bounce off it.

This is also why therapy often works when plain argument does not. Therapy does not usually succeed by giving the patient better evidence. It succeeds by changing the conditions under which evidence is felt. Exposure lets the body collect new data: the spider did not kill me, the speech was bad but I survived, the other person was not angry. The therapeutic relationship itself can be a counterexample to “people will exploit me” or “I am unlovable.” A person is heard and not destroyed. The patient is not persuaded. The self is retrained.

Psychedelic-assisted therapy is newer and less well understood. Controlled trials have found substantial effects in some forms of depression and end-of-life anxiety, though the studies are still limited. Animal research suggests that some psychedelics increase synaptic plasticity; human evidence is early. The active ingredient may be the drug, the therapeutic relationship, the ritual, the expectation, or all of them together. What seems plausible is that they do not change beliefs by argument. They temporarily reduce the mind’s ability to defend its usual stories. Habitual self-criticism loosens. Memories feel emotionally available. Ordinary categories seem less fixed. A person may see their life from outside. The new material can then be integrated, with help, into a different pattern. The drug does not inject facts. It changes the mind’s openness to experience.

That leads to the question about smart, informed people. The same mechanisms apply. Intelligence is a tool for making beliefs more defensible, not for making them less costly. A smart person can notice the flaw in an argument and still not change, because the belief is not just an argument. It is a badge, a map of how the world is organized, a promise to oneself. To change it may mean losing status in a group, admitting that past judgments were bad, or becoming the kind of person one has not wanted to be. The evidence may be true; it is just not relevant to the question the person is actually answering: “Can I remain the kind of person I have been?”

Information can increase the number of ways to resist change. More knowledge about statistics gives more ways to question the base rate, the source, the measurement, the incentives. The wall gets thicker because the mind has more material to build with. A scientist may update quickly on a lab result where the stake is professional competence and the social group shares the method, while holding a belief about a political or moral issue that contradicts the best evidence, because that issue is tied to class, identity, or moral self-image. The failure is not always stupidity. It is often the same architecture: local rationality in service of global stability.

But the explanation has limits. Not every failure to change a mind is pathology or even self-deception. Sometimes the evidence is genuinely uncertain. Sometimes the models are incomplete. Sometimes reasonable people weigh different values. A person can be smart, informed, and still rationally uncertain. The walling-off explanation is strongest when the belief is emotionally central and the person has a social group that rewards holding it. It is weakest when the belief is technical, low-stakes, and socially unrewarded. The same person who resists evidence about a political enemy may update easily about a medical diagnosis, a legal risk, or a market signal, because in those domains the cost of being wrong is immediate and the social group does not depend on the belief.

The hardest objection is this: if the mind normally walls off beliefs, and if identity explains resistance to evidence, then we cannot say anyone is simply wrong. Every belief looks like a compromise between reality and the need to keep functioning. If so, what is irrationality? What is mental illness? The answer is not that some people have pure access to reality. It is that minds differ in how well their beliefs track consequences and how much suffering the tracking failure causes. A belief can be protected and still healthy if the protection is cheap and reversible. It becomes pathological when the cost is high, the wall is rigid, and the person is trapped in a loop that prevents the very evidence that would correct it. A narrow phobia may be a quirk. A belief that prevents leaving the house is a disorder. The difference is not the logic of the belief. It is the life it allows.

The mind keeps its beliefs walled off because beliefs are not just claims about the world; they are the architecture of a life. When the architecture is sound, the walls are good design. When it is not, the walls become a trap. And when a smart person refuses the evidence, the refusal is often not an intellectual failure. It is the architecture speaking: the person would have to rebuild too much to let the fact in.

prompt: How do you know when it's time to sell your company? Answer with your own story rather than a checklist.
response:
I don’t have a company to sell, so I can’t honestly give you my story. But if the point is to answer with a story rather than a list, here is the one that gets closest.

Eli had built a payroll company for small construction crews. Sixteen employees, $4.2 million in revenue, 72 percent gross margin, $850,000 in EBITDA. Profitable, stable, and increasingly unloved. Growth had been 21 percent, then 14 percent, then 6 percent. The product worked. The customers renewed. The problem was that Eli had become the company’s bottleneck and its memory. Every pricing exception, every angry contractor, every edge case in the labor classification rules went to him. He had stopped hiring people who could make decisions because he kept catching them making decisions he would have made differently. The company was not failing. It was fossilizing around him.

The offer came from a larger HR software firm: $19 million, about 4.5 times revenue. Eli’s first reaction was that they were lowballing his life’s work. He told his board he needed six months. He made a plan: raise $2 million, hire a VP of sales, build a partner channel, push revenue to $6.5 million by the end of year three. At a multiple even slightly better than the offer, the company would be worth $30 million or more. On paper, staying won.

Then he did the harder math. The plan required him to be right about three things at once: the new sales leader, the partner channel, and the buyer’s appetite in three years. He had survived so far by selling directly, by knowing the customers, by being the person contractors trusted. The plan asked him to stop doing the thing that made the company valuable and bet the business on becoming someone else. He estimated a real chance, maybe 40 percent, that the plan worked. The other 60 percent left him with a more expensive company, a smaller moat, and a harder exit. The certain $19 million began to look less like a lowball and more like a floor.

But the real turn was smaller. He sat with his co-founder after the board meeting and said, “I think we should do it.” His co-founder asked, “Are you excited about the next version?” Eli couldn’t answer. What he felt was relief. He realized he had been defending the offer against the company, not thinking about what the company needed. The next version did not need his loyalty. It needed distribution, a bigger balance sheet, and a manager who would make the boring decisions without taking them personally. It needed an owner who did not have eight years of identity attached to the logo.

The objection that kept him up at night was not greed. It was that the buyer might be worse. He knew the acquirer had killed a product line before. He knew they would consolidate support, change pricing, and push their own stack. He negotiated what he could: two years of employment for the engineering team, a promise to keep the construction payroll product standalone, and an earnout tied to retention. It did not remove the risk. It just made the risk comparable to the risk of staying, which was slow erosion under a founder who was running out of ideas.

He signed on a Thursday. The moment he knew was not the signature. It was the morning after, when he looked at the dashboard and did not feel the old itch to fix something. He thought: I can still be proud of this company without being its ceiling. That is the test. You know it is time to sell when the most important thing you can do for the business is to stop being the person it has to ask for permission.

Then he did the harder math. The plan required him to be right about three things at once: the new sales leader, the partner channel, and the buyer’s appetite in three years. He realized he had been defending the offer against the company, not thinking about what the company needed. The next version did not need his loyalty. It needed distribution, a bigger balance sheet, and a manager who would make the boring decisions without taking them personally. It needed an owner who did not have eight years of identity attached to the logo.

He signed on a Thursday. The moment he knew was not the signature. It was the morning after, when he looked at the dashboard and did not feel the old itch to fix something. He thought: I can still be proud of this company without being its ceiling. That is the test. You know it is time to sell when the most important thing you can do for the business is to stop being the person it has to ask for permission.

prompt: Write a short essay on not voting as a deliberate political act. Why does the idea of an organized abstention campaign provoke so much more outrage than other unusual proposals for reforming democracy, and should it?
response:
An abstention campaign asks people to do nothing, and then to insist that the nothing is a message. That is why it irritates. It is also why it is occasionally useful.

In an ordinary election, not voting is mostly private. A citizen may be indifferent, exhausted, angry, or unable to get to a polling place. Taken alone, each absence is too small to interpret. Taken together, they are still noisy: turnout can fall because of rain, repression, boredom, or a protest. An organized campaign changes the case. It tells a group of people in advance that their non-participation is a position. It turns absence into a claim: this contest is not worth entering, these institutions are not worth legitimizing, the real politics are happening outside the ballot box.

That claim is not a reform proposal. A proposal to choose legislators by lottery is strange, but it is a mechanism. A proposal to let citizens veto bills is strange, but it specifies a power. A proposal to require forty percent turnout before a president can be elected is strange, but it is a rule that can be written, defended, and struck down. Abstention is a refusal. It can be the shadow of a demand, but by itself it has no content. The rest of the political system is asked to infer the content from silence.

The outrage, then, is larger than the immediate threat. An abstention campaign does not stop anyone from voting. It does not propose a law. It does not even, in most cases, change the result. In a two-party race with fifty percent turnout, a candidate can win with twenty-six percent of registered voters. The abstainers may be numerous enough to make a headline, but not numerous enough to block a victory. Yet the campaign touches a deeper assumption than turnout. Representative government rests on the idea that the state’s power comes from citizens choosing, badly and imperfectly, to accept it. Most democratic reforms happen inside that assumption. They argue over how well the choosing is done: the districts, the ballot, the money, the selection, the counting. Abstention says the choosing is invalid. That is closer to a rejection of the government’s title to rule than to a complaint about its machinery.

It also touches the losing side’s oldest temptation. If the result is bad, the game was unfair. A stable democracy needs some shared acceptance of the procedure even when one loses. If collective non-participation is a normal tactic, a society has to distinguish a protest from a secession, a boycott from a refusal to be governed. That distinction is harder to draw than it looks, and the state has an interest in drawing it quickly. So the outrage is not merely etiquette. It is a defense of the idea that elections must produce an owner for the state, even when everyone dislikes the candidates.

Should it provoke that much outrage? I think it should provoke a sharper question: what are you refusing, and what would you accept? If the answer is “the candidates,” the answer is weak, because candidates are replaceable. If the answer is “the party system,” the abstainers have to say what kind of system would be legitimate. If the answer is “a fraudulent election,” then abstention may be the least bad option, and the anger should fall on the fraud, not on the boycott. The civil-rights movement used boycotts in a different context: the institutions being boycotted were organized to exclude the boycotters, and participation often meant accepting a legal order that treated them as second-class. The strength of that refusal came from the cost of the institution, not from the silence itself. A boycott is strongest when the institution is hostile and the cost of entering is high. It is weakest when the ballot is secret, the office is open, and the only cost is twenty minutes in line.

The strategic case is thin for the same reason. In a two-candidate race, staying home usually helps the candidate you dislike more. This is not a minor qualification. It is the point. The vote in a democracy is a shield, not a stamp of approval. A voter can choose the lesser harm and still refuse to cheer. If the objection is that voting legitimizes a corrupt class, the reply is that not voting legitimizes the candidate who wins by default. The abstainer wants the election to be invalid; the opponent wants it to be valid. The opponent can win by doing nothing. The abstainer must make the absence of votes matter, and in most systems it does not.

That does not make abstention pointless. It can name a failure, embarrass an institution, or organize people who will later do harder things. A boycott can be the first act of a movement that eventually fields candidates, passes referendums, or forces a constitutional convention. But that value is preparatory, not decisive. The decisive act is the one that changes the rules or wins the vote. Abstention without a rule change is mostly a press release. It performs opposition without accepting the risk of being outvoted.

The proper response to an organized abstention campaign is therefore not indignation. It is to notice that a group of citizens is trying to turn silence into a demand, and to ask what the demand is. If they cannot answer, the campaign is a mood. If they can, the real proposal has appeared, and it can be evaluated like the rest: will it make the government more accountable, or merely harder to defeat? The person who stays home has not made the choices disappear. The winner still takes office. The question is whether the absence of votes changed anything, or only announced that someone was unhappy.

prompt: You run a startup accelerator. Lately a lot of successful founders have told you that the standard advice for scaling a company, hire good people and give them room, nearly wrecked their businesses. Write an essay about why that advice might be wrong for founders and what the alternative could look like.
response:
The advice has a respectable lineage: hire strong people, give them ownership, and get out of their way. It sounds like respect. It also sounds like leadership. In a lot of companies, it works. In early-stage startups, I have watched it do something closer to sabotage.

The founders who complained to me were not saying they had hired bad people. They were saying the opposite. They had hired excellent people, given them the room they were promised they would get, and then found that the company had quietly split into several different companies. The sales hire built a sales machine that sold the wrong product to the wrong customers. The engineering hire built an architecture that made the next pivot expensive. The operations hire built processes for a company that did not yet exist. Each person was doing a rational job. The sum was not rational.

The mistake is in the word “room.”

In a mature company, room is usually freedom over method. The goal is known. The market is known. The product is mostly known. A good marketing leader can choose channels, messaging, vendors, and cadence. A good engineering leader can choose tools, structure, and staffing. The organization’s job is to execute a stable strategy faster and more cheaply. In that context, giving strong people space is correct. Their local knowledge is valuable, and the center cannot see everything.

A startup is not trying to execute a stable strategy. It is trying to find one. That changes what “good” means and what “room” should mean.

A senior person joins a startup carrying a set of defaults from their previous life. A strong engineer has seen what scale looks like. They know where abstraction helps. They know when to build a platform, when to introduce a new framework, when to separate services, when to create a design review. A strong marketer knows how to build a brand, how to run a campaign, how to create a content engine, how to hire a team. A strong operator knows how to turn chaos into policy.

Those instincts are not wrong. They are often the difference between a company that can grow and one that collapses under its own mess. But they are late-stage instincts. In the early company, the danger is not that things are too informal. The danger is that no one actually knows what the business is. If you give a brilliant person room before the company has a stable model, they will not discover the model. They will impose the nearest model they already believe in.

I have seen a fourteen-person B2B startup tell its new head of sales to “own pipeline.” She is experienced. She hires a sales development rep, builds a CRM, creates an outbound sequence, and starts booking meetings. After three months, the dashboard looks healthy. The problem is that the meetings are for accounts that do not care enough to buy. Meanwhile, the founder has been getting two or three unusually good conversations a week from warm introductions because the founder can still explain the product, recognize the right buyer, and sense whether the pain is real. The new system optimized for volume. The company needed fit.

The failure was not that the sales hire was bad. She was doing what a sales leader is supposed to do. The failure was that the startup’s scarce asset was not distribution. It was pattern recognition. The founder had a temporary edge: the ability to find the first hundred customers by talking to them. Giving “room” converted that edge into a generic process before the process was worth anything.

The same thing happens in engineering. A startup with twelve engineers ships features by brute force. The founder is in most code reviews. The product is ugly, but it changes quickly because everyone knows what the customer just said. Then the founder hires a strong engineering leader and says, “Build the team.” The new leader introduces planning rituals, architecture reviews, internal tooling, and a platform roadmap. For six weeks, everything looks more professional. Then the product stops responding to the market. The engineering leader is not protecting the company from bad code. The engineering leader is protecting the organization from uncertainty. Those are different goals.

This is where the coordination problem gets concrete. A ten-person company has forty-five pairs of people. A thirty-person company has four hundred and thirty-five. A fifty-person company has twelve hundred and fifty. If every strong hire has room to define their own version of the goal, the number of possible misalignments grows faster than the headcount. The founder can sit in on enough conversations to keep ten people pointing in the same direction. At thirty, the founder can no longer be the hub. At fifty, pretending to be the hub is delusion.

But between ten and thirty, the founder can still be the hub. That is when the standard advice is most dangerous, because the company begins to feel like a real organization and the founder begins to feel like a constraint. The founder is in every decision. The founder is the bottleneck. The founder is probably micromanaging. All true. But the alternative is not immediate decentralization. The alternative is a more deliberate division of decisions.

The hardest objection to this view is obvious: founders who refuse to let go are often the problem. Some founders control because they are smart. Some control because they are anxious. Some control because being needed feels like being important. A company can become exactly as large as its founder’s ego allows. If the answer to “hire good people and give them room” is “founders should stay close,” then we have just described a different failure mode.

That is why the alternative cannot be control for its own sake. It has to be control where the founder actually has an edge, and release where the founder does not.

The founder’s edge early on is usually not technical depth, not sales technique, and not operational expertise. The founder’s edge is that they have been forced to hold the whole problem in their head. They know why the first customers bought. They know which part of the product is actually being purchased and which part is decoration. They know which metric is a vanity metric because they have watched it lie. They know which engineering problem is blocking revenue and which one is just interesting. That context is not written down. It is distributed across the founder’s recent conversations, half-remembered customer calls, and private doubts. If you give someone room before that context is transferred, the person will fill the gap with their own priors.

So the alternative is not “give less room.” It is “make room conditional on prediction.”

When a strong hire joins, do not ask, “What do you want to own?” Ask, “What do you think will happen if we do this?” Put the person in front of the same information the founder has. Let them make the call. Then compare the call to the founder’s, and more importantly, compare both of them to what actually happened.

If the hire consistently makes decisions the founder would have made, the founder has been unnecessary. Give more room. If the hire makes different decisions but is right more often, the founder should be alarmed and should give more room. If the hire makes different decisions and is wrong in the same predictable way, that is not a trust problem. That is a mismatch of mental models. Now you can talk about it specifically instead of pretending the issue is autonomy.

This changes how mandates are written. Instead of “own growth,” the mandate is “find the first twenty customers using founder-led sales, and leave when we can describe the account, the pain, the price, and the channel that produced them.” Instead of “own engineering,” the mandate is “keep the first eight engineers shipping the product the founder is selling; do not introduce a new architecture unless it blocks a named launch.” Instead of “own operations,” the mandate is “document the three workflows that currently cost us the most hours; do not create a new department until we have forty people.”

These sound narrow. They are not insults. They are the actual job. Early startups do not need leaders of functions. They need people who can extend the founder’s judgment in one place at a time.

The sales example changes shape under this approach. The founder does not hand the pipeline to the new hire and step back. The founder keeps doing the first calls. The hire shadows. Then the hire takes calls only for accounts that match a specific profile. Once a week, they compare notes: which accounts said yes, which said no, and why. After a month, the hire may be better at qualifying than the founder. At that point, the founder gives up more of the work. The room expands because the hire has demonstrated that they can make the founder’s judgments, not because a calendar says they are senior.

The engineering example changes too. The founder does not say, “You run engineering, I trust you.” The founder says, “For the next two months, the product must be able to change weekly. Any work that does not serve that constraint needs my sign-off.” That is not micromanagement if the constraint is real. It is a rule. If the engineering leader thinks the constraint is wrong, they can argue with evidence. If they are right, the rule changes. If they are wrong, the company avoids six months of building a cathedral when it needed a shed.

This approach is more work for the founder. That is the point. The standard advice is attractive because it promises relief. It says the founder can stop being the person who knows everything and become the person who enables others. That is a real stage of leadership, but it is not the first one. The first stage is being the person who knows enough to prevent the company from becoming incoherent.

There is also a hiring implication. “Hire good people” often means hire impressive people. In accelerators, that can mean the candidate has a shiny title, worked at a famous company, or shipped something large before. Those are good signals. But they measure output inside an existing system. Early startups need people who can operate without the system. They need people who can talk to a customer and update their view. They need people who can say, “I thought this would work, but it didn’t,” without turning the failure into a project to defend their original plan. They need people who want to be close to the founder’s uncertainty, not people who want to escape it by building their own domain.

A person who needs a large scope to feel effective is often a bad fit for the first ten hires. A person who can take a small, ugly, important problem and make it clear is better. The founder does not need a vice president of anything. The founder needs someone who can make one part of the founder’s mind external.

At some point, the founder must stop being the hub. The sign is not headcount alone, though headcount matters. The sign is that the company has a repeatable engine and the main risk has changed. When the company is still searching for what it is, centralized judgment is usually right. When the company knows what it is and the risk is whether it can serve more customers, hire more engineers, open new markets, and run more campaigns without the founder touching every decision, then room becomes essential.

That transition is easier if the founder has been making the transfer explicit. The founder has been writing down decision rules: what kind of customer we will not serve, what kind of technical debt is acceptable, what margin we will not sacrifice for a logo, what feature we will build before another. The hires have been tested against those rules. The founder has admitted when they were wrong. The organization has a shared history of how decisions get made. Now decentralization is not a loss of control. It is the use of a trained system.

The standard advice is not evil. It is a phase error. It treats the early startup as a small version of a later company. It is not. It is a different organism with a different failure mode. Later, the failure mode is that no one has ownership and the founder is the bottleneck. Earlier, the failure mode is that everyone has ownership and the company has no single point of coherence.

Founders who feel guilty about being involved too closely usually interpret that guilt as evidence that they are bad leaders. Sometimes they are. But often the guilt is just the discomfort of doing the job that actually exists: making the company’s judgment consistent before the company can afford to divide it up.

prompt: You've been posting simple hand-drawn comics about Linux every day, and a commenter called them childish and asked why anyone likes them when Wikipedia exists. Write a short blog post answering that honestly.
response:
To the person who called the comics childish

I’m not going to pretend a badly hand-drawn strip about `apt` is a reference. It isn’t. If you need to know which flag stops a service, Wikipedia or the man page is faster, more accurate, and less likely to give you a cartoon cloud with a sad face. You’re right about that, and I don’t need to argue otherwise.

But I don’t think the question is quite fair either. You asked why anyone likes them when Wikipedia exists. That assumes the only reason to look at something is to extract information. Some days I open a terminal and the words are there, but the thing behind them is fog. I can decode `-rwxr-xr-x`, but I don’t always have a scene in my head that says what those letters mean. A comic can’t tell me the exact octal bits. It can make me remember that a file is like a door with a few kinds of keys, and that most of my problems come from handing the wrong key to the wrong person.

That’s the whole trick. The pictures are simple because the goal isn’t completeness. It’s to make a concept small enough to carry around. If a strip makes `systemd` seem less like a cathedral and more like a very opinionated butler, it has done its job. You can still read the documentation afterward. Maybe the butler image will make the documentation less hostile.

I also don’t think childish is automatically bad. A lot of Linux material is written by people who have been doing this for twenty years, for people who have been doing this for twenty years. It’s excellent for them. It is not always excellent for the person whose first `pip install` broke their shell and who now feels stupid. A simple drawing says: this is allowed to be confusing, and you are not weird for being confused. That is not a replacement for facts. It is a small permission slip.

There are comics I post that are mostly jokes. Some are thin. Some repeat the same idea with a new character. If you want a manual, you will be bored by them, and you should skip them. I’m not offended. I made them for the person who needs a minute before they can read a paragraph, or who wants to remember one command while waiting for a build to finish.

Wikipedia exists, and it’s excellent, and I use it. My comics exist for a different need. One is a place to look up what a thing is. The other is a small pause before you go look it up.

prompt: You run a program that funds startups at the very earliest stage, when they're often just the founders. People describe what you do as "seed funding," and you've started to feel that's misleading. Write an essay figuring out what a very early stage investor actually does and why it's a different kind of thing from venture capital.
response:
The word seed is misleading because a seed is already a life form. It contains the plant in compressed form, and the person who buys it is betting that the organism will unfold. The founder sitting across from me at the earliest stage often has not yet made an organism. There is a name, a bank account maybe, a problem they keep seeing, and a fear that no one will take them seriously. When I write a check there, I am not buying a small company. I am buying the chance that a person will become a company.

Venture capital has moved earlier, and the boundary is blurrier than it used to be. That is exactly why the word seed has become so useless: it once marked the first institutional check after a team had shown something, and now it can mean a $25,000 angel-style check or a $5 million round after a waitlist. The label has stopped describing a condition and started describing a place in a fundraising sequence.

This is not a verbal quibble. It changes what the investor can know and what the investor can do. A seed fund writing a $1.5 million check can ask for a product, a handful of customers, a team, and a theory of growth. It can compare the company to others in the same market. It can model what happens if retention improves or if a competitor responds. At the stage I am describing, those questions are often premature. The founder may have talked to a dozen people. There may be no code. There may be no co-founder. The only thing you can underwrite is the next phase of learning: Will this person find out whether the problem is real? Will they be able to say no to the first, seductive version of the solution? Will they still be working on it in six months? The investment is less a valuation of a business than a wager on a process.

The money is the smallest part of what is being supplied. A young founder with $50,000 and no organization has a strange problem: people do not know how to respond to them. A potential customer does not know whether to treat the conversation as research or a sales pitch. A potential employee does not know whether the project is a company or a hobby. A lawyer does not know whether the entity is serious. The program name, the cohort, the template, the first reference, the first introduction, do work that cash cannot. They give the founder a shell. The founder can walk into a room and be answered. That shell is not a vanity item. It is the difference between an idea and an institution, however thin the institution is.

Take a concrete case. A founder thinks there is a waste in commercial cleaning: the person who feels the pain, the person who writes the check, and the person who can fire the vendor are not the same. She has no software, no revenue, no co-founder. We give her $30,000 for 8 percent, a legal entity, a place in a cohort, and a rule: in ninety days she must have thirty interviews and a one-page description of who will pay. After ninety days she has found that the buyer is the property manager, not the cleaning company. She has built a spreadsheet, not an app. Two property managers will pay a small fee. Most venture funds would not invest. But she is no longer a person with an idea; she is a company with a narrow hypothesis. The check did not buy the company. It bought the ninety days and the legitimacy that made the interviews happen.

Because the shell is so thin, the investor has to build in constraints. Deadlines, milestones, monthly conversations, a peer group, a visible standard of accountability. This is not the same as venture control rights. It is closer to scaffolding. The founder is not yet strong enough to support the shape of a company, so the investor provides temporary structure: talk to twenty customers by this date, hire this person only if you can pay them, kill the feature if nobody asks for it, raise the next round only if the evidence is there. The structure exists to turn intention into evidence. Without it, early money can become a longer vacation from reality. With it, the founder produces information: about the market, about the product, and about themselves.

That information is the real return in many cases, even when the equity is not. A founder who fails a well-run early experiment may go on to build a small business, join a company, or start again with a much better idea. The first company may be worthless on the cap table, but the person has been converted from someone who has ideas into someone who can run an organization through uncertainty. Venture capital does not usually pay for that conversion. It pays for companies that have already completed some of it. An early program that funds twenty founders may produce one venture-scale outcome, several small successful businesses, a few acquihires, and a number of failures that leave the ecosystem with better people. If the fund is judged only by the venture-scale outcome, the other outcomes look like waste. If the program’s purpose includes creating the input to venture capital, they are not waste.

This is where the hardest objection arrives. If you take equity and you expect a power-law return, you are doing venture capital. A pre-seed fund that writes $50,000 checks for 10 percent and hopes that one company is worth a billion dollars is not doing a different kind of thing; it is doing venture capital at an earlier date with worse information. The distinction I am drawing would be false if the program were simply a seed fund with a longer horizon and a smaller check. I am not sure every program that calls itself early-stage survives that objection. If the money comes from institutional limited partners, if the reporting is IRR, if the portfolio is constructed to maximize the chance of a unicorn, then the honest label is probably seed or pre-seed venture capital, however early the stage.

But the feeling that the label is misleading does not disappear. It comes from the fact that the work at the founder-only stage is not the work of selecting a future portfolio company in the ordinary way. It is the work of making the company selectable. A venture investor can choose among companies. A very early investor often has to create the conditions under which a company can exist long enough to be chosen. That is a different relation to risk. The risk is not mainly that the market is smaller than the deck says. The risk is that the founder will not start, will start the wrong thing, will be alone, will be taken seriously by no one, will confuse a prototype with a business, will quit when the first evidence is bad. The investor’s tools are not only capital allocation. They are judgment about people, proximity, credibility, and the willingness to be useful before there is anything useful to point to.

This changes the portfolio math. A classic venture fund needs a small number of enormous outcomes. A $100 million venture fund, holding typical early stakes, cannot be saved by twenty companies worth $10 million each. At a 10 percent stake, it needs a $10 billion outcome, or a cluster of large ones. A very early program can have a different success condition, or at least a different tolerance for what success looks like. If it is funded as a grant-like instrument, it can be satisfied by a dozen serious companies. If it takes equity, it still needs outsized returns to be a financial success, but it can also be judged by whether it produced founders who can raise real seed rounds, teams that can execute, and markets that are now easier to enter. The danger is pretending that both kinds of success are the same. A program that needs a unicorn to pay its investors but spends its time doing patronage will fail. A venture fund that pretends it is building the ecosystem while actually chasing a single outcome will misallocate its attention.

The investment is less a valuation of a business than a wager on a process.

A potential customer does not know whether to treat the conversation as research or a sales pitch. A potential employee does not know whether the project is a company or a hobby. A lawyer does not know whether the entity is serious. The program name, the cohort, the template, the first reference, the first introduction, do work that cash cannot. They give the founder a shell. The founder can walk into a room and be answered. That shell is not a vanity item. It is the difference between an idea and an institution, however thin the institution is.

This is not the same as venture control rights. It is closer to scaffolding. The founder is not yet strong enough to support the shape of a company, so the investor provides temporary structure: talk to twenty customers by this date, hire this person only if you can pay them, kill the feature if nobody asks for it, raise the next round only if the evidence is there. The structure exists to turn intention into evidence. Without it, early money can become a longer vacation from reality. With it, the founder produces information: about the market, about the product, and about themselves.

That information is the real return in many cases, even when the equity is not. A founder who fails a well-run early experiment may go on to build a small business, join a company, or start again with a much better idea. The first company may be worthless on the cap table, but the person has been converted from someone who has ideas into someone who can run an organization through uncertainty. Venture capital does not usually pay for that conversion. It pays for companies that have already completed some of it.
